Functors having a left adjoint which is also a right adjoint were investigated by Morita in {{cite:3bb4570c6b886cd00747805adde43de3b9147aa9}}, where it is shown that given a ring morphism {{formula:2ddffe81-3d44-4209-893d-f8e0eb74c2e8}} , the restriction of scalars functor has this property if and only if {{formula:4d25ee35-820b-4937-b426-7e029f8cf398}}  is a Frobenius extension: {{formula:490c4873-3658-4faa-91e4-6c25418a4f32}}  is finitely generated and projective in {{formula:a0c4f7a6-b6c7-488e-a054-07e7e2947d6d}} , and {{formula:ade18d29-79e5-4ac8-98bf-9045237708df}}  as {{formula:08f24b8f-6ac9-48e0-8910-a80f3acd4eb6}} -bimodules. Pairs of functors {{formula:ab5b21d3-ede6-4a9d-9e31-721c47a8e776}}  (between module categories) with the property that both {{formula:b0a5d340-e89f-44f9-8b7a-26b9e3a9f4f0}}  and {{formula:47d62d70-e7b0-4531-9e76-dcb2646ac79f}}  are adjunctions are called by Morita strongly adjoint pairs of functors. Later, a functor {{formula:f336543c-9894-40a3-ad05-d516d1937290}}  having a left adjoint which is also a right adjoint came to be referred to as a Frobenius functor ({{cite:8dd4d4c57edf8e06b7a964713411fc43844eadb0}}), and Morita's strongly adjoint pairs of functors are now known as Frobenius pairs.

The natural question arises of when various well-known and extensively used functors are Frobenius. Examples include the already mentioned case of the restrictions of scalars functor for a ring extension ({{cite:5bf02ad5c7316b795dd38dde91f1d4a5d3ef120d}}, {{cite:3bb4570c6b886cd00747805adde43de3b9147aa9}}), forgetful functor from Doi-Hopf (or Doi-Koppinen) modules to modules ({{cite:8dd4d4c57edf8e06b7a964713411fc43844eadb0}}), forgetful functor from {{formula:7e70ad88-ea33-400c-9c41-acda7e62e445}} -graded modules over a {{formula:a4b2fce5-3a11-4142-8ba8-992470a9fa87}} -graded ring to modules, where {{formula:bed06a69-9c78-445e-8f92-8b5952cd525b}}  is a group ({{cite:0ca86213743dee216f2aa240f6f6064d1934d9a0}}), corestriction of scalars through an {{formula:18b5e5d3-f9e0-467c-ab25-2a2cf6cca504}} -coring map {{formula:013eb3a3-0dc5-423a-bf18-37da5d07a74b}}  ({{cite:423e23c1f7298fc7c051a34b9b3838456fe6f098}}, or {{cite:b1c8a95a06c4ed4fabd3ca83494157b4a2898326}} in the more general setting of a map from an {{formula:4f5857f4-17d3-4e88-81cd-f775645a99db}} -coring {{formula:626b4f34-662e-4a12-82e3-c4d816d380b3}}  to a {{formula:a80d658b-591d-40b4-80b3-815e5b59b51a}} -coring {{formula:05d3797f-80f1-4148-9252-bf2ea26ffece}} ), and many more.

In this paper the point of view is the following one: we fix a complete, cocomplete category {{formula:beac3116-8c2f-4c6f-925d-a3d91e06e39a}} , and seek to characterize those small categories {{formula:35d6f5d5-1bfb-4b99-bbdf-4e9b549de850}}  for which the functors {{formula:e6079f55-a698-4eca-8b44-117da4a4ca40}}  sending a functor in {{formula:91a75b2b-9d00-47c0-9e8a-c358634cfeed}}  to its limit and colimit are naturally isomorphic. We call such a category {{formula:a48f8211-86b7-482a-a07c-80f45c390a57}} -Frobenius. The connection to Frobenius functors (hence the name {{formula:7d9c4dce-a911-4a55-bb9d-8e3d70072455}} -Frobenius) is highlighted by the following observation: the functor {{formula:44188a5f-89e9-4c0d-a98e-691fd9fd1066}}  is right adjoint to the diagonal functor {{formula:67ee3874-4191-41c2-9e12-a1f00d239649}} , whereas the colimit functor is the left adjoint to {{formula:ba9a494d-86b9-437d-a60c-d9a5dfaeee9b}} . Hence our question can be rephrased as follows: for which small categories {{formula:387b4f9f-125e-40f3-a5bc-9850f0d16818}}  (depending on {{formula:c3795688-0c63-4c2b-9756-f9f5ee43b787}} ) is the diagonal functor {{formula:9eb1e399-6d39-4ba3-a7d9-807641498e6a}}  a Frobenius functor?

This question is investigated in {{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}}, for discrete small categories {{formula:cbbaef15-95e3-48d2-82c9-4ac4155adb85}}  (i.e. sets), and categories {{formula:5d365a71-2860-4a83-a052-589327a09166}}  enriched over the category of commutative monoids (referred to as {{formula:2eac42b6-1097-4676-82d6-9ce17d620510}}  categories), and having a zero object. In that setting the problem is to find those sets {{formula:f4c9ad56-4b37-4085-88c4-1afca92ba83e}}  for which direct sums and direct products in {{formula:98b849bc-bc9b-4577-b054-a02b0fe852bd}}  indexed by {{formula:14e6f6ae-6bcd-47cc-83a5-1d329573fee5}}  are naturally isomorphic. The main result {{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}} says that under reasonably mild conditions, this is equivalent to {{formula:9e64bcd6-afac-4a52-88b4-f4214d2337d9}}  being finite.

Here, on the other hand, we focus mainly on connected categories {{formula:9a236d27-abc7-4d73-acff-f01cebc70959}} . The structure of the paper is as follows:

In Section  we introduce some conventions and prove Lemma REF , which allows us later on to break up the main problem into the two cases when {{formula:491dd757-37c5-4b13-9040-345c5421a7fd}}  is discrete (a set) or connected.

In Section  we introduce the class of categories {{formula:9c9db1c4-f6ad-4463-971f-df6a3b4e651f}}  we will be concerned with, which we call admissible, and also turn our attention to the case when {{formula:4f27536e-a249-46fd-a9c3-076efcbdc1e6}}  is connected. Two general results, Theorem REF  and Proposition REF , are proven in this setting.

In Section  necessary and sufficient conditions on {{formula:41a6bf0e-5673-43f2-89fe-e7a6923c83ad}}  are found in order that it be {{formula:28b93a8e-a7c4-48c9-bc72-5214f5b4ad08}} -Frobenius or {{formula:53f22fd0-e35a-4cb7-a2d7-8b1b83b52a81}} -Frobenius, where {{formula:a37806bb-9204-494a-a5bd-0f3103e8cda6}}  is a ring and {{formula:d3862bbb-eef3-449d-b8bd-1f406b424fb7}}  is the category of left {{formula:7b870b63-4b14-4b3c-880b-508f9327bb40}} -modules. Since both {{formula:0b59aa80-d861-469e-a46b-5bdd3fe9cb62}}  and {{formula:3879ecbe-6e9a-4ae0-bc94-32a5e29d582b}}  are admissible in the sense of Section , the results proven there can be applied to the two particular cases.

The conditions on {{formula:7f2b7409-7046-43c0-aad4-138da0b78e02}}  appearing in the main results of Section  (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2) are of a combinatorial nature. The full description of the statements of these theorems requires some preparation (Definition REF ), but they immediately imply, for instance, the characterization of {{formula:8660171f-594e-4551-9a68-148589b30d2d}}  or {{formula:c927e7b5-57d3-4f41-8f13-b2086c4b6637}} -Frobenius monoids {{formula:ab8e2934-2806-4e59-a424-34ae7b75b5a4}}  (as usual, we regard a monoid as a category with a single object). A consequence of Theorem REF  is that the {{formula:3e3cba59-c42c-4864-b5a3-e62cd4e269aa}} -Frobenius monoids {{formula:cc3d4ee1-912d-400a-a115-58037d43d3fc}}  are precisely those containing an element {{formula:9f06ef9b-fee9-4e44-a10b-89213eee0858}}  which is a fixed point for all left and right multiplications: {{formula:f7e24e88-f245-4e41-823d-53ee9208fc55}} . Similarly, Theorem REF  implies that a monoid {{formula:e2ebd2e9-7568-43c9-bdf9-aa847ce66f45}}  is {{formula:561d9016-42ff-4e10-8240-4fd679279186}} -Frobenius if and only if it contains a finite (non-empty) set {{formula:0491f0ac-379a-4e4d-ac65-68a102909495}}  on which all multiplications, left or right, act as permutations, and such that the cardinality {{formula:2c1af37e-54c2-4689-a4f4-b43cc1bfe67f}}  of {{formula:4ddf282f-8b4d-4bb2-b3b2-da9768241279}}  is invertible in the ring {{formula:4ecbe2b2-757f-44c8-aa82-8d849e474571}} . The full description of connected Frobenius categories {{formula:63178b5b-2181-482b-b50b-e0c2eb7b4a13}}  in the two cases is a natural generalization of this discussion.

Finally, in Section  we finish with some open problems for the reader.

Throughout this paper, {{formula:f5757fcb-9f18-4e78-bfc1-d3b0a827ac5b}}  will denote a complete, cocomplete category, while {{formula:8cef708b-196d-4b65-9e4c-021343803d8f}}  stands for a small category. In general, for notions pertaining to category theory, we refer to {{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}. The convention for composing morphisms is the usual one: given two morphisms {{formula:a2243cde-c8d5-411a-8e85-446fb6377fc0}}  and {{formula:ad2df10e-3caa-4540-8392-b80ee3e6f224}}  in a category, their composition is {{formula:8422a6ea-0a07-40cb-8bce-4d975b86d9a1}} . In order to keep the notation simple, if {{formula:09918c8b-3312-4e24-9c70-24e43b2075a9}}  is an object of {{formula:bc654868-d96c-4bfa-9eaa-7b8c9c5530fd}}  we write {{formula:3cfe6ef4-3d8d-461d-8201-fb9be5dee9eb}}  (rather than {{formula:d5e6d26d-dde8-4ec7-b7be-fb2498252658}} , for example). Sometimes, in order to make it easier to keep track of the objects involved in morphisms, we shall denote {{formula:03089ea9-6343-4650-bc58-91e39f44c371}}  by {{formula:8554e8ab-9511-4139-940d-86bcd18acfbf}} . Similarly, we might denote a subset {{formula:a5a5d0e8-2907-4ef5-8d46-549184fc970d}}  by {{formula:2e6a42a7-4245-4623-b2c3-897f5c056ee0}} . Given a set {{formula:2d7bdbba-c7a5-4bc5-9c8b-fc4ec0e20f80}}  and a morphism {{formula:42c58e55-c170-43b3-9f0f-030820d9bd70}} , {{formula:86b557c8-cdeb-40d9-925b-8a4109feb9d0}}  stands for the set of all morphisms {{formula:914e92c0-c9fa-4bc9-9114-2cc603d2a0cb}} ; similarly for {{formula:66aad640-d2d3-4b88-867c-94818b6b6cb4}} , when the composition makes sense. Given categories {{formula:14963ddc-2417-405b-b1bd-69683bad8974}} , we denote the category {{formula:695fabdd-9bcc-4a3f-90dd-8a27b6f308a0}}  simply by {{formula:8bce95d8-e71e-43a5-bf29-c854863bb965}} . All functors are covariant, except when explicitly mentioned otherwise.

Definition 1.1

Let {{formula:ca2163de-186f-4a19-8b3b-2542ea568df0}}  be a complete, cocomplete category. A small category {{formula:b4674c68-2af6-46fb-99fe-a9c237aac6cf}}  is said to be {{formula:ef361815-492d-45c0-b54b-692e609e2941}} -Frobenius if the diagonal functor {{formula:950c8ab2-77b6-46dc-b0e0-0530266f8077}}  is a Frobenius functor.

Remark 1.2

The left adjoint to {{formula:83a271bc-24ad-48d0-a079-7fc078b6552d}}  is the functor {{formula:22bc2bdd-d1cd-43d8-8dd8-011fd635e914}} , sending {{formula:e3f54fa8-91d1-4772-a931-e444e9886e69}}  to its colimit {{formula:6f3e1583-8e81-45c7-a8c4-8aa8a9fb620d}} . Similarly, the right adjoint to {{formula:8b757f0f-969f-44ef-9267-7ec812c6da75}}  is the functor sending {{formula:3657e158-e48a-4e9e-b827-88eb67ade8db}}  to its limit {{formula:d15a6ef7-9aff-4b88-8bd7-bb63d534279c}}  ({{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}). Consequently, saying that {{formula:015e833d-5dec-4a74-97ad-191420da205d}}  is Frobenius is the same as saying that {{formula:83202025-8796-4f03-a262-710d8765486b}}  and {{formula:32253a59-1da7-4c0d-8a17-770894328aaa}}  are naturally isomorphic. This means that we can find, for each functor {{formula:51ec517f-187c-43eb-92ca-9ae45e368d6d}} , an isomorphism {{formula:5fd5de4c-52e2-4f63-a299-7814baac3abe}}  such that for every natural transformation {{formula:f3b22ea9-5f70-4dc1-aa39-9906541be1f0}}  one has the commutative diagram
{{formula:a029af4e-dcc2-4405-bd43-59d1c04acec4}}

Remark 1.3

Notice that the empty category is {{formula:17b9d382-b88a-4c21-bcff-033986db4a74}} -Frobenius if and only if {{formula:2b1e8ae9-846b-493d-9189-4cfb580bb102}}  has a zero object. In order to avoid splitting the arguments into cases, we assume from now on that all our categories are non-empty.

We remarked earlier that we would be concerned primarily with the case when {{formula:a108e1c5-6d7d-401f-a918-7a53129e9631}}  is connected. In fact, as the following lemma shows, the general problem of finding the {{formula:4e3208c5-9fe6-46cd-8e33-919a7621a19f}} -Frobenius small categories {{formula:53f31d43-052a-48fb-b398-602eee650dc7}}  for a given {{formula:f99677fd-3259-4650-8e87-1943e3f2dde1}}  breaks up into the connected and the discrete case under certain conditions which do occur in the cases of interest.

Lemma 1.4

Let {{formula:d90eb60c-0135-4399-92fe-cb1d6bdcfb32}}  be a complete, cocomplete category and {{formula:54c2fa2b-1c6d-41d5-b16e-55054c8109be}}  a small category with connected components {{formula:cfef482d-b715-42df-ae36-7e05bb340d9e}} . Then:

If each component {{formula:e3917408-6f3e-41c0-9e13-7dc3ac403558}}  is {{formula:a69db840-ae78-4b67-957c-7c9c444060bc}} -Frobenius and the set {{formula:719bc378-105b-4e27-beec-eaca8f219d58}} , regarded as a discrete category, is {{formula:de1b223a-cc82-4a51-a517-9ccf3741db5a}} -Frobenius, then {{formula:e2f8bee2-20ce-4420-b31b-db0323a09d9d}}  is {{formula:b0883747-db31-4c79-8dc3-779595356ccd}} -Frobenius.

If {{formula:de0ce6a5-5e3a-4c1d-a00a-a1f7a852d72d}}  is {{formula:7293dc46-18fb-4c4a-8b6c-c736e6c5259d}} -Frobenius, then {{formula:c2cb4581-8f99-4c29-9ee0-6bce083094cd}}  is {{formula:8877aea3-9ec6-4df8-966d-ba2d901517e8}} -Frobenius.

The converse of {{formula:16b171df-591b-43db-8966-d22a6a889389}}  holds if {{formula:31e908df-4145-4dbb-90fb-5babbfb15c4d}}  has a zero object.

Before proving the three assertions, we make some observations useful in all three arguments. Fix a functor {{formula:ff40d46b-8453-4fed-b278-68c2a12e08a7}} , and consider the contravariant functor {{formula:5c9e00f9-d94f-4bb7-9dcd-dd1a40f10099}}  defined by sending each object {{formula:1a48ea18-c673-4d15-b6cb-d0b8ecc6b02c}}  to the set of cones {{formula:9380e841-ad93-4066-9b68-5b4a7969e10f}}  (Mac Lane's terminology and notation; see {{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}). The set of cones can also be defined as the object set of the comma category {{formula:7cdb92d2-cf4f-45ec-be7b-3901f96d4701}}  ({{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}). Since {{formula:9e0086a0-87bb-41d5-8326-cd4176ea046d}}  is small, the comma category is indeed small, so it makes sense to talk about its object set. Notice that the limit {{formula:6126922d-38c8-4bad-b6d9-9fe6b90d9a05}}  is precisely the representing object of {{formula:eaed68e4-b4d7-4d26-966a-b7f6a756ce77}} . Moreover, {{formula:81586afa-e949-4df4-9622-364af895467c}}  is natural in {{formula:c1175fc7-661d-44a4-8140-a6fa0b901697}} .
On the other hand, again having fixed {{formula:5d3aeca7-26c7-4cda-8537-35123bf4c977}} , consider the functor {{formula:d4e8c21c-5e83-4350-bdae-06b2ee66c7b5}}  sending {{formula:7e062dcd-235d-4661-9ab9-8e321e729b0c}}  to collections of cones {{formula:c9288635-f6e0-4806-a24e-c246cd96c326}}  from {{formula:e411bf86-4e4e-49e1-968d-1111a079f2ed}}  to the restrictions of {{formula:c52006a9-f8fc-44d9-8bc0-ebaec21b13a7}}  to the connected components {{formula:fccda7e2-536c-48f6-91c6-fcb4705ca099}} . By the definition of limits, the representing object for {{formula:c33604c7-9975-4695-8616-8a01494fa509}}  is {{formula:862a904c-bbf8-4b7e-ab63-6acb6ababf24}} . Notice however that, since there are no morphisms between distinct connected components, the functors {{formula:5a108038-6ce1-4ffe-a91f-b60a677afb29}}  and {{formula:b2a9d8b4-8477-4a79-a4e9-3bdba13391c9}}  actually coincide. In conclusion, the representing objects {{formula:9942e838-6cfa-467a-9cab-1e9fec640361}}  and {{formula:35da4a53-e2c8-44a3-9fae-fa74e4114638}}  are in fact isomorphic; the isomorphism exhibited here is natural in {{formula:2f5726cf-e8d5-4cd3-acc6-69edf065f54f}} , because {{formula:1dc37fc3-9234-476b-ba85-726164f99775}}  is. Similarly, {{formula:5e00b815-08b0-48bf-acc3-12ad4fdb3b06}} . We are now ready for the proof proper.
(a) We have just seen that {{formula:274ebeb4-fed5-4f9e-bb0a-d7e363bc7778}}  naturally in {{formula:95bf9539-7464-4725-bab4-9f1d3de3cd10}} . Each {{formula:86e76e87-49d7-4f62-ac21-0afc6ef84803}}  is Frobenius, so the latter is isomorphic to {{formula:e96525dc-23db-49f2-a13e-a77555dc92e0}}  (naturally in {{formula:88028c61-4268-4ea9-ab75-919eedbaf255}} ). The component set {{formula:80044155-a6ba-4590-b0a3-af416049ad27}}  is Frobenius, so this is isomorphic to {{formula:5c7139e3-a390-45e3-b37c-e584f9606534}}  (again, naturally in {{formula:cf5dc366-5783-428e-b6cb-48d41182ca7d}} ). Finally, the above discussion shows that this is isomorphic to {{formula:8927e74a-a2d6-4ce4-ab79-1c57d3ed7999}} .
(b) Instead of looking at the whole of {{formula:46402547-bbc9-47c8-9130-a985a03f2ffc}} , consider only those functors {{formula:69af90db-49b9-489c-98ad-5639ee9d7110}}  which restrict to constants on each component {{formula:65286284-9753-4ed0-a231-73d0b86e633d}} . These are precisely the functors factoring through the canonical functor {{formula:489b1396-6a9a-4388-b20b-3f0cc1e1d084}} , which sends each {{formula:51c43398-8f71-4083-8b7c-f177514ea6be}}  to {{formula:31db4b39-4766-4abf-817a-a533bf5a783b}} . Again, use the isomorphism {{formula:cdda3bf8-241c-4591-8c57-b092b6ae65b2}} : the limit of a constant functor on a connected category is easily seen to be precisely the image object (with all structural morphisms equal to the identity); it follows that in the case at hand, when {{formula:bbbdd5f7-e752-49b1-bca8-4bc2ec123246}}  restricts to a constant on each component, {{formula:a4986bb7-6f5c-4447-bd03-5899c248bedc}}  is naturally isomorphic to the product of the objects {{formula:8388b08f-bcad-4651-a531-01ed021233e4}} . The same discussion applies to colimits: {{formula:6209f763-dfac-4c86-80eb-afb56d6e75be}} . The desired conclusion that {{formula:feb8cb38-2ede-4952-808b-0659a2495f2f}}  must be {{formula:ae72f682-60a4-4896-b92f-2501d1c7ea50}} -Frobenius follows.
(c) In view of (b), we must show that given the additional hypothesis of a zero object, each {{formula:c582e79a-b90e-4915-b607-221dab0f56bf}}  is {{formula:daa66c1a-2f68-4b13-b0d5-d9c616d3a764}} -Frobenius. Fix some index {{formula:837b3000-b953-48e9-a7ef-592daa7252d1}} , and consider only those functors {{formula:2b73c5d5-4e15-4e70-89b0-1dca4e15d36c}}  which send each component {{formula:1bf8636a-5254-44d2-994c-f40a1a6125e6}}  to the zero object 0. Using once more the discussion at the beginning of the proof, we conclude that for these functors, the limit is naturally isomorphic to the product {{formula:aac67eb2-e67a-4d38-95c5-a9de62fc0cc7}} . Since in any complete category product with the final object is naturally isomorphic to the identity, we conclude that {{formula:c57b83ec-00d8-4291-a25d-79dab7f7d83d}} , naturally in {{formula:db7c359d-06b8-4689-a36c-a43c32f3b23c}} . Similarly, the colimit of {{formula:5dd7c121-1d3f-43f8-b017-4f04bbe2c9c7}}  is isomorphic to that of {{formula:cd59a8af-341e-4230-85d3-d984c330005b}} , so {{formula:ce16fec6-025f-4710-82cb-586b35b1a1c9}}  must indeed be {{formula:7d94548f-d3d8-429b-8845-2145557ac1ee}} -Frobenius if {{formula:cd8e0572-a282-426c-9257-87279d096dfb}}  is.

In the end, we are going to find the small categories {{formula:06c89507-58f3-4c69-807d-b6e90a4017c8}}  which are {{formula:349e3dc0-8dcb-4bf4-887f-7ef261febb84}} -Frobenius and those which are {{formula:89093539-4aa4-41f0-ad4a-db16a49b4d33}} -Frobenius for a given ring {{formula:d9cc8491-6e91-4845-9c93-88894297b9bf}} . Part of that proof will be unified by the results in this section, dealing with a certain class of categories {{formula:ee66f04e-a903-4008-944a-1f241e07674a}}  which contains both {{formula:cae89eb6-a9fe-40a9-a97a-5c06215c361e}}  and {{formula:9f312bdd-6db9-470e-8476-12325547369b}} , and many more familiar categories. We introduce this class below:

Definition 2.1

A category {{formula:895bdf8f-c1b5-4662-bb48-9af48346ac19}}  is called admissible if:

it is complete and cocomplete

there is a faithful functor {{formula:3a7caa58-319d-49b6-aecd-c15545d25fca}}  which has a left adjoint {{formula:29a8212d-75a4-4d33-95d4-e34bb5bac4ae}}

for at least one object {{formula:8bd4c47f-38a9-4f06-85de-c79d2802d8d2}}  of {{formula:8087dd50-b074-4698-bd22-1fe846d79b78}} , the set {{formula:39ca9948-2101-4c3a-b195-cbb2f65b2d06}}  has {{formula:78b48945-67cf-4649-95ef-1c31ed4a6556}}  elements

for any set {{formula:8e64f5c4-9ed9-4cdf-a2e2-7c42767def04}}  and any element {{formula:527bfe52-6a62-4996-ac19-53f4b42c1b38}}  of the set {{formula:5a9006c6-d9cd-4f37-b6f5-f487aa855c35}} , there is a smallest finite subset {{formula:01f627ed-2a7e-441a-8a56-c2058638ce61}}  such that {{formula:d5f5f08a-eaf4-43fe-8a16-593b33ce6f24}}  belongs to the set {{formula:f201453b-bcfc-44f1-948c-a68dcfdc500b}} .

For a set {{formula:7a036691-f31e-4f81-884d-7ba7eeca2805}} , we denote the free object {{formula:bb7f4261-2631-4ff6-a7ce-27f7c9819e83}}  by {{formula:394a66c9-9dd0-456b-9a99-76d78f8b277d}} . The faithful functor {{formula:c5ee4a88-ac45-460b-9b38-b3157d8caa74}}  makes {{formula:d0c97cc4-41e2-4171-91d8-d4cc09543925}}  into what is usually called a concrete category. Most of the time we will simply omit {{formula:9111837c-e3c5-4a3c-9561-e62a51fdb4b7}} , and regard {{formula:87aebde8-fbd5-48f1-8e1b-a41e3a2037ca}}  as a category whose objects are sets (with “additional structure”; that is, we keep in mind that the same set might correspond to different objects), and whose morphisms are functions between these sets.

Remark 2.2

Condition (3) implies that for each set {{formula:23717046-216b-459b-82aa-cbd2304f132b}} , the component {{formula:b343117a-e831-4349-926d-19865fc97d9f}}  of the unit of our adjunction {{formula:3a45880d-bf3f-4c98-b6b6-2abac52a653b}}  is mono. Indeed, if {{formula:5357f8c9-3d95-4a71-a1af-eadcd0636adc}}  is an object of {{formula:6b4b55f9-9197-4a35-931d-46f41ff087d7}}  such that the set {{formula:1ada3430-359b-46a4-a75d-051db9f1d45a}}  has at least two elements and {{formula:4ea2dc7b-621f-43dd-bee6-4e85ddbfa8c4}}  is any set, then any two different elements of {{formula:757a4696-58d1-43c3-a4a1-096dab01e824}}  can be mapped to different elements of {{formula:da523025-e99d-464b-babb-1f8d37df3aa5}} , meaning that any two different elements of {{formula:baac1954-a5c8-44e0-821b-cf81a09533b9}}  must have different images in the set {{formula:0e66a0a1-f91b-4d9b-9ce7-afb7e14e079e}} . Hence, from now on we will regard {{formula:4af0cdf8-47df-4a92-9ba1-7729aa79d384}}  as a subset of {{formula:310b3906-c8f1-483f-b2ef-1c36412521ec}}  (or of {{formula:0b39a2b9-5cf0-4b8c-8460-0bbef81485f5}} , with the convention in the previous paragraph). Also, condition (3) implies that {{formula:65558e12-0aa4-43ef-a437-c49a92a5db6c}}  is not isomorphic to any of the other free objects, a fact that will be useful at some point: {{formula:636bca16-7f3d-40fe-a3e9-c2b11f4479d2}}  is initial, whereas any other free object admits at least two morphisms to any object {{formula:a92559ff-f3b6-4876-9c9e-27e5736cd453}}  such that {{formula:18d1f2ca-76ef-4dda-95f3-b44d7f723e5b}}  has at least two elements.

Remark 2.3

Another observation which will be used tacitly from now on is this: inclusions of sets {{formula:2fa56401-db30-4261-aa3b-27348e07cb55}}  induce inclusions of sets {{formula:5c8d689d-562a-4afd-9052-7ec8d4250f00}}  (we omit {{formula:8b573e9d-edd0-4f2f-8831-4925be86ee34}}  in this remark). When {{formula:86d71e0a-bf29-4335-820a-3745c9e965b8}}  this is clear: every monomorphism of sets {{formula:7b0e7d61-2e83-4420-9635-892bcaf5b4d4}}  is then a coretraction, and functors preserve coretractions. When {{formula:56ab9a89-86aa-4715-8c01-9545e9683c4e}} , on the other hand, {{formula:b9925c1b-b899-44bd-9ae3-73404659fccf}}  is the initial object of {{formula:3058c26b-f103-49e7-ba76-01507e8b364f}} . The initial object can be constructed, in any complete category, as a subobject of any weakly initial object (see {{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}). More precisely, it is the equalizer of all endomorphisms of any such object. By weakly initial we mean object admitting a morphism (not necessarily unique) to any object. Free objects are all weakly initial (unless {{formula:0f94d943-f3a6-41ae-9541-700e2091e3fd}} , in which case there is nothing left to prove), so {{formula:9eaf991b-5bf7-444b-bd71-c149c38c4e63}}  is a subobject of each of them. Right adjoints (such as {{formula:4e4cf0ab-b5b1-4cf8-8893-639ba2091e0c}} ) preserve monomorphisms, so, given a subset {{formula:ca459b43-5d3c-4600-afdf-b5cc40899116}}  of {{formula:f45a384d-8816-4b94-b9fd-fb8c37bd60b3}} , we will regard {{formula:0609ff30-fa0a-4863-ae09-1c7bcc5863c6}}  as a subset of {{formula:7100dd01-646d-4d20-b7d6-966d262ec094}} ; the inclusion is always the one induced by {{formula:c74ef31e-7f16-4f7c-9b15-8e69de185944}} .

Here we make a short digression to identify many familiar categories which are, in fact, admissible. These are the so-called varieties of algebras, in the sense of Universal Algebra. For definitions and a detailed treatment we refer to {{cite:2203f598f963f2efd52132991e2de51ea90230ca}}. Also, there is some discussion on the topic, from a more category theoretical point of view, in {{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}; here the main definitions are given, and the proof for the existence of free objects is sketched, using Freyd's Adjoint Functor Theorem ({{cite:9a167d9fd4d622832b0843ee9a5656fc06738694}}).

We will not give complete proofs or definitions here. Given an {{formula:0d7e0c2b-3e19-4863-b2d7-247c65f45d5b}} -graded set {{formula:e2238e2f-205e-4634-a910-85dcfa0e79df}}  whose elements are called operations, an action of {{formula:c9dee965-f036-4870-9532-f6e4effe2de4}}  on a set {{formula:4211914a-a140-4b79-a84b-108906cc0f0c}}  is a map assigning to each {{formula:1e42494a-f28c-444b-bbea-6a0ec229fe3a}}  of degree {{formula:10740988-c9fe-465b-9788-fd55d08c4e04}}  a function {{formula:056db8a6-74a2-431e-9111-2a22048b9532}} . The degree {{formula:3bc32da2-96bb-4e5e-948d-fedb1b186178}}  is also called the arity of {{formula:e9e630c3-3d09-4ffc-b5ed-07d73a52a923}} . From the operations in {{formula:2fab0bc6-7911-472a-9ca4-bc53a71128b0}} , named fundamental operations, others can be derived, by composition and substitution; see the reference from Mac Lane. A set {{formula:2507b64e-614b-464e-81b0-6d7bd1547de4}}  of equational identities is a set of pairs {{formula:1ca871e4-e360-41d7-8d54-05fdee26e877}}  of derived operations having the same arity. A set {{formula:c2eca7d4-7f70-4747-8dd4-45c3c6e1db19}}  with an {{formula:226e29f1-d0fc-4557-9993-df8d1f97aef3}}  action is then said to satisfy the equations {{formula:58cd65da-54e7-4892-8374-04b0909ff3f7}}  if {{formula:d1e3a6f6-2893-4fc0-a3bc-6f996aa572ad}}  for all {{formula:bb542c2a-4772-4ccb-a56f-0c7493aee712}} . The class of all sets with an {{formula:2eafe6e4-3939-4acc-a7f4-8bd1b192f4e3}}  action and satisfying the identities {{formula:1822b4ba-012d-48e2-9551-2eb7c2d0df66}}  will be denoted by {{formula:d12e8865-0261-4f31-8907-c178aa8d8c3d}} , and a member of this class will be called an {{formula:a3257cc6-0f95-413c-8422-9f7b572b5180}} -algebra.

A morphism between algebras {{formula:e87277a7-8850-47b6-8468-eaf778a20399}}  is a map {{formula:092c46c5-54a8-4c07-9d97-f7d2e45b77f5}}  which, for each {{formula:a9d8b821-ba28-4cff-8c58-f57b5da6d6bc}} , makes the following diagram commutative:
{{formula:f884a7a5-d34e-4dd7-9cf8-d311d57652f9}}

We now have a category {{formula:cc51cfd9-e059-4cc5-9d08-b82586db6aec}} . Examples include the categories of sets (no operations at all), monoids, groups, rings, modules over a ring {{formula:e1ad4841-b421-4462-9ab0-c3a1cbcb1c38}}  (these are abelian groups with some unary operations describing multiplications with scalars in {{formula:00b58926-a119-4259-8ce4-9661137ea2df}} ), Lie algebras, etc. Notice that we allow the underlying set of an algebra to be empty, although the authors of {{cite:2203f598f963f2efd52132991e2de51ea90230ca}} do not. A variety contains the empty set if and only if there are no nullary operations (i.e. operations of arity 0).

The definitions allow for a variety of algebras not to satisfy condition (3) of Definition REF . Assuming it does, however, it can be shown that {{formula:ec0e81f3-a27b-4142-acab-eb6e55294f8a}}  is admissible, with {{formula:d49b72bc-db5d-46dc-9823-b0760421db76}}  (from Definition REF ) being the forgetful functor, which sends an algebra to its underlying set, and a morphism of algebras to the corresponding map of sets. We will not give the complete proof here. As mentioned above, Mac Lane proves the existence of free objects indirectly, using the Adjoint Functor Theorem. In {{cite:2203f598f963f2efd52132991e2de51ea90230ca}} an explicit construction of free objects is given. Condition (4) follows from the fact that a filtered union of {{formula:79cbd248-92f8-4d34-be17-4b56f68c0ee6}} -algebras is again such with an obvious structure; it is easy to check the required universality property for the union of all {{formula:fe9e350a-ef66-4ee7-b036-61cde38b4c49}}  as {{formula:2cc912d4-14f2-4994-994c-4e9814e48e61}}  ranges through the finite subsets of {{formula:6754de2b-dc7c-43dd-a058-233dd4a751df}} , which makes it into the free object on {{formula:7d77e4be-a86b-437b-beb4-5839c0e61733}} ; hence, elements of free objects are contained in finitely generated free subobjects. Finally, (4) is proven by noticing that for varieties of algebras, one always has {{formula:b7427e71-f018-4301-b417-ee95ff705fe4}}  (including the case when there are no nullary operations, and the second set in this equality happens to be empty). This can be seen by constructing the free objects explicitly. For completeness and cocompleteness one can mimic the usual constructions of products, coproducts, equalizers and coequalizers from group theory, for example.

In particular, {{formula:1ae4c881-8e2d-460d-9313-9909142f3384}}  and {{formula:1c1bd853-c3bf-436e-aae4-703f46217348}}  are admissible. Of course, this can be seen directly.

We will need the next lemma in the proof of Theorem REF .

Recall that a directed graph (digraph) is said to be strongly connected if for any two vertices {{formula:82e00c9d-2e5e-4e85-804c-474020b2d17b}}  there is a directed path from {{formula:419f1011-5b66-471a-9544-fae00330d07e}}  to {{formula:8c1f397b-cc3a-4894-b2ae-a0e37b1eebc0}} . A digraph is said to be transitive if whenever we have directed paths {{formula:92029948-1340-4ecc-a013-527a75ab3156}}  and {{formula:38966346-2686-4437-9a6e-ef84a09ca331}}  we also have a directed path {{formula:6a7395a9-371e-46a7-ab3d-58c4c2078066}} . The underlying graph of a category is transitive, for instance. If a digraph is transitive then strong connectedness is equivalent to having an edge {{formula:9af09a71-6845-4ebc-bb11-2c17659ae460}}  for any pair of distinct vertices {{formula:d7fc4ba5-fa27-4fb2-8dea-7b80979681f6}} .

Let {{formula:4d1e17cb-68c5-44c1-8604-1da7c06c133c}}  be an admissible category, and {{formula:cc6b867f-e07d-46d4-844a-bbb2ce191de3}}  a small, connected, {{formula:daff8c8a-7fd0-4084-83d9-a1bf9c29674b}} -Frobenius category. Now consider the functor {{formula:738da879-9d9d-4cf0-8fa6-aab86f04e8bb}}  which restricts to the constant functor {{formula:e321c9d2-0d4b-4ef0-b574-e045119ed443}}  on {{formula:6f90d0eb-82ad-475a-9bb7-4411b5b6d983}} , to the constant {{formula:1dcc7721-b82b-4bc2-aae4-d9f6998a7f1b}}  on {{formula:53d327f7-4d4d-4f31-82b6-4d0fee89bf85}} , and sends all morphisms {{formula:73dcc685-e911-4e9b-b066-06e6e9594e9a}}  onto the unique morphism {{formula:4fe61550-2dc8-4a60-94a4-6c66d33be044}} :
{{formula:e4411705-c457-495e-b8cd-7798abb8d51b}}

Remark 2.5

Notice that in the above proof, instead of the unique arrow {{formula:6fb2ffb6-bb4f-4d05-b813-8b7b85cb73f1}}  we could just as well have taken the unique arrow from an initial object to a non-initial object. Hence the statement holds for any (complete, cocomplete) category {{formula:ece874c2-68a4-4b28-8279-7b400e41c61e}}  having at least one object which is not initial.

The following definition is crucial in subsequent results. {{formula:443f8431-68a4-4683-8991-f004bce6fea5}}  stands for a small category.

Definition 2.6

A left invariant system (LS) of {{formula:bf6b0bf3-4a10-4d0d-94a3-e7651c39b66c}}  is a collection of finite, non-empty sets {{formula:f9278ef7-1eeb-473f-80fb-012ca5812900}} , one for each pair {{formula:a9525767-01e2-47e9-8a2e-9a801bb28eeb}} , such that composition to the left with any {{formula:4ab9cbdf-80c3-4bb9-ae86-4cc1d57085d4}}  sends {{formula:58f4a9b6-a974-41b4-8423-c56f76a903ce}}  bijectively onto {{formula:468cadca-1a32-435b-9781-d868b26269b4}}  for all {{formula:fe0f818c-1624-4351-bf13-c11985cd0507}} .

A right invariant system (RS) of {{formula:abb8f77f-ec81-4e3c-baca-fffb88f34b40}}  is a collection of finite, non-empty sets {{formula:61b474cb-5d5b-4b4d-9e61-1230a347afb3}} , one for each pair {{formula:1260d0ac-d034-4ae8-a66a-cf0a2929ddae}} , such that composition to the right with any {{formula:d11f4f1b-da9c-403f-bfd7-6e4f6bb9b9cc}}  sends {{formula:0cb863de-08fc-4266-9a88-1a63b918eb6b}}  bijectively onto {{formula:92d5b271-823b-4beb-bd95-cb719d7bb9f5}}  for all {{formula:d4684617-c845-44bc-8928-c8453ef53b96}} .

An invariant system (IS) of {{formula:a2e5d360-f75e-4007-ba4d-368e8ccd0e34}}  is an LS which is also an RS.

The main result of this section follows:

Theorem 2.7

Let {{formula:bab93659-0cee-4afe-8630-359399374488}}  be an admissible category, and let {{formula:b2844481-6de5-4216-a238-1ed1804d88c0}}  be a small, connected, {{formula:fc422aad-e3d9-4efd-ab76-f57b96e0a726}} -Frobenius category. Then {{formula:2bbb097f-a330-4125-9262-47807f37d96a}}  has an IS.

By the {{formula:18a21b50-cd23-48dd-91c6-99354257dc81}} -Frobenius property we can identify {{formula:fdaebaeb-14b3-4240-88f6-14e771688f6a}}  with {{formula:f679296c-b4cd-4f05-a3b3-5b21605450ce}}  as well. We will denote by 1 the element generating {{formula:b276922b-7bce-4ffa-ad09-156c0e549c2e}} ; in the present context it corresponds to the image of any morphism in {{formula:a8d27ccf-6693-4838-b4b8-4b1984b00941}}  through the canonical map {{formula:84ac4c0b-c678-48c6-84bb-ecaf2a154c9c}} .
Let {{formula:3bfbd8df-1beb-4825-a5f8-068145ecfca9}}  be the structure map of the limit, and denote by {{formula:5b396c99-6a03-47ba-b42a-1d353d72420f}}  the element {{formula:0bf355b4-cb85-4c94-b424-2fefd1ab9e8c}}  (keep in mind the convention made after Definition REF : we regard the objects of {{formula:f635a572-165d-45c0-ab8b-97712afd5f6e}}  simply as sets, omitting the faithful functor {{formula:c10ceb3b-b826-49da-ba29-6ad80da424cf}} ). In this section we characterize those small {{formula:6b4d473c-d3da-4eec-94ce-da30c6a82773}}  (not necessarily connected) which are {{formula:a2eb6ec4-74d3-463d-ac6c-18d8ca6666b6}} -Frobenius and {{formula:e205f10a-1e95-4166-9303-f59a10e6e20b}} -Frobenius for a ring {{formula:79d3bf9f-fb33-4427-97a8-5f72eb297e2f}} . Section  and Section  will allow us to obtain both necessary and sufficient conditions on {{formula:4dab9ea7-68cb-4dd9-83af-e2d2499d9dc5}}  in order that it be Frobenius for these categories. We have already remarked in the discussion on varieties of algebras above that {{formula:3cba8e9d-0134-4ef4-a1f0-37ccc4059235}}  and {{formula:120f6c7c-2876-4f33-b1e0-96c5f24f60d0}}  are admissible categories, so the results in Section  apply in both cases. Remember that all our categories are non-empty.

The following theorem describes the Set-Frobenius categories:

Theorem 3.1

A small category {{formula:5da5bdcf-6d1a-444d-8b22-629641881292}}  is {{formula:17a0c2ee-5ff2-45ff-89fb-f856e796a846}} -Frobenius if and only if it is connected and it has an IS consisting of singletons {{formula:a26badd4-cba6-472f-808b-b618debd0088}} .

Assume {{formula:b76daf07-e05a-45be-a6ac-b17ec38fc051}}  satisfies the conditions in the statement. Then the group {{formula:8afd3974-28f8-4b97-b095-c92bc10b0394}}  introduced in the discussion before Proposition REF  is the trivial group. From Proposition REF  we know that in order to conclude that {{formula:7253682c-d268-4d89-898f-978ec1137858}}  is Frobenius, it suffices to check that {{formula:cd3fd7ca-5f61-44aa-b733-26accfa3ddf3}}  is. It is clear that the trivial group is {{formula:d72868f5-c2bb-48a9-8987-d130c1c1429a}} -Frobenius for any complete, cocomplete category {{formula:848e74a9-f652-480d-b8b5-05e2a53770bb}} , and the proof of this implication is finished.
Conversely, suppose {{formula:04c3d831-33e2-4385-b592-d0e3fd60cdd0}}  is {{formula:8b2084df-83b8-4ce3-b6cb-be62a027235e}} -Frobenius. Lemma REF  (b) then tells us that the set {{formula:a94425c4-d20d-43d4-b5ca-cb9585695901}}  of connected components of {{formula:dc4e91a1-54c8-47ba-8c53-bfe5b972a89d}} , viewed as a discrete category, must be {{formula:c6660227-bc0a-4a83-9c14-5d7d73fd044c}} -Frobenius. The only non-empty {{formula:7c4f443a-9287-4139-922b-eacc0c724590}} -frobenius discrete category is the singleton: notice for instance that the product of a non-empty set and at least one copy of the empty set is empty, whereas the disjoint union of all these sets is non-empty. Hence {{formula:63889bfb-c4fa-42b7-8b3d-59bf18a98ddf}}  is a singleton, i.e. {{formula:5a884db5-04c1-4db3-870c-4a63003e9b13}}  is connected.
Now Theorem REF  applies to show that {{formula:debbea24-6c1e-49f4-aeed-86b9fe05dedc}}  has an IS consisting of finite non-empty sets {{formula:091429ae-8021-4bea-a460-de4dd91bb3b6}} . Now we go once more through the argument in the first paragraph, in reverse: Proposition REF  says that {{formula:4c2d1b9f-1a90-494c-8792-5fcaadd98883}}  is {{formula:867af0a0-cbbd-4fa1-a687-99c120be2c23}} -Frobenius if and only if the finite group {{formula:0ccd9e37-55da-4adb-9f09-fd8f2813bdcd}}  is, so we have to prove that the only {{formula:4c23c077-9555-4a4d-ac95-c2badc9713cf}} -Frobenius finite group is the trivial group.
Functors from {{formula:98aba8ea-ffe6-49c0-bc8c-c20eed970c36}}  to {{formula:410c9c43-a276-44ae-a408-69bce5a9ed77}}  are actions of {{formula:87d86198-7f83-42e0-ba63-72882c2ff58b}}  on a set. They have easily described limits and colimits: the limiting cone of an action of {{formula:08dc1b55-ece8-468d-acfe-aa4068c78a04}}  on the set {{formula:dad2d9df-8107-4cea-9492-5ed18846cd90}}  is the inclusion of the set of points in {{formula:1dd0ebb0-294e-4bda-bfe8-d050e2cafa2a}}  fixed by all elements of {{formula:4ffe1471-1b79-467d-8a0e-428ed576ece4}} . The colimiting cone, on the other hand, is the canonical projection of {{formula:6f552f87-336b-4a37-9bbd-9e2decc55a41}}  onto the set of orbits of the action (sending each element onto its orbit). In particular, we see that the colimit of an action on a non-empty set is always a non-empty set, whereas one can always find actions on non-empty sets with no fixed points whenever {{formula:d08b5fdc-574a-43fd-9893-ee26139a35a1}}  is non-trivial: simply make {{formula:26a046b1-4372-4ba4-88e5-8ec9d6c101f0}}  act on itself by left multiplication, for example.

For {{formula:ee4856bf-79c1-4e5c-a10b-c2ec53511afe}} -modules, the result reads as follows:

Theorem 3.2

Let {{formula:a1dbaa76-cb07-42d4-a144-c40c0d369e0a}}  be a ring. A small category {{formula:151b0956-d08f-4da4-964a-2747b06a0138}}  is {{formula:aadc33a3-a981-4d96-a217-654d62084785}} -Frobenius if and only if it has finitely many components, each of which has an IS consisting of finite sets {{formula:cf7572f4-9407-44ae-8fda-09580737e698}}  such that {{formula:3f024ba8-b6f4-41ba-a7d3-cff5a7d06ef1}}  is invertible in the ring {{formula:bd6c2015-5853-41fe-9b41-e59493595b55}} .

In the course of the proof we will make use of the following result regarding discrete categories:

Proposition 3.3

Let {{formula:0d11fc88-1625-4859-90d6-459f049fb690}}  be a ring, and {{formula:a01fb368-76af-48e9-8e4a-6ce0198c8ae4}}  a set. The discrete category {{formula:c9da19cb-bb9c-4df6-8f9e-da1d5dc6d58d}}  is {{formula:9682b8e9-400d-41c7-a03e-769504af3d66}} -Frobenius if and only if it is finite.

This is {{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}}. In that paper it is both an immediate consequence of the main result {{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}}, and proved separately using a finiteness result on Frobenius corings ({{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}}; see also {{cite:364429b530fddf8141cb4b3e31dfb203fa1c4679}} for definitions and relevant results on Frobenius corings). We give here a different proof, relying on another proposition found in {{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}}.
On the one hand, it is well-known that finite sets are {{formula:1e35d439-ac78-46e4-86e2-9a5179ca25b8}} -Frobenius. In fact, products and coproducts are canonically isomorphic in any additive category.
Conversely, assume that {{formula:f2890572-9e5e-4fac-92d6-ee6bf8967d62}}  is {{formula:076b599c-c67d-4a1c-922f-ba9b7aa09b1c}} -Frobenius. Now {{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}} says that the canonical map {{formula:77b2c433-a9b8-4cf1-8080-0873ec504065}}  is a natural isomorphism. Consider the composition
{{formula:a9be769e-55e0-476e-ba96-afdf40bdf107}} 
in which the first arrow is the map with all components equal to the identity on {{formula:df4b0e8a-1e33-4d35-a9a1-1a6f58acbfad}} , while the second arrow is the inverse of the canonical isomorphism {{formula:a4ea86fe-d93e-4586-83bf-e008d4e4fff0}} . It is a morphism from {{formula:2ce53eca-72c0-47b5-979a-5e325653ac7a}}  to {{formula:09d512df-ffec-4fa4-8771-d4e2ba998ac5}}  having the property that the image of {{formula:7ba9f70d-4bea-49f0-bd1d-42a792f69fed}}  is not contained in any {{formula:618ebba0-ea50-4319-a08c-f3f3d28e96da}}  for {{formula:a6b994a2-3ca1-4bf2-8755-1167e16e4d41}} . As {{formula:b597e5c3-ff83-42da-bdda-ef911dfa0a76}}  is a finitely generated {{formula:779eea82-c671-484f-bee9-5354cc741bba}} -module, however, its image is certainly contained in a finite direct sum. Hence {{formula:5b68f8d1-6328-4f57-b11b-cf4d63a6468d}}  must be finite.

Remark 3.4

It is clear that the direct sum of infinitely many non-zero modules is strictly smaller than their direct product. However, note that the proof, arranged as above, applies to all (complete, cocomplete) abelian categories having a non-zero small object. We say that an object {{formula:de7ebe52-815d-4f27-9eab-aa6d14927d4e}}  in a category with coproducts is small if any morphism of {{formula:43696b45-c2d0-45cb-8234-a5c5a5a9ebe9}}  to a coproduct factors through a finite coproduct. Indeed, {{cite:cf38123c9883ef8b5208b8147aceafaf74a02868}} covers this situation as well (and in fact holds for all categories enriched over the category of commutative monoids and having a zero object), and all we need to do is replace {{formula:8b44b764-5fff-4524-b984-bf21cd16b03e}}  in the above proof with a small, non-zero object.

A cocomplete abelian category with a small projective generator is equivalent to some {{formula:997b893e-4531-40ee-981f-03f74fbe77ab}}  ({{cite:9bee669bafbdc0e5e8412446951981f105a05871}}). There are, however, examples of complete, cocomplete abelian categories with a non-zero small object and which are not equivalent to some {{formula:892f28e0-7eda-42b3-ac82-228a44b4a098}} . We give such an example below.

Example 3.5 (Torsion modules)

Let {{formula:3fb6dc66-2539-4fa6-bdb6-1f8d9c0a14e7}}  be a DVR (discrete valuation ring), and let {{formula:1c95cc2c-2dea-4d60-a8e1-ea1cc0dd02f8}}  be the full subcategory of {{formula:bca9afef-512e-4d92-9c0a-dc4f5f2767b2}}  consisting of torsion modules. {{formula:1cb7c172-66e6-4ab4-bb94-0406cd54ba10}}  is an abelian category, because kernels, cokernels, finite direct sums, etc. of morphisms of torsion modules are morphisms of torsion modules. Completeness and cocompleteness are, again, easily checked: the direct sum in {{formula:750b2f80-d973-4d41-9c93-a0ea9bfd7385}}  is also the direct sum in {{formula:e8f5b64b-1e58-4e0a-9601-b7c530e09977}} , and the direct product in {{formula:192a74e1-02e7-4fec-bf60-c5ff0eff528d}}  is the torsion of the direct product in {{formula:d06218aa-41f6-4007-b1d1-9ca71659700b}} . Finally, the category has non-zero small objects: any non-zero finitely generated torsion module will do. A small projective object in {{formula:db54cd91-3c0e-49cc-bfcf-d03c0b14e353}}  must be finitely generated, and the structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID now easily shows that {{formula:06aad69b-fd74-42a4-8f09-65a0deae775e}}  has no non-zero small projectives, hence cannot be equivalent to some {{formula:7ad74f8e-1df5-45d7-8f66-9462f061a894}} .

Remark 3.6

Although we will not prove this here, with a little more work, it can be shown that the previous example still works if {{formula:8cf7aa48-7460-40e2-9d58-38d02e12652d}}  is taken to be any noetherian local integral domain (which is not a field).

At the other end of the spectrum, when working with connected categories, we will need the following characterization of {{formula:f8b7125a-a0eb-442f-8ef3-ec185db778b5}} -Frobenius groups:

Proposition 3.7

Let {{formula:cc72b482-d067-454b-b6c5-90eea373ef37}}  be a ring and {{formula:ae2e5e81-a07d-4dd4-9eda-26db347c530c}}  a group, regarded as a one-object category. {{formula:cac18f9d-bd5d-433e-8fd1-a15a7cef4c42}}  is {{formula:3a9fee0b-ee07-44e7-af1b-81171bf6b5ac}} -Frobenius if and only if it is finite, and the natural number {{formula:7b1deb5f-1d8d-4efb-9703-be35ee88b11d}}  is invertible in {{formula:fc3ef226-0916-4fe3-928d-3232f7ad39bf}} .

Functors {{formula:1fd2bd37-d0ae-4adc-a124-8be8b010154d}}  are precisely {{formula:ed4137cd-4981-4280-813e-eb053c42dec0}} -modules with a {{formula:1a1a32e6-505d-4f4c-8666-2b64c1891609}}  action, or, in other words, {{formula:ccecd6b8-9786-4be3-80e3-3f243481c7f3}} -modules. The diagonal functor {{formula:e12f4ec2-b52f-464c-84fe-c591ac22c4d2}}  associates to each {{formula:5d77e919-d099-41ee-904a-9a98fa69effb}} -module the same module with trivial {{formula:6e14932d-9618-48ff-bb57-fbdb94e867a9}}  action. This means that one can identify the diagonal functor with the restriction of scalars from {{formula:bc9f0b57-946c-44bd-9abd-fef609c08fd6}}  to {{formula:2d23031b-4228-491e-b692-35c8b7a415d7}}  through the augmentation {{formula:8d851660-7eaa-428a-b882-3d68c2990c14}}  (the unique ring morphism sending each element of {{formula:bc79b407-1a59-408e-8713-98c917eaf4df}}  to the identity {{formula:33f93019-2f9c-4775-8b16-0c0f19bde5c4}} ).
The problem has now been reduced to the classical question of deciding when a restriction of scalars is Frobenius. By a well-known result of Morita ({{cite:3bb4570c6b886cd00747805adde43de3b9147aa9}} or {{cite:5bf02ad5c7316b795dd38dde91f1d4a5d3ef120d}}), restriction of scalars through a ring morphism {{formula:594e9079-a53d-4c67-9ad6-f0e1f4d27a96}}  is Frobenius if and only if {{formula:56f46ac7-c6c0-4e24-8920-435b5ca2333e}}  is left {{formula:884c9285-d55c-4e0e-b2dd-d5060c06cb69}} -projective and finitely generated, and {{formula:461082b2-3139-448f-804a-b06ccab4f348}}  as {{formula:867f541c-fc13-4eae-ac0c-91539a13e279}} -bimodules. We are going to apply this characterization to the ring extension {{formula:6b74aaae-f946-44a5-b915-d17fb772e8ed}} .
{{formula:aa04fe73-aa3c-4a17-808d-4445fcf8db73}}  is left {{formula:3b66e59c-eb73-48d3-a8b2-c0e260f9443c}} -projective if and only if the augmentation {{formula:f379ae4b-2bf6-43f7-bcf8-dd063d15fec7}}  splits through some left {{formula:af2e6aa8-7320-4ba0-971f-e111abf73eb3}} -module map {{formula:71d1c722-2a51-4f8b-9d40-be032db1913a}} . For any such splitting, {{formula:22eda98c-98e6-4b2e-b61c-1367a6e6861a}}  is some element {{formula:c789b66d-e01e-49fd-802e-84026a6d6edc}}  of {{formula:47827d9b-f7f1-4009-a6df-7b1e9f27223b}}  fixed by left multiplication with any element of {{formula:99788941-3ff5-4fd0-a6ad-a293beef64e0}} . This shows at once that {{formula:cd7c07e2-535c-40fe-946a-1be82ae59579}}  must be finite, and that {{formula:a65e77ed-c1c0-4372-a45c-378d357d3a5b}} . Finally, from {{formula:08947df1-e2dd-41a2-a0e0-392a1febccff}}  we find that {{formula:a605a519-b790-473a-9712-99766f7c9fa2}}  must in fact be the inverse of {{formula:37323a47-a9d3-432f-bd0f-421397f0251c}} . Conversely, if {{formula:f9287394-71f2-47cf-a54a-97d111a16372}}  is invertible in {{formula:5470616a-ea22-4c2f-901c-e5ffa4c14253}} , simply consider the {{formula:759901cb-d53c-4c47-a9fe-ace378b4700c}} -module map sending {{formula:f2562d4c-f304-4887-9fdd-c2df07a9e208}}  to {{formula:fa931616-c00b-4e0f-b019-8842e2d15bb4}} ; clearly, it is a splitting for {{formula:83ece3bf-5cec-4ce8-a9e0-9cf1fc2bb151}} .
We still have to prove that when {{formula:e17cd5c6-2031-4f44-9a7d-f00690edd7cd}}  satisfies the condtitions in the statement of the proposition (and hence, as we have just seen, {{formula:4b4be9e0-1f98-4bba-90a3-fdffb50e9f60}}  is left {{formula:e41e9d03-dc0a-4bb3-ba55-be8b1e07b23c}} -projective), we also have an isomorphism {{formula:cf38ed11-496a-4702-9a80-32f8fddbb4d6}}  in {{formula:5ba5112c-03b5-4727-892b-aa2c15ec7b32}} . The second term is canonically isomorphic to the {{formula:b2ba3489-a50e-47ba-bcac-39a8a5e482bf}} -sub-bimodule of {{formula:8239d0dd-c592-481d-b56e-323c9fb353c7}}  generated by the central idempotent {{formula:661b0624-4510-473f-b67b-b8769a4847c1}} ; there is an obvious {{formula:589ca700-fa65-46d7-b09b-b4ed40d95251}} -bimodule isomorphism of {{formula:7a7c59ae-ee58-4714-9ea3-7334b4359c22}}  onto this bimodule, sending 1 to {{formula:c44ed92a-4107-4584-bde2-4dcfa80b36c9}} .

We are now ready to prove the theorem.

Since {{formula:9bdcd106-1114-466d-8747-eaacd0ce4802}}  is a complete, cocomplete category with a zero object, points (a) and (c) of Lemma REF  show that {{formula:93a96c93-3f0a-4cf7-b5e1-4fd0031741c9}}  is Frobenius if and only if (i) its set of connected components {{formula:581dbed9-a74c-436a-94c1-1254961fc34d}}  is Frobenius, and (ii) each connected component is Frobenius. Hence the problem breaks up into the discrete and the connected case.
Proposition REF  says that the component set is {{formula:ab2ba4df-7c30-4dce-9b7d-02018eb12da8}} -Frobenius if and only if it is finite. In the connected case we can apply the results in Section . Theorem REF  and Proposition REF  together imply that a connected category is {{formula:4b4dbc8b-3efc-4c0f-a9fd-61fff0438ee3}} -Frobenius if and only if it has an IS such that the group {{formula:1cd26301-6aa3-4075-92c6-9e9d450a9828}}  is {{formula:5f8f9c7d-72b9-4a3a-a6ce-887a0c99ed9c}} -Frobenius. Finally, apply Proposition REF  to finish the proof.

The problem posed here, of finding the {{formula:a8b5ac97-dff1-4cc2-b0c2-f5e787d40771}} -Frobenius categories {{formula:0a62218f-0189-4769-b278-21eccb28f816}}  for a fixed complete and cocomplete {{formula:1596f06c-c267-4ddf-aae1-2d0773748ed8}} , has variations which would make interesting topics for further inquiry. We give only a few examples.

For one thing, we would like to extend the results obtained in this paper to various categories (or perhaps large classes of categories) which were not covered here. One conspicuous example is that of the category of (left or right) comodules over some {{formula:2e3b716f-c7fb-4e30-ae14-ffe87e9113b8}} -coring {{formula:b6de5c2e-4773-47e2-9d07-e5aed9c366bf}} . This would cover the case of {{formula:64390ed2-b565-4b35-a85a-4c4bbe8fa545}} -modules, since these are the simply the comodules over the Sweedler coring {{formula:05d3306a-e97f-442a-a903-de6c290dbfd5}}  over {{formula:762af405-bd50-42f0-8853-25698e5a9709}}  ({{cite:364429b530fddf8141cb4b3e31dfb203fa1c4679}}). Choose right comodules, in order to fix the notation. Because we want the category {{formula:c49faa32-68e8-4b8c-8e7f-9d4fa7f5ac23}}  of right comodules to be complete and cocomplete, we impose the condition that {{formula:2718c18f-7355-4b49-bfb3-cf64424aa4fa}}  be flat (see {{cite:364429b530fddf8141cb4b3e31dfb203fa1c4679}}).

Problem 11

Given a ring {{formula:397d08c6-802f-45c1-814c-37b09e41878b}}  and an {{formula:7d45cbaf-d139-41fe-bbd9-b834322ee07d}} -coring {{formula:f3df7425-869a-4dc4-a164-c4869266518e}}  which is flat as a left {{formula:3f3639f5-d20a-4bae-be65-898f3e54ccf5}} -module, find the {{formula:61bf34b1-67ed-4e58-a362-bcd63ce22b32}} -Frobenius small categories {{formula:4efdebd9-e1af-4496-bb59-ba6c6166854e}} .

Even within the realm of admissible categories, treated here, the results we have proven give rise to some interesting questions. For example, Theorem REF  and Proposition REF  together reduce the problem of finding the connected {{formula:9f515a1c-e267-4f58-a2bd-3fdc9e9cd024}} -Frobenius categories to that of finding the {{formula:26c35b15-40cf-4c88-a7c9-75cf234dac02}} -Frobenius finite groups, whenever {{formula:eccd352b-890a-4ad6-90e9-f469d5f19583}}  is admissible. We have already seen two classes of groups arising as the class of {{formula:0bb2686a-55c7-4b36-8207-1ecfab1dff46}} -Frobenius finite groups for various {{formula:8a334da3-ee7d-4185-9cb4-dc062a16ca28}} : the trivial group if {{formula:2fb15f4e-7b84-4d87-bc3f-1f1449908377}} , and the finite groups whose cardinality is invertible in {{formula:f14ed820-269f-4b66-9fe8-d59951f77d01}}  for {{formula:41f0b278-01fc-48d8-99ee-49722f1dee32}} . Can all such classes of finite groups be described?

Problem 22

Which classes of finite groups arise as the class of {{formula:11782a3e-0461-46d0-96a9-0a1dc9f4d234}} -Frobenius finite groups for some admissible category {{formula:b800890b-7a00-4b17-bb2a-8744b5f53960}} ?

We can turn this question around, and ask for a characterization of those admissible categories {{formula:c096ef23-0346-402b-b499-aad774e9bcf4}}  having the property that the only {{formula:a5eded81-6854-4df9-a722-607d0edc1b00}} -Frobenius finite group is the trivial group. We have already seen in Theorem REF  that {{formula:ffb3f07c-0b15-4a65-b04b-35a0e10639a0}}  is such a category. Although we do not prove this here, it is not difficult to see that {{formula:24207dd9-fbdf-4d12-8b19-5f0f80e30e9f}} , the category of groups, is another example. Note that Grp is a variety of algebras, so it is indeed admissible.

Problem 33

Find simple necessary and sufficient (or, alternatively, only sufficient) conditions on an admissible category {{formula:86a12125-feec-462f-8cd4-64fe93ef0a16}}  in order that the only {{formula:1841ebcd-b7e9-4ae6-93cd-f7943fae3a9e}} -Frobenius finite group be the trivial group.

The author wishes to thank Professor Gigel Militaru, who posed the problem and suggested this line of inquiry, for the insight gained through countless discussions on the topic, as well as the referee for valuable suggestions on how to revise an initial version of this paper.

Noise in calorimeter readout electronics has been treated in some
detail {{cite:4474ec580b81b7b5cec209bd6af4ca4658a1f387}}, {{cite:37394b5e876539d508805adc26c6e368e82005b6}}, {{cite:e4a256971c5928aed1762685fd2fcf17ec9575b9}}.
However, since each author builds the details of
their particular situation into their analysis, it is worthwhile
to review the subject in light of our own experiment. Most
previous studies assume that a single measurement will be made
at a well determined time. Furthermore they assume that filtering
preceding the digitization is limited to relatively simple
analog devices. Since we have chosen to solve our lack of
knowledge of the event time by recording periodic samples,
applying digital signal processing techniques is natural.
This also raises questions about the required sampling rate
and the quantization error that don't occur in the
usual scheme.

Electronics noise and filters are usually analyzed using
Fourier transforms {{cite:772159a2b317e3995a82a34164c7f5c3b07acaa3}}, {{cite:7ee370cb39a793424886e24c77577953c598aaeb}}, {{cite:0b864466fb791c0480ec5b9dcdb588eca37b91bf}}.
In the frequency domain, filtering, differentiation,
integration, and time shifting are all represented by
multiplications. Stochastic noise is most easily
represented by its power spectral density (which is the
Fourier transform of the more complicated auto-correlation function in
the time domain). Many questions such as the signal to noise
ratio for particular parameters and filter design can be
handled entirely in the frequency domain.

Figure REF  shows a simplified version of the calorimeter
input circuitry. Figure REF  shows a noise equivalent
representation of the same circuit. The right hand portion represents
the input FET. This is one of many possible equivalent representations
{{cite:d10d1dcfe7b4aaefbf5365e9ad30c1afd3ac0bec}}{{cite:772159a2b317e3995a82a34164c7f5c3b07acaa3}}.
This particular one has a relatively
simple connection between the physical processes which generate
noise and the elements of the representation. The spectral densities
of the noise generators will correspond to the those given in
manufacturers specification sheets.

{{formula:03eebf5e-2fb2-460b-b78a-954a5ff4d40d}}  is a current generator corresponding to the signal generated by
the interactions in the calorimeter. It will be represented by the
function:

Heaviside unit step function.

The Fourier transform of {{formula:24a25dd6-43f6-4c54-9a7a-8202ce4ce6ea}}  is

by the leakage current in the photodiode. This has a “white”
(independent of {{formula:86a1038c-d21d-4485-b646-e2259681dcbd}} ) spectrum with the value

Since we average two diodes we can use the equivalent

A photodiode with these properties is the 1N2744.

As much as possible, the discussion will be restricted to the
electronic regime. However, some effects depend on the efficiency
of the conversion of calorimeter shower energy into charge.
When this number is required, I will use the value of
3000 photo-electrons per MeV in each diode.

a few picofarads to tens of picofarads depending on the choice of FET.
We will return to this choice later.
In the circuit it functions in parallel with {{formula:65ec806f-8b41-4440-97d6-1ab063729317}} .
Not shown in the figure since they are much less than {{formula:dacf6009-f637-47ef-ab6e-6e8f900b6185}}  are

I will call the sum {{formula:cb3b4f32-367f-4f01-9209-b10c23664f78}}  simply {{formula:43ffd6de-9980-4734-920b-2fe78d80da69}} .

{{formula:7e565b79-4897-4123-915e-641da83bf2d9}}  is a noise generator corresponding the input current noise
of the FET. It is primarily due to the gate leakage current,
although for very large gate areas the effect the thermal noise
of the real part of the input impedance should be checked.
The shot noise acts just like the diode shot noise and the two
leakage currents may be added. In practice the FET gate
leakage current is of the order of picoamperes and is negligible
compared to the diode leakage current. Let

{{formula:ccefe010-2b87-499b-99b1-78a710c566df}}  is a voltage noise generator representing the input voltage
noise of the FET. This is primarily due the thermal noise
in the FET channel. Many authors put a formula,
which shows the dependence of this noise
on the temperature and the forward transconductance, into
their equations {{cite:d10d1dcfe7b4aaefbf5365e9ad30c1afd3ac0bec}}. I prefer to keep {{formula:d06d2ab7-9056-4a60-8af5-a039cc9d3c35}}  as an
explicit term.
The value of {{formula:629477b1-f631-4e69-9c8d-039e0782980f}}  is usually given on specification sheets and is
also easy to measure.
For junction FETs, {{formula:984289c3-5cba-4a0e-a00f-cd324e45db63}}  is approximately independent of
frequency over the range of interest to us. Typical
values are 1 to 2{{formula:858b3e6a-4043-4d0a-847c-04a5fad43527}} /{{formula:9879c52c-4bfe-4efb-a191-018b59442564}} .

In order to be more specific I'll take as an example the SANYO
2SK932 JFET.
{{formula:7ac68b30-442b-42e4-97cf-a9b12447f303}}  is 20{{formula:d7fd3ae5-8d98-4f86-9bb8-e43086242e94}}  and {{formula:5602889b-94bd-433e-a386-39cd04452ffe}}  is {{formula:90b46bad-4b3b-4a01-bd64-968238b6655a}} .
Because
we average the outputs two diode-FET-preamp
combinations on each crystal, we divide
by {{formula:cc4eef99-113a-44c1-a9e0-f8d10d2f391b}}  to get 0.5{{formula:e4a6613b-23d8-4d66-9808-8a7f263a576d}} /{{formula:975598d5-b9bf-4203-879b-4d631374041a}} .
This is a good FET but not optimally matched to
our problem. We'll return to this issue after we have developed
the signal to noise formulas.
{{figure:8fceb7d5-b6d4-4919-8e38-188e9c248dab}}

{{formula:e8ba4d72-f1d9-4ef5-88e7-7890742fc57d}}  is a current noise generator representing the sea of photons
generated by particles lost from the beam. This noise resembles
shot noise in that near impulsive elements arrive at random times.
It differs in that the pulse shape is not a delta function but has
the shape of the signal and there is a distribution of pulse areas
instead of just the electron charge.In radar theory, noise
with these properties is called “clutter.”
If we return to the
derivation of the shot noise formula {{cite:772159a2b317e3995a82a34164c7f5c3b07acaa3}},
we see that
the first difference can be treated by giving this noise the
power spectrum of the signal (the Fourier transform of each pulse
is the same as that of the signal
except for phase and magnitude). The second is handled by noting
that the shot noise formula is really a pulse area squared times
a rate: {{formula:b4ca10f9-596a-45c4-8134-06cdc00e129b}} . {{formula:8fd06c91-34af-4779-98fc-b5b6b98366aa}}  is the size of the pulse and
{{formula:b338c7d6-35d7-4498-a010-d0279da3f769}}  is the mean rate of their occurrence. Therefore we can
get the low frequency limit of the noise spectral density of the
background by doing the integral:
{{formula:5f07950d-4a6f-4529-8652-d838b3ea642e}}

where {{formula:3337ed42-ca6b-49bc-bb4a-6ba5438d05fa}}  is the rate of background events per pulse area interval
per time interval. The value of this integral can be
inferred from the statistics of histograms such as those
in B A B AR Technical Design Report Figure 12-9 {{cite:de804d3291f646f8c67793ee8a7c0c0195fd67dc}}.
Here I use more recent calculations of the background {{cite:a0a10dc757e8fa0fb5652c6aa1868ebe46a14c7c}}.
Assuming {{formula:660bb670-487b-4eb4-bd0c-d8a116d191b2}} , the result for an average crystal
is {{formula:9b3b95dd-2b1a-4e18-9cee-a9117443ea28}}  at nominal background.

For convenience
I'll use the symbol {{formula:53691b2e-d60a-4c72-bc2e-e475dcd5f6f7}}  to represent this low frequency limit
and put the frequency dependence into the formulas explicitly.
Since {{formula:73b3c13b-a12c-4c44-a677-6b98187d17e3}}  and {{formula:b2bd25bf-0c68-44b4-9fd0-09d9be5b3322}}  are approximately independent of frequency,
I can then treat {{formula:fea12b7c-0967-405d-8483-381ade552c13}} , {{formula:3518ee12-202b-4c93-8e39-cd633eed818e}} , and {{formula:a97da4d5-f88c-45c7-bb4f-dc735c2a4117}}  as constants.

Note that individual crystals can differ from the average by factors as
large as 4. In particular, compared an average barrel crystal,
an average endcap crystal has {{formula:74537aac-3a61-4401-91d1-bd93fe2c5025}} th the hit rate,
twice the average energy deposit, and an {{formula:8d43bda6-05b4-4e3c-8ffd-3b280df37c2f}}  twice as large.

Figure REF  summarizes all the noise sources.

The treatment of background as noise is a good description if the
background signal after all processing contains significant contributions
from many background events. If this is not the case, the data
may fall into two classes, those showers little affected by background, and
those with a large background contribution. The former will have
a distribution of measured values consistent with electronic noise,
while the latter may have a wider, highly skewed distribution.
While the background as noise treatment may give a near optimal
procedure for minimizing the rms error, it will widen the
distribution for that class events unaffected by background.
Depending on the physics objective, treating the background
affected events as an inefficiency rather than events with
errors may give the better result.

How well does our case satisfy this many hit condition?
In the background calculation in the preceding paragraph, an average
crystal had {{formula:cd216689-56fb-4169-abe2-4fa562943811}} . Assuming a window of {{formula:4c4d288d-b0b0-40ac-8d9c-9ffb3d088681}}  and
a sum of 25 crystals, this implies 5.5 background hits contributing to the
measurement during nominal conditions. This is enough to give reasonably

With the same assumptions about filtering

requirements on the quantization error. We assume there is a low

Under such conditions, quantization error may be referred back to the
input where it appears as another current noise source.

The treatment of background as noise is a good description if the
background signal after all processing contains significant contributions
from many background events. If this is not the case, the data
may fall into two classes, those showers little affected by background, and
those with a large background contribution. The former will have
a distribution of measured values consistent with electronic noise,
while the latter may have a wider, highly skewed distribution.
While the background as noise treatment may give a near optimal
procedure for minimizing the rms error, it will widen the
distribution for that class events unaffected by background.
Depending on the physics objective, treating the background
affected events as an inefficiency rather than events with
errors may give the better result.

How well does our case satisfy this many hit condition?
In the background calculation in the preceding paragraph, an average
crystal had {{formula:cd216689-56fb-4169-abe2-4fa562943811}} . Assuming a window of {{formula:4c4d288d-b0b0-40ac-8d9c-9ffb3d088681}}  and
a sum of 25 crystals, this implies 5.5 background hits contributing to the
measurement during nominal conditions. This is enough to give reasonably
Guassian behavior. However, much of {{formula:1b561ddc-319d-4c72-b625-94dde8d01467}}  is generated by the high
energy tail of the background distribution. If we count down from high
energies until get a mean number of hits of at least 2, the cut would
be in the vicinity of {{formula:b0238708-e3f0-4234-9bc6-9b351cf4fcea}} . At 10 times nominal this cut would be
close to {{formula:d4168fa5-f2cf-40d9-9068-5532beb0c96d}} .

Another consideration is that an approach which
tries to separate a background tail from other noise
is hardly likely to succeed if the magnitude of the background
contribution is of the same size as other errors. The size of the
intrinsic error depends on the size of the signal. For a {{formula:824d946e-6d07-4415-b269-dc2d07f959e0}} 
shower the expected error is {{formula:9cf4abea-f45b-4b5e-965e-e07ce8e3f358}} .
Assuming that background contributions
must be at least {{formula:11977ccf-cdd3-426e-949f-bdeaf969060d}}  before they can be separated from
noise seems conservative.

If only background hits with energies below {{formula:b9446a29-3091-4024-b0ba-98b5ca6d11e8}}  are included,
{{formula:7c907d2f-6b2b-4f44-bf05-0383079d495f}}  falls to {{formula:e6940fbd-b33e-4fba-af3a-af514491dfa9}} .
