Analytic cross sections for processes can be produced by CompHEP{{cite:9a855f67dd39ceedc7ca0828fbd6a92d72185bc0}}.

These review studies have
led to an appreciation of uncertainties in the parton distribution functions, uncertainties about the correct {{formula:f8d97148-534b-4641-8fa9-d314630e25d5}}  to useRef {{cite:ea40f4daf3ed6338906708699e20ed24b80e9d9f}} suggests using {{formula:6850790a-34a8-4f18-b10c-2f41035e8cde}}  or whatever energy scale is relevant to the particles being produced., and uncertainties in the process of hadronization of the outgoing partons. All these uncertainties contribute to significant uncertainties in the background of which new physics must be discovered, and to uncertainties underling model-dependent, cross-section-dependent determinations of particle masses.

Particle detectors have finite capabilities which limit what we can learn.
We will discuss the effects of finite energy resolution later in this thesis.
Here I focus on the lack of the traditional tracks one sees in event representations.

The early history of particle physics shows beautiful
bubble chamber tracks of particles.
Studies of Pions and Kaons relied on tracks left in bubble chambers or modern digitized detectors. In the case of the {{formula:89c77b12-9187-4921-89b9-fafab65e3c5c}}  the lifetime is {{formula:8a08c85f-7ced-4044-b60f-9e4b7c5460ad}}  seconds or {{formula:b5cabfb3-2e4c-4d01-a544-5b0d1ff71d63}}  cm, or equivalently the decay width is {{formula:832444b2-140a-4f60-897f-5a8613d444b3}}  eV.
A particle with a width of {{formula:04ceccef-5e0e-4b11-88e2-fbb061c46304}}  eV has a lifetime of {{formula:c096262e-b740-409b-bec0-ec028c61bc35}}  seconds with {{formula:120f48ec-4b44-4e28-b465-8ea0f65f30fd}} .
The more massive known states of {{formula:5821b921-0ee4-446e-8c4a-8465b2308756}} , {{formula:88566da0-2bb6-449b-9b95-3cb68a9a6695}}  bosons and the top quark have widths of {{formula:77e47a5d-e5a6-480f-add6-89b2e5d9f85a}} , {{formula:f06de28d-1195-4003-ab04-0f6ee3cfb50f}} , and {{formula:d2e296e1-002d-4b90-9fff-a9633a5168d0}} .
These decay widths give these states tracks with {{formula:687d7b7f-f542-409c-9cbf-87dcc510f41a}}  fm or about {{formula:ce2868c8-10da-42b3-a9f6-19f9cfc5b9f4}}  the size of an atomic nuclei.

Most supersymmetric states, depending on the model, have decay widths between around 1 MeV and 2 GeV This is not a universal statement. Some viable models have long lived charged states ({{formula:5a456559-b919-4d4c-8955-a9bab4ce2931}}  cm) {{cite:b073ba1b1bdf636a55a38abb52d1b73e7dd28c2f}}, {{cite:0395db6b958f4b7f3f714a2f744a0523e4c9c495}}, {{cite:9dd3791f88b80a0468e193a1263637ec0baa0c35}}..
These observations, while trivial, make us realize that new physics discoveries will most likely need to deduce properties of the new states from their decay products only.
The fact that all events effectively occur at the origin creates combinatoric problems because we cannot know the order in which the visible particles came off of a decay chain or even to which decay chain they belong.

We now turn to existent tools to overcome the challenges inherent in
mass determination at hadron colliders in the presence of missing transverse momentum.

Lorentz invariant distributions are optimal for making a distribution independent of the unknown frame of reference.
Fig REF  shows a two-body decay and a three-body decay.
{{figure:06d2e7d7-ca94-4703-8c8f-4cd7ceb84364}}

The decay products from {{formula:bbaddf6d-41e5-45c9-b700-947ba5de6d92}}  in both cases involve a dark-matter particle {{formula:2212a6be-684b-45a7-9ef2-ddac184b1768}}  and two visible states with 4-momenta {{formula:91955203-2d07-480f-8511-f3e37f89f421}}  and {{formula:9c8fc0cd-03c6-49ad-ab41-e384bc783d24}} ; we will abbreviate {{formula:ee62f1e4-194f-4a1a-9f03-c1ca6825cc57}} . The Lorentz invariant mass of these two visible states is defined as
{{formula:0a23ea03-965b-4d4d-ad03-332bf5d57e4a}}

Assuming no spin correlation between {{formula:ec1adbe0-21d2-4815-873c-eebb2aeecf3e}}  and {{formula:63b8bfa5-54f7-47a8-b235-fd95d7a40a87}} , the distribution for the two-body decay looks more like a right-triangle whereas the three-body decay case looks softer.
Spin correlations between these states may change the shape and might be used to measure spin in some cases {{cite:efec5ddf94f0bdec55708af01481afd510ae5a2f}}.
The distribution shape can also be affected by competing processes in the three-body decay.
For example, the degree of interference with the slepton can push the peak to a smaller value{{cite:25ceb846af33346facdc6462bdb84b26da9b95b0}}.

The end-point of the distribution gives information about the masses of the new particle states.
In the two-body decay case the endpoint gives
{{formula:c29f95c7-e6da-4c91-9775-55db790c095d}}

and in the three-body decay case
{{formula:9f1a2de8-ceae-4674-ba8c-1602064cd12e}}

These edges in invariant mass combinations provide information about mass differences or mass squared differences but not about the mass-scale itself.
Measuring these edges requires some model of the events creating the distribution in order to simulate the effect of the detectors energy resolution.
For this reason, even end-point techniques,
although mostly model-independent, still require some
estimate of the distribution near the end point to get an accurate end-point measurement.
Radiative corrections also
play a role in shifting this endpoint slightly{{cite:cd7371d7359b8fa6572e6edfbb6d70c1d3e26249}}.

These techniques have been studied to select a model if one assumes a particular set of starting models {{cite:daffdd5c8091b7d5300a69f3d582fa1dc5dd782c}}. They have also been used with Bayesian techniques to measure the mass difference between slepton states {{cite:339caa809922c8321cb9ba4beccb3cfb07f2ba33}}.

If there are many new particle states produced at the collider,
then we can use edges from cascade decays between these new states
to provide constraints between the masses.
Given some luck regarding the relative masses, these constraints may be inverted to obtain the mass scale.
Fig REF  shows a cascade decay from {{formula:a0841186-e5fa-4cee-83ec-1d4d28832582}}  to {{formula:dc59a4d5-5aa4-4dba-a197-293127f277fc}}  to {{formula:952477a1-da4e-4be8-a552-b2d8c1a12811}}  ending in {{formula:bd07f53e-2b89-41a7-9906-a553c263220b}}  and visible particle momenta {{formula:9c903523-b3ed-4407-ace4-1d84238f6ed3}} , {{formula:cceff3dd-e9c6-4f89-8537-f3e16a9de316}} , {{formula:b299956e-a0a6-4485-8a82-c9de3f59e768}} .

There are four unknown masses and potentially four linearly-independent endpoints.
In addition to Eq(REF ), we also have {{cite:246dca572ed9397ab75135146dea46d67573c99d}}, {{cite:daffdd5c8091b7d5300a69f3d582fa1dc5dd782c}}
{{formula:55f5f77a-fc5f-43aa-9ded-e7b7b8c4407a}}

and
{{formula:eb330ce1-884a-468e-b4d6-b082f54cc653}}

The fourth endpoint is
{{formula:c64bbbc7-e9df-451f-ab9d-1dad41da6d02}}

Depending on whether we can distinguish
visible particles 1, 2 and 3 from each other,
some of these endpoints may be obscured by combinatorics problems.
If the visible particles and the masses are such that these four can be disentangled from combinatoric problems, and if the masses are such that these four end-points provide independent constraints, and if there is sufficient statistics to measure the endpoints well-enough, then we can solve for the mass spectrum.
{{figure:12f61df7-e990-4bf7-801a-35660dabc56d}}

This technique has been studied in {{cite:deb6d46c125cbd88b5481273fcb3937f08abd962}}, {{cite:246dca572ed9397ab75135146dea46d67573c99d}}, {{cite:daffdd5c8091b7d5300a69f3d582fa1dc5dd782c}}
and subsequently by many others. In some cases, there is more than one solution to
the equations. This degeneracy can be lifted by using the
shape of these distributions {{cite:1262575081b628e94f7cf7c411cf5ddc62d32fa6}}, {{cite:17db4dffa8f5fd4588f62d3a4c6baa0681fdb2e7}}, {{cite:c45b33e2ad0c675811bdfd2128993beb18670d84}}.
Using the Supersymmetric benchmark point SPS 1a,
this technique has been shown to determine the LSP mass to {{formula:ffd9c784-b499-4276-b59f-98109f00d41b}}  with about 500 thousand events from {{formula:4ad8d72b-a4a7-4495-8185-4e6c0379620d}} .
They are able to determine the mass difference to {{formula:e7385e7e-25e9-4d59-8309-4a8fa86a7049}}  and {{formula:c768dee3-245d-4354-adf9-23198144e6ce}}  {{cite:1262575081b628e94f7cf7c411cf5ddc62d32fa6}}.

What if there are not as many new-states accessible at the collider, or what if the masses arrange themselves to not enable a solution to the four invariant mass edges listed above?
There is also a series of approaches called Mass Shell Techniques (MST)The title MST is suggested in Ref. {{cite:888980905ddb0c201c30db26c521e1a691504984}}. where assumption are used about the topology and
on-shell conditions to solve for the unknown masses.
{{figure:135ed2ee-75b3-42a2-b6f0-930a637f0a49}}

An MST was used in the early 1990s by Goldstein, Dalitz (GD) {{cite:0d0a890959fe5130dc31d5b42015898f23ab7d45}}, and Kondo, Chikamatsu, Kim (KCK){{cite:e43ee0e28c2e94d1a77726eac16d5de674134f0d}} as a suggested method to measure the mass of the top quark.
The top-quark pair production and decay has the topology
shown in Fig {{formula:29c14824-7879-4bca-94ee-69e2bcf868e1}} .
Here {{formula:c951c1e6-7953-4076-98ff-9a3dfc8f363f}}  or {{formula:2feada92-c9b3-4083-91d3-3562a5ef1d58}} , {{formula:00e1e4f0-9fec-442f-97e9-bd336e6bc196}} , {{formula:e2f20d36-c0fa-4f27-8bd5-70845611b95e}} , {{formula:cffa889d-491b-4041-a5a3-5e8bc9bd1be9}}  and {{formula:c6860c9a-318f-4e7a-8168-dd858af8dc6a}} .
In each event, one measures {{formula:f5636069-0ca4-47c9-83e6-bf585d9f93bc}} , {{formula:5edb8ed0-f31b-4fe0-a6dc-cdc3b8f3361c}} , and the
missing transverse momentum {{formula:49ebce82-8478-4ed7-8f61-3c1ce71c36fa}} .
The resulting mass shell and missing momentum equations are
{{formula:caf5bd17-7070-4ad7-8225-b1f91403a285}}

If we assume a mass for {{formula:ab629965-3c67-450f-af20-f31ebea0ae52}} , then we have 8 unknowns
(the four components of each {{formula:2c022d1c-e6b6-470d-916e-c4aab8e3efb3}}  and {{formula:7a72f303-f6c3-41a2-800c-9b6c64aa1061}} ) and

to the intersection of two ellipses which have between zero
and four distinct solutions.
In GD and KCK, they supplemented these solutions with some data from the
cross section and used Bayes' theorem to create a likelihood function

The approach has a systematic bias {{cite:deca71f35335f8f4682f5e4c3227ff30b8e7e125}}{{cite:bb8465bb11a9612adedbe43748871001ad34739c}} that must be removed by modeling {{cite:daae44da8d33d5be984a18e832e487a301ee1259}}Details of this bias are discussed more in Section  REF.

A modern reinvention of this MST is found in Cheng, Gunion, Han, Marandella and McElrath (CHGMM) {{cite:6482955dabf1746e5d045b4e8635076adbcc9bab}}
where they assume a
symmetric topology with an on-shell intermediate state
such as in Fig {{formula:b1d315f6-5eac-4de0-af44-12e276a2754c}} . This reinvention assumes {{formula:cbaaddcb-1dfe-4cfb-99a0-5cf03a8b5171}} ,
{{formula:3cd05591-33a4-4e94-a4cf-e8ba55e435a0}}  and {{formula:7d3a1210-9dec-4c90-8061-41ee5df7a71b}} .
CHGMM do a test of each event's compatibility with all values of {{formula:1d9131d7-8df0-4e66-a102-7926ab5a9ed8}} .
Using this approach, they find that with {{formula:89dd7fa3-82c9-46c5-bc90-1079b32e6847}}  of events that they can determine the LSP mass to {{formula:ed1007ae-6b6a-4572-a386-4a8649d5d89a}}  GeV. Unlike GD and KCK, CHGMM make no reference to Bayesian techniques.

Another MST assumes a longer symmetric decay chain and assumes the masses in two events must be equal {{cite:ac9f6f98cbeeb2c6bdf454c493e4c89467cd44c8}}.
This results in enough equations to equal the number of unknowns to solve for the masses directly.
For SPS 1a after {{formula:c3678bf8-ca5c-499b-8d5a-58694dd554d3}} , they reach {{formula:5d4cb099-d551-4f99-a055-e65f5a0e0f73}}  using 700 events satisfying their cuts but have a {{formula:c7322803-f53c-46b7-ba55-7a33b5620d17}}  systematic bias that needs modeling to remove.

Finally there is a suggestion for hybrid MST where one combines on-shell conditions with the information from the many edges in cascade decays {{cite:43f26218b508598253c597e079530d8cce57501f}}. The {{formula:057effc9-2f6c-4459-a294-1ae783886589}}  variable introduced in Chapters  is a simple
example of such a hybrid technique that predated their suggestion.

The invariant mass distributions are Lorentz invariant.
In events with one invisible particle, like the neutrino,
leaving the detector unnoticed, we only know
the neutrino's transverse momentum inferred from the missing transverse momentum.
If a parent particle {{formula:024d7843-ea32-41a3-87dd-b8ea8a53ab64}}  decays into a visible particle with observed 4-momentum {{formula:eb0050d1-d9f0-4648-a8f9-017e6cd2e8eb}}  and an invisible particle {{formula:94d21dd2-b1fd-4b7d-b8be-09d89dd7bb1a}} , then what progress
can be made in mass determination?
There is a class of techniques which, although not Lorentz invariant,
is invariant with respect
to longitudinal boosts along the beam line.
The 4-momentum {{formula:965a4380-e2aa-4397-86ad-f8deab02018b}} 
is cast in new coordinates

From the missing transverse momentum, we can deduce the transverse components {{formula:d7929527-eaed-4200-8251-0ca9f6af78e2}}  and {{formula:dc4cc571-6550-4a42-869c-d310085c79b8}} . If we know the mass of {{formula:ccbe322d-1064-4565-8f9d-4da1af7d2e72}} , we can bound the unknown mass of {{formula:e2273987-e267-4ddd-ba61-c42eab7b0bb4}}  from below by minimizing with respect to the unknown rapidity {{formula:844d6d69-d991-4983-a4a8-8ee1ee28108a}} .

This technique is used to measure the {{formula:ff17eefe-fde2-48ae-89d2-89e9cf6d21b0}}  boson's mass with the identification {{formula:9804cbe8-61e7-434f-a783-efc19ae4a77d}} , {{formula:4569a100-230c-4915-a81b-616552fcad50}} , and {{formula:dfd0175a-0931-497b-b1d0-395aa25b31af}} .

If a hadron collider pair produces dark-matter particles, then there are two sources of missing transverse momentum, each with the same unknown mass. The `stransverse mass' {{formula:ecda2389-5996-4179-a4f7-3a17e19422f7}}  introduced by Lester and Summers {{cite:a7122a793da3b761c0143edf85ffdcd0df4de3f9}}, {{cite:49540485f3ca9c02b43d677a465c7e6460cd4f7f}} adapts the transverse mass {{formula:a39dbad6-5488-4573-a052-d08c784c2aaf}}  to this task.
{{formula:13bf4853-6255-45fa-be44-b3984f2ebd48}}  techniques have become widely used with Refs. {{cite:a7122a793da3b761c0143edf85ffdcd0df4de3f9}}, {{cite:49540485f3ca9c02b43d677a465c7e6460cd4f7f}}
having more than 45 citations.

The stransverse mass is used to determine the mass difference between a parent particle and a dark-matter candidate particle given an assumed mass for the dark-matter candidate based on a topology similar to Figs REF  or REF .
The variable {{formula:a7d38e00-8f64-4c40-8a75-728b304edfa0}}  accepts three inputs: {{formula:21ad13aa-0ad0-4d01-b168-a4343e7864c8}}  (an assumed mass of the two particles carrying away missing transverse momenta),
{{formula:89648290-f005-40d7-b580-a124f3603c75}}  and {{formula:aca5fde1-82d6-47a6-bcf7-2236d5b966bf}}  (the visible momenta of each branch), and {{formula:ffa68016-9559-4050-a869-dbcf9db6b075}} 
(the missing transverse momenta two-vector). We can define {{formula:37c0e658-beba-43eb-a02c-f7b8e9fe2e5c}}  in terms of the transverse mass of each branch where we minimize the maximum of the two transverse masses over the unknown split between {{formula:9980d25f-d454-440f-8abe-5f4ed8f88acb}}  and {{formula:5bed3719-48f5-4ef7-a464-726344295a66}}  of the overall missing transverse momenta:
{{formula:2e7cdd91-5146-4d05-9ee3-bb26d5fc5e19}}

In addition to invariance with respect to longitudinal boosts, {{formula:54b191f8-38a6-485e-8cdd-c892e9e55d1a}} , in the limit where {{formula:fe228c93-cec5-4ea3-a3b0-78f1f0b92d43}} , is also invariant with respect to back-to-back boosts of the parent particle pair in the transverse plane {{cite:d4912d2eadd857397c24bfc31cdb7f7aef332737}}.

In this chapter, we have introduced the need for making mass measurements in a model independent manner of collider-produced dark matter. We have outlined many approaches based on edges of invariant mass distributions, mass shell techniques, and transverse mass techniques. Each technique has distinct domains of validity and requirements. In the remaining chapters of this thesis, we introduce and test new model-independent techniques to determine mass of dark-matter particles.
Which approach turns out to be best is likely to depend on what scenario nature hands us, since the various techniques involve different assumptions. Having different approaches also offers the advantage of providing a system of redundant checks.

In this chapter, we propose an improved method for hadron-collider mass determination of new
states that decay to a massive, long-lived state like the LSP in the MSSM. We
focus on pair-produced new states which undergo three-body decay to a pair of
visible particles and the new invisible long-lived state. Our approach is to
construct a kinematic quantity which enforces all known physical constraints
on the system. The distribution of this quantity calculated for the observed
events has an endpoint that determines the mass of the new states. However we
find it much more efficient to determine the masses by fitting to the entire
distribution and not just the end point. We consider the application of the
method at the LHC for various models under the ideal assumption of effectively
direct production with minimal
ISR and demonstrate that the method can
determine the masses within about 6 GeV using only 250 events. This
implies the method is viable even for relatively rare processes at the LHC
such as neutralino pair production.

This chapter, which is based on
work first published by the author and his supervisor in Ref. {{cite:3f9e8e0fc39ef90f2ee5d224b131e3618627723e}},
concentrates on mass determination involving the
production of only two new states. Our particular concern is to use the
available information as effectively as possible to reduce the number of
events needed to make an accurate determination of {{formula:7dc71c49-3a88-42bc-8025-5f51ce899737}}  and {{formula:19bab1a9-8869-484c-818b-40eb086225f5}} . The
main new ingredient of the method proposed is that it does not rely solely on
the events close to the kinematic boundary but makes use of all the events.
Our method constrains the unobserved energy and momentum such that all the
kinematical constraints of the process are satisfied including the mass

(ii) the angular dependence of the {{formula:7ee6592c-1859-4bf6-af61-6f2ac133619a}} 's momenta in the rest frame of {{formula:3015d512-9b53-49ff-9537-98c9434b1a50}} . In

{{formula:f74b0a76-e01b-405e-8424-d4f20e41ad1a}} , {{formula:3ae4ec5a-e806-4e7c-ae0c-4372ed1eee8a}} 's momentum is distributed

universally true it applies in many cases and hence is a good starting point
for analyzing the efficacy of the method.

Under what conditions is the uniform distribution true? Note that the
{{formula:0a3cf7d4-03cc-4b72-b36a-a2f76c336134}} 's spin is the only property of {{formula:cfd1d478-f7de-423c-b703-37a8cf9d13bd}} 
that can break the rotational symmetry of the decay products. For {{formula:a503254e-d61a-423d-94b2-40b23079bf67}} 's spin to affect the angular distribution there must be a
correlation of the spin with the momentum which requires a parity violating
coupling. Consider first the {{formula:0c4d7697-051b-4c08-883d-021079eaa2f3}}  contribution. Since we are integrating over the
lepton momenta difference{{formula:bb4432a1-5a2b-4c47-be0f-91df679ba8db}}  only depends on the sum of the two OSSF lepton momenta that follow from a decay of {{formula:c268a52d-efeb-4e8f-9c87-4f082dc7236a}} ., the parity violating term in the cross section coming from the
lepton-{{formula:9caf36ed-fe79-4e0b-b6ab-6d3b23f2fac3}}  vertex vanishes and a non-zero correlation requires that the parity
violating coupling be associated with the neutralino vertex. The {{formula:c64e38e4-a4cf-4a9f-8e68-e303f5bbadd6}} -boson
neutralino vertex vanishes as the {{formula:9dc327e3-7eea-42ac-b73f-a8ef08abeb69}}  interaction is proportional to
{{formula:df7c74d2-8c6b-404c-8c4b-7855697202d1}}  or {{formula:f938285e-1a2c-4a77-bf72-7ae79da8f8a8}}  depending on the relative sign of {{formula:d9e36699-01e1-496b-a74b-5580ae814dbd}} 
and {{formula:582b2463-8be5-4f1a-a8dc-fafee5896f79}}  eigenvalues. However if the decay has a
significant contribution from an intermediate slepton there are parity
violating couplings and there will be spin correlations. In this case there
will be angular correlations but it is straightforward to modify the method to

How big an effect could spin correlations
have on the shape of the {{formula:932e02d5-b0ff-4f73-a2a6-6481b04623ec}}  distribution?
To demonstrate, we modeled a maximally spin-correlated direct production process.
Fig REF  show the spin-correlated process that we consider, and the {{formula:a277388b-5611-4e6c-915d-f40108e19556}}  distributions from this process compared to the {{formula:9fb37b3b-c9d7-4370-982c-b9dd68d348a2}}  distribution from the same topology and masses but without spin correlations. The modeled case has perfect energy resolution, {{formula:4835f2db-c246-49be-adca-a3b1f431dddf}}  GeV, {{formula:0c6dc78d-caed-42a5-b90c-240c32aee280}}  GeV, and {{formula:a502306a-9f0b-4065-9678-1fa7bb9f57ba}}  GeV. Our maximally spin-correlated process involves pair production of {{formula:b690329f-9ac6-44ef-8cae-f8c1a9ce27c3}}  through a pseudoscalar {{formula:310b1248-7306-40b5-b055-855a1d83d931}} . The fermion {{formula:23d73ddc-02c8-4730-abf3-1fc28f60c2ae}}  in both branches decays to a complex scalar {{formula:33e67409-6977-441e-97c4-2dd21a5a232d}}  and visible fermion {{formula:506912ce-58e6-4fbe-96c3-faa29db4ebc3}}  through a purely chiral interaction.
The production of the pseudoscalar ensures that the {{formula:a41265d4-0453-446a-809d-624ba3d45984}}  and {{formula:c20c3ff5-76de-4e5c-b921-86b2b08f7a1a}}  are in a configuration {{formula:bb2c8446-5c5f-4b13-bbfe-405237392f7b}} .
The {{formula:da126b67-d372-4c44-94df-67bc5b158843}}  then decays with {{formula:c3724bc3-eabe-4f0a-867d-60204f3ad89b}}  preferentially aligned with the spin.
The {{formula:e27a61a6-6c6c-4590-a148-b6b7e7b4fbf5}}  decays with {{formula:4c61a291-f3e1-42a7-9259-0c0a705bf7a8}}  preferentially aligned against the spin.
This causes the two sources of missing transverse momentum to be preferentially parallel
and pushes {{formula:baaa3a53-6a54-4e58-99ad-c5f2f58b1d6f}}  closer to the endpoint.
For this reason the spin-correlated distribution (red dotted distribution) is above the uncorrelated distribution (solid thick distribution) in Fig. REF .
For the remainder of the chapter we assume no such spin correlations are present as is true for neutralino pair production and decay to leptons through a {{formula:e88127dc-e902-44c4-8c53-344bd2a0df78}}  boson.

We have proposed a method to extract the masses of new pair-produced states
based on a kinematic variable, {{formula:ef9aecf2-238c-44f5-b326-ce341701e4d0}} , which incorporates all the known
kinematic constraints on the observed process and whose endpoint determines
the new particle masses.
However the method does not rely solely on the
endpoint but uses the full data set, comparing the observed distribution for
{{formula:a52130a5-6bf3-4064-ae95-03866be7dcaa}}  with the ideal distribution that corresponds to a given mass. As a
result the number of events needed to determine the masses is very
significantly reduced so that the method may be employed at the LHC event for
processes with electroweak production cross sections.

This chapter is an initial feasibility study of the method for several
supersymmetric models.
We have made many idealized assumptions which amount to conditions present if the new particle states are directly produced.
We have included the effect of detector resolution but not
backgrounds, or cuts. Our modeling assumed that {{formula:6ffb2be4-109c-48c1-a490-4a615fcf2f00}} .
We demonstrated that for
some of the models studied we are able to determine the masses to within 6 GeV
from only 250 events.
This efficiency is encouraging,
a study
including more of the real-world complications follows in Chapter .

The constrained mass variables we advocate here can be readily extended to other processes.
By incorporating all the known kinematical constraints, the information away from
kinematical end-points can, with some mild process-dependent information, be
used to reduce the number of events needed to get mass measurements. We shall
illustrate an extension to three on-shell states in Chapter .

In the previous chapter, we introduced the {{formula:d151efa9-3db6-4ef7-beea-61233432b147}}  kinematic variable which gives an event-by-event lower
bound on the dark-matter particle's absolute mass given the mass difference between the dark matter candidate and its parent. The previous chapter focused on direct pair production with minimal initial state radiation (ISR).
In this chapter, we introduce a complementary variable {{formula:f91f1e2e-bbfe-4676-aa20-56b02f456282}}  which gives an event-by-event upper bound on the same absolute mass.
The complementary variable is only relevant in the presence of large upstream transverse momentum (UTM).
Our study shows that the technique presented is as good if not better than other model-independent invisible-particle mass determination techniques in precision and accuracy.

In this chapter, which is based on work first published by Barr, Ross, and the author in Ref {{cite:302025c7c429f6072bf6a564288b609c0d793b09}}, we demonstrate the use of the variable {{formula:0f9cf0fa-7803-4d0b-b4cf-2a13051c832b}}  and {{formula:6e16f051-a8f6-4272-86bd-325bf0fc1d9c}}  in LHC conditions.
The variables {{formula:507a74e0-9377-41b5-8134-afda0417de6a}}  and {{formula:ccad30b7-3f58-4b9c-a080-106d3740ce28}}  give an event-by-event lower-bound and upper-bound respectively on the mass of {{formula:fe192296-a24e-4246-94a6-f4bd53703922}}  assuming the topology in Fig. REF  and the mass difference {{formula:1883940e-be02-447e-aa10-3098b968d1be}} . To get the mass difference, we use events where {{formula:5f33f058-86b6-4a7e-a98d-b2df886571c0}}  decays into {{formula:80cb9286-8c5d-49c0-b0aa-f8a5f26198c3}}  and two visible states
via a three-body decay
in which we can easily determine the mass difference from the end point of the visible-states
invariant-mass distribution, {{formula:822b9e49-444f-4120-9b4e-89ea311724df}} .
One might also conceive of a situation with {{formula:43b7d736-8f21-48d8-9085-f774763846e9}}  supplementing an alternative technique that gives a tight constraint on the mass difference but may have multiple solutions or a weaker constraint on the mass scale {{cite:1262575081b628e94f7cf7c411cf5ddc62d32fa6}}{{cite:a93a9d1165bd6371a3cd21375d4bb4559d16f891}}.
Given this mass difference and enough statistics, {{formula:7fc8e7c6-2d3f-40f7-a95b-bf7bb947bdf0}} 's endpoint gives the mass of {{formula:9b1e6860-0689-4298-a89c-1db2cd80f908}} .
However the main advantage of the {{formula:91b298cc-d964-4944-9d5d-c98a4aa68b34}}  method is that it does not rely simply on the position at the endpoint but it uses the additional information contained in events which lie far from the endpoint. As a result it gives a mass determination using significantly fewer events and is less sensitive to energy resolution and other errors.

To illustrate the method, in this chapter we study in detail the performance of the {{formula:92b82aaa-49dc-4a35-8fd0-f268a65fc509}}  constrained mass variable in a specific supersymmetric model.
We study events where each of the two branches have decay chains that end with a {{formula:db9bfd04-038b-411e-aee2-8b229ca61f85}}  decaying to a {{formula:42a5f4bb-cd9e-4ddd-bb97-e5141894799a}}  and a pair of opposite-sign same-flavor (OSSF) leptons.
Thus the final states of interest contain four isolated leptons
(made up of two OSSF pairs) and missing transverse momentum.
Fig REF  defines the four momentum of the particle states with {{formula:041fad8e-2570-43f8-b622-5b1a8310305f}} , {{formula:0f54b081-4f51-40cc-b3d7-a27d5ee73670}} , and the OSSF pairs forming the visible particles {{formula:4bf4f437-22db-4127-98ab-5a69b1309d75}} .
Any decay products early in the decay chains of either branch are grouped into {{formula:512f2138-d446-46e6-9d6e-7330d6266072}}  which we generically refer to as upstream transverse momentum (UTM).
Nonzero {{formula:764972de-7f67-4ddb-9b04-e8c928ef4d31}}  could be the result of initial state radiation (ISR) or decays of heavier particles further up the decay chain.
Events with four leptons and missing transverse momentum have a very small Standard-Model background.
To give a detailed illustration of the {{formula:05fab801-8d3b-4424-85a1-8a6cf5a0a4aa}}  methods, we have chosen to analyze
the benchmark point P1 from {{cite:2885256b8175641b48acd10898bf5acd922cd5be}} which corresponds to mSUGRA with {{formula:a1da032b-e466-42cb-9fdf-4a4f214312c5}}  GeV, {{formula:1f7ea9c6-7336-41e7-a740-ed0fc3744d09}}  GeV,
{{formula:fc3ea5ce-d686-446e-b681-aba02c2fb27a}} , {{formula:17a81675-6268-4493-86b1-fb63ec76bb7b}} , {{formula:9a13b9c3-bf49-4b05-b93f-a7d76ee65dbb}} . Our SUSY particle spectrum was calculated with ISAJET {{cite:4eb2d3f2c7a2517fee17350e92647432965678dd}} version 7.63.
We stress that the analysis technique employed applies generically to models involving decays to a massive particle state that leaves the detector unnoticed.

A powerful feature of the {{formula:9f63ba00-d683-415f-9bd7-2324d0d2f023}}  distribution is that, with some mild assumptions, the shape away from the endpoint can be entirely determined from the
unknown mass scale and quantities that are measured. The ideal shape fit against early data therefore provides an early mass estimate for the invisible particle.
This study is meant to be a guide on how to overcome difficulties in establishing and fitting the shape: difficulties from combinatoric issues, from differing energy resolutions for the leptons, hadrons,
and missing transverse momentum, from backgrounds, and from large upstream transverse momentum (UTM) Our references to UTM correspond to the Significant Transverse Momentum (SPT), pair production category in {{cite:348e5f35889b9524254b0651a1999f0d05c1c888}} where SPT indicates that the relevant pair of parent particles can be seen as recoiling against a significant transverse momentum.. As we shall discuss, UTM actually provides surprising benefits.

As a specific example of the application of the {{formula:f723cca0-71f9-42fc-9fd4-a875d18e0afb}}  method, we have chosen a supersymmetry model mSUGRA, {{formula:7e1266e1-46aa-4c8c-824a-d2d3d516dd63}}  GeV, {{formula:5d99992a-ede3-427c-8ca9-a46332b90a0f}}  GeV, {{formula:546f64ad-c4e0-47df-a179-9ec4bcc5f778}} , {{formula:1b82603e-3c72-464d-9530-a4a1b3196558}} , {{formula:37b613a5-3bf7-4ea4-9579-ec4ffa30c45b}}  This was model {{formula:b2637d8d-0b63-4771-aa5a-cc0ffb90c9cc}}  from {{cite:2885256b8175641b48acd10898bf5acd922cd5be}} which we also used in {{cite:3f9e8e0fc39ef90f2ee5d224b131e3618627723e}}.. The spectrum used in the simulation has {{formula:2f484646-47a1-423c-b181-3e9835cacb8e}}  and {{formula:40d6a0bd-e355-4d56-8aff-54708d5400f2}} .
We have employed two simulation packages. One is a Mathematica code that creates the `ideal' distributions based only on very simple assumptions and input data. The second is HERWIG {{cite:0c828633ccd49479610dba8034f2ce3f04fd0421}}, {{cite:c41d3eb6fb4d403a67326302f26b1579dc346e12}}, {{cite:aa34ed4d8ef34392279223dbb9368eae204ae9a3}} which simulates events based on a SUSY spectrum, MSSM cross sections, decay chains, and appropriate parton distribution functions.
If the simple Mathematica simulator predicts `ideal' shapes that agree with HERWIG generator, then we have reason to believe that
all the relevant factors relating to the shape are identified in the simple Mathematica simulation.
This is an important check in validating the benefits of fitting the {{formula:5049dbdc-aeee-4d03-beb6-2d498dda89f9}}  and {{formula:6c726131-399b-4076-9f65-f739dbc5dbba}}  distribution shape as a method to measure the mass of new invisible particles produced at hadron colliders.

Our `ideal' distributions are produced from a home-grown Monte Carlo event generator written in Mathematica. This generater serves to ensure that we understand the origin of the distribution shape. It also ensures that we have control over measuring the parameters needed to determine the mass without knowing the full model, coupling coefficients, or parton distribution functions. We also use this simulation to determine on what properties the ideal distributions depends.

The simulator is used to create events satisfying the topology shown in Fig REF  for a set of specified masses.
We take as given the previously measured mass difference {{formula:0daddeed-1dd2-474e-a338-4b992f0e7224}} , which we use in this chapter's simulations.
We neglect finite widths of the particle states as most are in the sub GeV range for the model we are considering. We neglect spin correlations between the two branches. We perform the simulations in the center-of-mass frame because {{formula:b24b5181-7e3a-4c96-a93b-40aef2517950}}  and {{formula:12e52bb8-4593-42ff-96ac-c9446b8d1cef}}  are transverse observables and are invariant under longitudinal boosts. The collision energy {{formula:a5e89cb0-378b-42cf-975e-69c5df95c681}}  is distributed according to normalized distribution
{{formula:3d5cbc98-2c22-4e76-923f-9e20cfd63730}}

unless otherwise specified. The {{formula:d22c9208-8927-4df5-a87c-90dc6eed1b59}}  is produced with a uniform angular distribution, and all subsequent decays have uniform angular distribution in the rest frame of the parent. The UTM is simulated by making {{formula:24cfc625-67ee-497e-a432-2aad164722ab}}  equal to the UTM with {{formula:246c95cd-1ffc-4759-ba25-3986ac082cf4}}  (unless otherwise specified), and boosting the other four-vectors of the event such that the total transverse momentum is zero.
As we will show, these simple assumptions capture the important elements of the process.
Being relatively model independent, they provide a means of
determining the mass for various production mechanisms.
If one were to assume detailed knowledge of the production process, it would be
possible to obtain a better mass determination by using a more complete simulation
like HERWIG to provide the `ideal' distributions against which one compares with the data.
Here we concentrate on the more model independent simulation to demonstrate that it predicts
the {{formula:54bffd69-0dc4-44fb-9973-5790a8f1e99f}}  and {{formula:04590c37-0c7b-4412-80a8-9e68666ef7cf}}  distributions well-enough to perform the mass determination that we demonstrate in this case-study.

In order to obtain a more realistic estimate
of the problems associated with collision data,
we generate samples of unweighted inclusive supersymmetric particle pair production,
using the HERWIG Monte Carlo program with LHC beam conditions.
These samples produce a more realistic simulation of the event
structure that would be obtained for the supersymmetric model studied here,
including the (leading order) cross sections and parton distributions.
It includes all supersymmetric processes and so contains the relevant background processes
as well as the particular decay chain that we wish to study.
Figure REF  shows the {{formula:86ff2401-2a98-4cc0-992b-d7cd24aeb534}}  and {{formula:cc5a1692-41cd-49a3-8c99-11480fa5df31}}  distributions of a sample of HERWIG generated signal and background events.

Charged leptons ({{formula:90091654-50ef-4d4a-b576-59ce05c3c8cd}}  and {{formula:31d5ff88-a289-49b2-995d-7a9aa1b575ae}} )
produced in the decay of heavy objects (SUSY particles and {{formula:8602dae8-defa-4038-b871-851d56f85693}}  and {{formula:9e881c56-d925-4ee2-8506-cc00b389a5c3}}  bosons)
were selected for futher study
provided they satisfied basic selection criteria on transverse momentum
({{formula:40b3ab21-5f29-4ca2-aa16-8afdecbd5d42}}  GeV) and pseudorapdity ({{formula:81d59026-31cf-4ed7-a6c9-39a1ff793612}} ).
Leptons coming from hadron decays are usually contained within hadronic jets and
so can be experimentally rejected with high efficiency using energy or track isolation criteria.
This latter category of leptons was therefore not used in this study.
The acceptance criterion used for the hadronic final state was {{formula:033dac44-22f3-4446-80e0-a23e90416ffb}} .
The detector energy resolution functions used are described in Section REF .

There are several factors that control or
affect the shape of the {{formula:0f1c0f2d-b3e4-44ee-8b55-a8e68271867f}}  and {{formula:dbc03321-f19c-43b6-adcd-8ceef60b9fa5}}  distributions. We divide the factors into those that
affect the in-principle distribution and the factors that affect
the observation of the distribution by the detector like
energy resolution and selection cuts.

The in-principle distribution of these events is influenced by
the presence or absence of spin-correlations between the branches, the
{{formula:6c176a37-d334-431a-bc11-1afe5b9a1d5b}}  distribution of the visible particles, any
significant upstream transverse momentum (UTM) against which the system is recoiling (e.g. gluinos or squarks decaying further up the decay chain), and background coming from other new-physics processes or the Standard Model. As all these processes effectively occur at the interaction vertex, there are some combinatoric ambiguities.
These are the factors that influence the in-principle distribution of events that impinges on the particle detector.

The actual distribution recorded by the detector will depend on further factors. Some factors we are able to regulate – for example cuts on the missing transverse momentum. Other factors depend on how well we understand the detector's operation – such as the energy resolution and particle identification.

Where the effect of such factors is significant,
for example for the {{formula:6271cd36-23b5-4045-b202-f0df1077a649}} , {{formula:a6b6618a-2452-4cf3-af1f-5115932be915}} , and background distributions,
our approach has been to model their effect on the ideal distributions
by using appropriate information from the `data', much as one would do in a real LHC experiment.
For the present our `data' are provided by HERWIG, rather than LHC events, but the principle is the same.

Mass Difference and Mass Scale

The end-point of {{formula:d0a19c6c-e559-40f6-bffe-78ec14266730}}  and {{formula:3db61b70-84c4-4105-8f22-502d2447c54e}}  distributions give the mass of {{formula:728b9d3e-9400-4741-9f06-d9be34bd69db}} . Therefore the mass scale, {{formula:ea63e7da-ebd0-4fc3-b423-129409724b8d}} , is a dominant factor
in the shape of the `ideal' distribution. This is the
reason we can use these distributions to determine the mass scale.
Fig REF  shows the {{formula:834fa2cf-6983-4b46-8133-65b6cf0c9214}}  and {{formula:d7fef19d-2cad-495b-b825-f5261eb16b76}}  distributions
for five choices of {{formula:47ec6816-e798-48f2-8db8-84e98053ae7b}}  assuming the HERWIG generated
{{formula:63828a1e-1ed8-49a5-8226-2a56f4e5767e}}  and UTM distributions.
{{figure:d2f6042f-013d-44ee-9fc5-364d364c3d47}}

How does the shape change with mass scale? The shape is typically sharply peaked at {{formula:05886f50-df9c-41b2-bc87-2450ffe38087}}  followed by a tail that ends at the mass of {{formula:8438f2f6-d60a-4871-a97d-9d3518a9d748}} .
The peak at {{formula:1d25db7b-6bb6-4c51-b388-2086abf5f327}}  is due to events that are compatible with {{formula:007b57d8-3913-4e2f-b770-6e212bd9129f}} . We say these events give the trivial constraint. Because we bin the data, the height of the first bin depends on the bin size. As {{formula:feada35b-db2c-485e-9a6e-5731b5137191}}  becomes larger, then the non-trivial events are distributed over a wider range and the endpoint becomes less clear. In general if all other things are equal, the larger the mass, the more events in the first bin and the longer and flatter the tail.

The distribution also depends on the mass difference {{formula:fb58fce8-2ccf-4cb9-a890-9de41773fd3d}}  which
we assume has been determined.
We expect that experimentally one should be able to read off the mass difference from the {{formula:6624fbeb-0ecd-454f-8a63-6aeaba155064}}  kinematic end-point with very high precision.
Gjelsten, Miller, and Osland estimate this edge can be measured to better than {{formula:a39a8501-7ecf-414f-9d9c-c5031d9c23d8}}  {{cite:1262575081b628e94f7cf7c411cf5ddc62d32fa6}}, {{cite:c45b33e2ad0c675811bdfd2128993beb18670d84}}
using many different channels that
lead to the same edge, and after modeling energy resolution and background.

propagated from the error in the mass
difference in the limit of {{formula:6979be1b-372e-46d6-bc7c-203dd1ab40a9}}  are given approximately by
{{formula:5f0e6e92-652f-4d36-ae47-9aeeb81b9113}}

where {{formula:937b68a7-d906-4511-aabf-0a1807b2fb74}}  is the error in the determination of the mass difference
{{formula:014189e1-6a22-4106-bb06-2990b3fed9a8}} . An error in {{formula:50570f38-a2e3-4708-be79-5e53952f8901}}  will lead to an {{formula:3c4eef77-dcf3-42ed-a0b5-c1a63d37d5c2}}  distribution with a shape and endpoint above or below the true mass in the direction indicated by Eq(REF ).

To isolate this source of error from the uncertainty in the fit, we assume that the mass difference is known exactly in our stated results. The UTM makes the distribution have a sharper endpoint and thereby make the mass easier to determine. This is equivalent to having a sharper kink in {{formula:c958bea6-60bb-4e83-b84c-312f69cdb489}}  in the presence of large UTM {{cite:348e5f35889b9524254b0651a1999f0d05c1c888}}.

Backgrounds

{{figure:bd7032ad-d647-41dc-9b43-997f5e6a2c63}}

Backgrounds affect the shape and, if not corrected for,
could provide a systematic error in the estimated mass. In Section  we will see that the position of the minimum {{formula:a3c06ae0-4c8c-4b7b-95b4-23abd19e583a}}  in a fit to {{formula:52e90199-5f79-4092-870b-ebeefa63e6f9}}  is barely affected by the background. The main effect of the background is to shift the parabola up, giving a worse fit. To improve the fit, we may be able to estimate the {{formula:13d72461-1b75-4c5c-88f0-dc6243b7e749}}  and {{formula:dfe7dab9-db9f-44a7-9ae0-f20fc588c9db}}  distribution and magnitude of the
background from the data itself.
We first discuss the sources of background, and then we describe a generic technique using a Dalitz-like wedgebox analysis to estimate a background model which gives approximately the correct shape and magnitude of the background.

One reason we study the four-lepton with missing transverse momentum channel is because of the very-low Standard-Model background {{cite:c7c028bb5a29232cda5dd507c401fcc6db3ed45a}}, {{cite:1c7ffb43da3911f4247d3218a45d1f3b84018718}}. A previous study {{cite:1c7ffb43da3911f4247d3218a45d1f3b84018718}} estimates about 120 Standard-Model four-lepton events (two OSSF pairs) for {{formula:be5c1355-dff2-49a1-a7c4-2161ba81fafa}}  with a {{formula:d0a7fa7e-836d-41da-839b-56b6acc7b41c}}  GeV cut. They suggest that we can further reduce the Standard-Model background by requiring several hadronic jets. Because we expect very-little direct {{formula:21e3b89f-065b-4284-a635-58326a80dc3a}}  pair production, this would have very little effect on the number of signal events. Also, because {{formula:ee8a8a83-bde2-4216-a9b5-da5a1f3a005f}} s are a part of the intermediate states of these background processes, very few of these events will have {{formula:214db69a-5e68-4fe9-8566-bf650a15a491}}  significantly different from {{formula:5a559fa6-c16d-4918-96c3-20612dc9b266}} .

What is the source of these Standard-Model backgrounds? About {{formula:bf7a06fb-f4dd-417b-bfcf-beebdef9ecb2}}  is from {{formula:5014ae7b-1194-41d2-9699-3746d5ddfda9}} -pair production events with no invisible decay products, in which the missing transverse momentum can only arise from experimental particle identification and resolution errors. This implies that a slightly stronger {{formula:0b2fd9bb-02f4-4b8e-8eb4-721fa3bc2501}}  cut could further eliminate this background. Another {{formula:3b212e25-778f-45f1-be16-68e47f8305fe}}  are due to {{formula:ad248a83-985f-4455-8160-909bbffa00a0}}  production.
Not explicitly discussed in their study but representing another possible source of backgrounds are events containing heavy baryons which decay leptonically.
If we assume {{formula:5fac210d-ba32-4a44-a994-fdda9f09473c}} -quark hadrons decay to isolated leptons with a branching ratio of {{formula:dad25435-33f6-4593-9d10-2ea402e6a2a8}} , then LHC {{formula:427e9bde-e1fb-49c4-8397-fc7c5b1766ba}}  production will lead to about 10 events passing these cuts for {{formula:c2cfd07f-c37f-48d1-be24-4cfb9917c2e5}}  where both OSSF leptons pairs have {{formula:c1643b40-1b67-4c1e-9487-a97d5df43cd1}} .

Tau decays also provide a background for our specific process of interest. The process {{formula:34190f3e-3f95-4706-8958-ac7c8b71f1dc}}  will be misidentified as {{formula:f150593d-3d97-4f50-be39-4631149f043e}}  or {{formula:7b0f544a-5fa4-4c95-b203-92b9bcd01803}}  about {{formula:c2f4483a-674d-4cb4-a9e5-72965f6e41ce}}  of the time ({{formula:69648653-bc83-409b-8ccc-d63f47f37649}}  total). Because the {{formula:deeac3ec-ef77-4482-a5a0-d36812e77a13}}  decays introduce new sources of missing transverse momentum ({{formula:4cc9259a-9922-432e-a3ee-aee3de0958df}} ), these events will distort the {{formula:4c24c422-db91-40d7-9945-56729980f87d}}  calculation. This suggests that the dominant background to the {{formula:9154c286-6a86-4480-b8a1-e13e8bc1734c}}  hadrons will be from other SUSY processes.

We now create a crude background model from which we estimate the magnitude and distribution of the background using the `true' HERWIG data as a guide.
We follow the suggestion of Ref. {{cite:888980905ddb0c201c30db26c521e1a691504984}}, {{cite:1c7ffb43da3911f4247d3218a45d1f3b84018718}} and use a wedgebox analysis plotting the invariant mass {{formula:1177413a-018d-4637-9705-a81080d7078a}}  against {{formula:a28ef2df-c146-4124-af6e-fa8ebc777a5a}}  to supplement our knowledge of the
background events mixed in with our signal events. This wedgebox analysis, seen in
Fig. REF  for our HERWIG simulation, shows patterns that tell about other SUSY states present. The presence of the strips along 91 GeV indicate that particle states are being created that decay to two leptons via an on-shell {{formula:1f302bd8-453e-4b35-a13b-1420dd62f49d}} . The observation that the intensity changes above and below {{formula:56471a72-ec1c-4239-b222-4c2c3407f3c2}}  GeV shows that many of the states produced have one branch that decays via a {{formula:2c311d84-382a-4217-a92a-5aaf7d51ef3c}}  and the other branch decays via an on-shell {{formula:6543c733-337c-4a28-a950-0b5b68cc8767}} . The lack of events immediately above and to the right of the {{formula:c8e65e9f-593d-447b-86fb-25bad5ec07dc}}  coordinate but below and to the left of {{formula:5586fc23-8d2e-4c47-8eb3-93c845d9e7a2}}  coordinate suggest that symmetric process are not responsible for this background.

We also see the density of events in the block above {{formula:0005c467-c88b-47c4-b37a-321800217227}}  and to the right of {{formula:c6947533-d2b1-44e8-9f23-ab1ac55cd43f}}  suggest a cascade decay with an endpoint near enough to {{formula:78b7bf56-42a8-491b-9a3c-2370df72d201}}  that it is not distinguishable from {{formula:5c091efe-d3ac-4bc4-9b4b-f55b817b646f}} . Following this line of thinking, we model the background with a guess of an asymmetric set of events where one branch has new states {{formula:44ca8879-9244-4af3-bcb5-613f144a0bd9}} , {{formula:5a034dd5-7e9e-43fb-8d53-c607fd0fafe8}}  and {{formula:891d2a18-74c2-4214-9c37-4353683e3a64}}  with masses such that the {{formula:0564ca77-ab76-47a4-a00e-7103d62d915e}}  endpoint is
{{formula:3bcb867a-026a-4b32-bb3c-387583919572}}

and the other branch is our {{formula:367d269c-d4a4-4490-a552-3c14bfb7cfde}}  decay. The masses one chooses to satisfy this edge did not prove important so long as the mass differences were reasonably sized; we tried several different mass triplets ending with the LSP, and all gave similar answers.

We now describe the background model used in our fits. One branch starts with a massive state with {{formula:81dc3b7a-be48-43ac-b46a-d018069028f3}}  which decays to a lepton and a new state {{formula:038c2bc5-bd70-4c03-a6b2-0cff43f03503}}  which in-turn decays to a lepton and the LSP. The second branch has our signal decay with the {{formula:00ab3acc-d0de-4f0f-bd1e-bdc14aeb3485}}  decaying to {{formula:ef6804c6-fd50-4fb3-92db-2b999ab8a946}}  and two leptons via a three-body decay. We added UTM consistent with that observed in the events.

By matching the number of events seen outside the {{formula:2b1c48d8-4aab-48a0-a810-7b07c260579a}}  region, we estimate the number of the events within the signal cuts that are due to backgrounds. We estimate {{formula:7156d829-5697-49ce-8e7a-6373301abbae}}  of the events with both OSSF pairs satisfying {{formula:914844ab-a556-40cc-a0b1-d2ba07c08fc9}}  are background events.
The model also gives a reasonable distribution for these events. Inspecting the actual HERWIG results showed that actual fraction of background events was {{formula:60de717c-9d83-498a-bb38-30cf49435ca1}} . If we let the fraction be free and minimize the {{formula:7f2b86f8-209f-449e-a1b5-edfcf5562a86}}  with respect to the background fraction, we found a minimum at {{formula:54a01963-3d6f-48d9-9a4b-5994dabb20e9}} .

Our background model is simplistic and does not represent the actual processes, but it does a good job of accounting for the magnitude and the shape of the background mixed into our signal distribution. Most of the HERWIG background events came from {{formula:1ee4be60-9b14-49c5-9dc6-3916a47f2aa9}}  and charginos which introduce extra sources of missing transverse momentum. Never the less, the shape fits very accurately and the performance is discussed in Section . It is encouraging that our estimate of the background shape and magnitude is relatively insensitive to details of the full spectrum. Even ignoring the background, as we will see in Section , still leads to a minimum {{formula:59ecaff6-e03b-4d50-8d51-931458d5550e}}  at the correct mass.

Combinatoric Ambiguities

If we assume that the full cascade effectively occurs at the primary vertex (no displaced vertices), then the combinatoric question is a property of the ideal distribution produced in the collisions.
There are no combinatoric issues if the two opposite-sign same-flavor lepton pairs are each different flavors (e.g. the four leptons are {{formula:cb1a032b-0911-4a57-8cdf-c3e6cc7b55f0}} , {{formula:10c89666-7376-46bd-9760-7953454cb9ff}} , {{formula:ad50deaf-259f-41b3-9752-a1356b4bd0dc}}  and {{formula:c686427f-6992-4a5d-bf48-500efcb2342a}} ). However if all four leptons are the same flavor, we have found that we can still identify unique branch assignments 90% of the time. The unique identification comes from the observation that both pairs must have an invariant mass {{formula:9079f996-152b-432c-b41d-964105d9b1a4}}  less than the value of the {{formula:fd2b9697-8db6-4bb2-94d8-f0014766b4c9}}  edge. In {{formula:37861d09-99b2-4430-8ee8-135eed7f203a}}  of the events, there is only one combination that satisfies this requirement. This allows one to use {{formula:3647f58f-3395-4e61-bac1-e873f14c7b98}}  of the four lepton events without ambiguity. The first {{formula:2abed0bd-7782-488c-b663-767818eeb0f7}}  are identified from the two OSSF pairs being of different flavors and {{formula:752a2eab-b20c-4c81-a57d-cd6f271214b8}}  of the remaining can be identified by requiring that both branches of OSSF lepton for an event's combinatoric pairing satisfy {{formula:92b0de9f-a217-4d49-8016-ab6e15cb9c39}} . The events which remain ambiguous have two possible assignments, both of which are included with a weight of {{formula:ca704427-37f9-460b-9ac0-f9cfbcb41593}}  in the distribution.

As just described, the `ideal' in-principle distribution is created from the observed {{formula:70bf2ba6-bf59-42c0-8a1b-e3995298e6d6}}  distribution and the observed UTM distribution. We include combinatoric effects from events with four leptons of like flavors. Last, we can estimate the magnitude of background events and their {{formula:9439b4f3-ddb2-4e14-a85d-69a701d8dbb8}}  and {{formula:b8177612-4eef-49c2-99ed-121f10dba68a}}  shape.
We now modify the in-principle distribution to simulate the
effects of the particle detector to form our final `ideal' distribution
that includes all anticipated effects. The two main effects on the {{formula:85cd4865-3f77-48be-9ae3-2db17bfdf033}}  and {{formula:02df31dc-64cc-4c9e-8dd8-9d73ec4d346a}}  distributions are the energy resolution and the {{formula:861d3550-3d45-4dc4-96ac-67231e4ed7d9}}  cuts.

Shape Dependence on Energy Resolution

Energy resolution causes the {{formula:bc846cb7-4d6f-49ca-bd10-0607e3beb822}}  and {{formula:2d5eb1b0-e47d-4336-8bd3-27c6e80e42aa}}  distributions to be smeared. Here we assume the angular resolution is negligible.
For both the Mathematica Monte Carlo model and the HERWIG events
we simulate the detector's energy resolution by scaling the four vectors for electrons, muons, and hadrons by
{{formula:b0ea08f5-c480-42d4-8367-c7dd6044598d}}

respectively
{{cite:3d447a7ab763ebea675b1f3c994bb4d17208915c}}{{cite:5c59b90aa2f70cb96f42a891557d7a6891f0e571}}. The muon energy resolution is different because they are typically not contained by the calorimeter.
A more detailed detector simulation is of course possible,
but since we do not know the true behavior of any LHC detector until the device begins taking data,
a more sophisticated treatment would be of limited value here.
In practice the dependence of the ideal distribution shapes
on the missing transverse momentum resolution should reflect
the actual estimated uncertainty of the missing transverse momentum of the
observed events.

Smearing of the distributions decreases the area difference between two normalized distributions, thereby decreasing the precision with which one can determine the mass from a given number of signal events. This expanded uncertainty can be seen in Section .

The {{formula:c8a1f679-733b-4130-b08e-c4e98ac19e22}}  calculations depend on the mass difference, the four-momenta of the four leptons, and the missing transverse momentum. As the lepton energy resolution is very tight, the missing transverse momentum's energy resolution is dominated by the hadronic energy resolution. We model the energy resolution of the UTM as a hadronic jet. This significantly increases the uncertainty in the missing transverse momentum because hadrons have about five times the energy resolution error.

In our Mathematica model, we represent the UTM as a single four-vector {{formula:f3797430-5b84-43d3-95f8-e74e8ab8a466}} , but in reality it will be the sum of many four-vectors. Because we apply the energy resolution smearing to {{formula:07e7694f-ca53-4fb5-9b8f-2634c1b1471b}} , if {{formula:a2aa6ca6-46e9-45b2-b2c7-7d48d9cdb215}}  is small the simple Mathematica model will have a smaller missing transverse momentum resolution error.
However, an events with almost 0 UTM could have a large missing momentum energy resolution if it has a lot of hadronic jets whose transverse momentum mostly cancels.
Fig REF  shows that most of the time we have considerable hadronic UTM, so this effect is a minor correction on our results.

Shape Dependence on Missing Transverse Momentum Cuts

A key distinguishing feature of these events is missing transverse momentum. To eliminate the large number of Standard Model events with four-lepton and with no {{formula:4e617f9c-b3a1-4db2-a967-a8c9194c5468}} , we will need to cut on this parameter. Fig. REF  shows the HERWIG simulation's missing transverse momentum versus the {{formula:d395e026-19e3-4300-ba9d-ff0cbb08a080}} . A non-trivial {{formula:39643905-1c29-4761-a101-bc9fe5875a2a}}  requires substantial {{formula:ecd80e74-a0bf-4874-a105-5f94ea0f1419}} . Small {{formula:9ba6a5e0-3467-41ba-903a-a9f002962ab2}}  of less than about {{formula:17b258ff-4827-4f0a-bb53-76b897059596}}  only affects the {{formula:47702628-237e-43f0-b5be-cd0884505fba}}  shape below about {{formula:e802b530-00fd-49fa-b048-b80176dfee23}} . The shape of the {{formula:cda829f7-0a36-4ff4-aa48-92611f9fe2f9}}  therefore will require a higher fidelity model from which to train the shapes. Instead, we just choose to not fit bins with {{formula:b3a1074e-b529-4017-a481-7422634e3118}} .

All events near the end of {{formula:3116de92-fcdc-480f-a146-077f35e58125}}  distribution require significant {{formula:db6643f5-b084-4d10-ac83-1a1534ded607}} , therefore {{formula:e4235f16-37f7-4b53-a375-74adc441fb6a}}  cuts will not affect the part of this distribution which we fit. The number of events with no non-trivial upper-bounds will also be affected by {{formula:631688e7-46bc-4968-8e83-4feae29c4925}}  cuts. We only fit the {{formula:9851ef28-5f23-43bb-96ed-b769a4b86dcd}}  distribution up to about {{formula:75c83bc7-cb0f-4054-ac8e-db2b1a58446b}} .
{{figure:51c5580e-406c-4c3f-8fa1-72e20da82cba}}

Determining the mass based on the shape of the distribution enables one to use all the events and not just those near the end point.
We fit both upper-bound and lower-bound shapes to the data as described in the Appendix . As one expects, fitting the lower-bound shape more tightly constrains the mass from below and fitting the upper-bound shape more tightly constrains the mass from above. Combining the two gives approximately even uncertainty. We calculate ideal distributions assuming {{formula:dc8314e7-9a2d-4be3-89b8-9cf6adf946a4}}  at five values 50, 60, 70, 80, and 90 GeV. We then fit a quadratic interpolation through the points. Our uncertainties are based on the value where {{formula:c9269450-994c-48d7-a8f2-4babe89dc717}}  increases by 1 from its minimum of this interpolation. This uncertainty estimate agrees with about {{formula:ab731216-710f-413c-bd58-8adcb8503662}}  of the results falling within that range after repeated runs.
Our uncertainty estimates do not include the error propagated from the uncertainty in the mass difference (see Eq(REF )).

The error in mass determination obtained with limited statistics can be estimated using Poisson statistics. In our studies we find that, as one would expect, increasing the number of events by a factor of four,
we bring down our error by about a factor of two.
This means that one could expect {{formula:596900ea-62ba-4459-b47d-5a4f84f340f7}}  after about {{formula:ce22378b-da98-4654-82b2-eff10731aea0}}  which represents 100 signal events and 75 background events.

Despite adding some of the complicating effects one would encounter with real data, we have discovered other factors which demonstrate that one could obtain an even better precision than estimated in Chapter .
There, we used only our simple Mathematica model and neglected most sources of realistic uncertainty.
We assumed all the events could be modeled as being direct production without spin-correlations. With these simplifications, we argued the mass could be determined to {{formula:ee580105-9a09-462e-a848-c98ed00c50b1}}  using 250 signal events.

In this chapter, we performed a case study to show that that the relevant {{formula:cf7b2719-b776-4143-963b-c700e38b9af2}}  and {{formula:7bba80fb-5dca-47bb-a539-e0e47f05df8f}}  shapes can be successfully determined from the mass difference {{formula:2c5271a9-499e-4d7a-9932-5b7f8384f80a}} , the {{formula:fab3e2e9-862e-4a37-9be4-b97fecd8ecfd}}  distribution observation, the upstream transverse momentum (UTM) distribution observation.
We included and accounted for many realistic effects: we modeled the large energy-resolution error of hadronic jets. We also included the effects of backgrounds, {{formula:32479a6b-824c-4f7f-a197-b7b8a4ef2c80}}  cuts, and combinatorics. Our signal and backgrounds were generated with HERWIG.
We discussed how a Dalitz-like plot can estimate the background fraction and shape. Observed inputs were used in a simple model to determine ideal distribution shapes that makes no reference to parton distribution functions, cross sections, or other model-dependent factors that we are not likely to know early in the process.

Despite these extra sources of uncertainty, we found a final mass determination of {{formula:df1cdd16-28f0-4ddd-9133-ba364f32ddf7}}  with about 400 signal events which is still better than the appropriately scaled result from RS {{cite:3f9e8e0fc39ef90f2ee5d224b131e3618627723e}}.
The sources of the mass determination improvement are twofold: (1) the prediction and fitting of upper-bound distribution, and (2) the sharper end-point in the presence of large UTM.
Under equivalent circumstances, the sharper endpoint is enough to give a factor of 2 improvement in the uncertainty over the direct production case assumed in {{cite:3f9e8e0fc39ef90f2ee5d224b131e3618627723e}}. Fitting the upper bound tends to improve the determination by an additional factor of {{formula:256876e3-b635-49f1-a1a1-742b92a6e48a}} . This improvement is then used to fight the large hadronic-jet energy resolution and background uncertainty.

Mass determination using {{formula:48bc5d1b-36fb-4560-acdd-f3d5d3118950}}  and {{formula:5a69b47a-f8d9-4d2b-af0f-4afb495209a4}}  applies to many other processes. We have focused on cases where the mass difference is given by the end-point of an {{formula:5963a359-cc35-4b62-b5cb-b33dc32213e1}}  distribution involving a three-body decay.
If there is not a three-body decay, then the mass difference may be found by applying other mass determination techniques like the mass shell techniques (MST) {{cite:6482955dabf1746e5d045b4e8635076adbcc9bab}}, {{cite:ac9f6f98cbeeb2c6bdf454c493e4c89467cd44c8}}, {{cite:43f26218b508598253c597e079530d8cce57501f}} or edges in cascade decays {{cite:deb6d46c125cbd88b5481273fcb3937f08abd962}}, {{cite:17db4dffa8f5fd4588f62d3a4c6baa0681fdb2e7}}, {{cite:c45b33e2ad0c675811bdfd2128993beb18670d84}} or {{formula:f4da9b7e-7961-4572-a352-09bf2ed68e78}}  at different stages in symmetric decay chains {{cite:a93a9d1165bd6371a3cd21375d4bb4559d16f891}}.

How does our method's performance compare to previous mass determination methods? Firstly, this technique is more robust than the {{formula:2eace05d-33f8-4ac0-93fe-d917393001bb}}  `kink' because in fitting to the shape of the distribution, it does not rely entirely on identification of the events near kinematic boundary. One can view {{formula:5cfac3fd-a72b-4f2b-8310-7f522185a531}}  and {{formula:36179a0a-0f78-4a86-ac5c-2e1755de81e3}}  as variables that event-by-event quantify the `kink'. Other than the `kink' technique, the previous techniques surveyed in Chapter  apply to cases where there is no three-body decay from which to measure the mass difference directly. However, each of those techniques still constrains the mass difference with great accuracy.
The technique of {{cite:deb6d46c125cbd88b5481273fcb3937f08abd962}}, {{cite:1262575081b628e94f7cf7c411cf5ddc62d32fa6}}, {{cite:17db4dffa8f5fd4588f62d3a4c6baa0681fdb2e7}}, {{cite:c45b33e2ad0c675811bdfd2128993beb18670d84}} which uses edges from cascade decays determines the LSP mass to {{formula:bf32cb4a-9870-49c7-ad9c-f7a8efd2217b}}  with about 500 thousand events from {{formula:b8cd2116-b60a-43f6-9db1-b27d904e5b90}} . The approach of {{cite:ac9f6f98cbeeb2c6bdf454c493e4c89467cd44c8}} assumes a pair of symmetric decay chains and assumes two events have the same structure. They reach {{formula:3f50203a-ba73-4499-8c19-e98962c6a467}}  using 700 signal events after {{formula:f597b113-d38f-4487-9c4d-ee56fc91f98b}} , but have a {{formula:c17935cf-e5a8-4053-9e4a-c295e73b990f}}  systematic bias that needs modeling to remove. By comparison, adjusting to 700 signal events we achieve {{formula:cc6252e9-71c0-4831-a864-8c00a5d35507}}  without a systematic bias after propagating an error of {{formula:22620ac4-cc74-45ea-b1fc-8439961c6d50}}  in the mass difference and with all discussed effects.
Uncertainty calculations differ amongst groups, some use repeated trial with new sets of Monte Carlo data, and others use {{formula:f1b4a470-f009-412d-87e9-cd1ff570f34f}} .
Without a direct comparison under like circumstance, the optimal method is not clear; but it is clear that fitting the {{formula:5f0c6b1c-b802-44ba-8838-b3586c0bb9e7}}  and {{formula:81933802-1691-4519-ace4-dd9cbd486561}}  distributions can determine the mass of
invisible particles at least as well, if not better than the other known methods in both accuracy and precision.

In summary, we have developed a mass determination technique, based on the constrained mass variables, which is able to determine the mass of a dark-matter particle state produced at the LHC in events with large missing transverse momentum.
The {{formula:dfb84a5b-4d27-4611-8393-a87751994391}}  method, which bounds the mass from below, was supplemented by
a new distribution {{formula:a160c820-1109-4b38-b601-35a660f97b21}}  which bounds the mass from above in events with large upstream transverse momentum.
A particular advantage of the method is that it also obtains substantial
information from events away from the end point allowing for a
significant reduction in the error.
The shape of the distribution away from the end-point can be determined without detailed knowledge of the underlying model, and as such, can provide an early estimate of the mass.
Once the underlying process and model generating the event has been identified the structure away from the end-point can be improved using, for example, HERWIG to produce the process dependent shape.
We performed a case-study simulation under LHC conditions to demonstrate that mass-determination by fitting the {{formula:8e90dc52-f4e7-46fc-b563-4326d7c4e76d}}  and {{formula:0e0dadc9-3614-4c25-8967-490670911cc1}}  distributions survives anticipated complications. With this fitting procedure it is possible to get an early measurement of the mass - with just 400 signal events in our case study we found we would determine {{formula:a76e46cd-8443-4600-8b3b-a35dbd08fa06}} . The ultimate accuracy obtainable by this method is {{formula:16604e9d-1fb8-4e21-99f3-506d5911e8c5}} . We conclude that this technique's precision is as good as, if not better than, the best existing techniques.

The main concept of the constrained mass variable {{formula:9c1cf0d6-f871-4dc9-b095-187a5bc98b75}}  {{cite:3f9e8e0fc39ef90f2ee5d224b131e3618627723e}} {{cite:302025c7c429f6072bf6a564288b609c0d793b09}} is that after studying several kinematic quantities we may have well determined the mass difference between two particle states but not the mass itself. We then incorporate these additional constraints in the analysis of the events. We check each event to test the lower bounds and upper bounds on the mass scale that still satisfies the mass difference and the on-shell conditions for the assumed topology. Because the domain over which we are minimizing contains the true value for the mass, the end-points of the lower bounds and upper bounds distributions' give the true mass.

The subject of this chapter is extending the constrained mass variable to the case with three new on-shell states as depicted in Fig REF . The constrained mass variable for this case will be called {{formula:acf342cc-8454-4618-8610-a898bfdacbc4}} .
We structure the chapter around a case study of the benchmark point SPS 1a {{cite:dbbddc5f2f78bfea5566c41eae136910b95c033d}}.
In this study, the three new states are identified as {{formula:708b74fe-5270-454d-8f8c-c6dc028fce30}} , {{formula:c61fceb2-6420-48b4-a8f2-374d45b0b925}}  and {{formula:cc4425ea-00a9-486d-9810-833e8febdb80}} . The visible particles leaving each branch are all opposite-sign same-flavor (OSSF) leptons ({{formula:b47a6d42-381e-47fb-b8cf-505d01544d9d}}  or {{formula:af85f04a-7492-41bd-90a2-7f2faea3f643}} ). This allows us to identify any hadronic activity as upstream transverse momentum.

The chapter is structured as follows:
Sec.  introduces the definition of {{formula:bb808e01-af74-4e73-abe5-deb4c04ea349}}  and how to calculate it. Sec.  discuses the dependence of {{formula:d8f00d8d-0317-432b-a9b3-6fa9ea8eae90}}  on complications from combinatorics, large upstream transverse momentum (UTM), {{formula:87e77976-e73d-44a6-9405-830283efb09e}}  cuts, parton distributions, and energy resolution. Sec  applies {{formula:bea1a8a9-dfa1-43fc-9bce-f1c9740a4c12}}  variables to HERWIG data from the benchmark supersymmetry spectrum SPS 1a. Finally we summarize the chapter's contributions.

We will now introduce the definition of {{formula:80bd9b8b-e9d3-4e2a-8ed1-a6df368950de}} , how to calculate it, its relationship to previous mass shell techniques.

The upper bound and lower bound
on the mass of the third lightest new particle state in the symmetric decay chain is the constrained mass variable {{formula:c984096c-73bf-4423-9216-42eddb88eb66}}  and {{formula:aa4eaa44-fd20-4f5f-8d3d-7d511bfabaed}} .

We initially assume that we have measured the mass differences from other techniques. For an on-shell intermediate state, there is no single end-point that gives the mass difference. The short decay chain gives a kinematic endpoint {{formula:accfe580-25a2-47e6-8539-2a4cf74326d6}}  described in Eq(REF ) that constrains a combination of the squared mass differences. Unless two of the states are nearly degenerate, the line with constant mass differences lies very close to the surface given by Eq(REF ). The two mass differences are often tightly constrained in other methods.
The mass differences are constrained to within {{formula:7eb48a0d-cf8b-40be-9f86-17eeff2aac03}}  GeV from studying long cascade decay chains where one combines constraints from several endpoints of different invariant mass combinations {{cite:1262575081b628e94f7cf7c411cf5ddc62d32fa6}}.
The concepts from Chapter  also provide another technique to determine the mass differences. After initially assuming that we know the mass difference, we show that our technique can also find the mass differences.
The {{formula:92e9a502-e005-4029-b6d4-272d9655df8f}}  distribution shape is a function of both the mass scale and mass differences.

The variable {{formula:b078182e-1de6-466c-bd31-91301bd1dd65}}  is a hybrid mass shell technique{{cite:43f26218b508598253c597e079530d8cce57501f}}.
In Chapter  we reviewed other mass shell technique that measure the mass in the case of three new states.
Cheng, Gunion, Han Marandella, McElrath (CGHMM) {{cite:6482955dabf1746e5d045b4e8635076adbcc9bab}} describe counting solutions at assumed values for the mass for {{formula:342fb96a-97ac-4961-adf6-4ebe74675c5d}} , {{formula:3f466d64-49a9-4322-981d-f2f4bde40a85}} , and {{formula:4ae3c569-c9d0-4ef4-9adc-f65dcc171231}} .
By incorporating a minimization or maximization, we enhance CGHMM's approach because we have a variable whose value changes slightly with slight changes of the inputs instead of the binary on-off that CGHMM has with the existence of a solutionI am grateful to Chris Lester for pointing out to me the importance of this feature..
We also incorporate knowledge of the added information from other measurements which accurately determine the mass differences.
Finally, the quantity {{formula:a35372c9-92a8-409a-a17f-0104fa8291e5}}  can form a distribution whose shape tells us information about the masses.
Because for most events there is only one `turn-on' point below {{formula:e7a3a792-8f89-4f52-9b6b-467e4dfacd24}} , the distribution {{formula:27172eba-7d4c-4b60-be58-1ced16740f36}}  is very similar to the derivative of the figure 8 of CGHMM{{cite:6482955dabf1746e5d045b4e8635076adbcc9bab}} to the left of their peak and {{formula:1adcbf05-00a7-4440-b3f3-d8f082cce25f}}  is similar to the negative of the derivative to the right of their peak.
They differ in that there may be multiple windows of solutions; also CGHMM's Fig 8 is not exactly along the line of fixed mass differences; and the effect of backgrounds and energy resolution are dealt with differently.

We also hope to show that the use of the distribution's shape enables us
to exploit the essentially non-existent dependence of the distributions on the unknown collision energies and incorporate the dependency on UTM directly. This diminishes the dependence of the measurement on the unknown model while still allowing us to exploit the majority of the distribution shape in the mass determination.

After studying previous MSTs, we were tempted to use Bayes theorem with a parton distribution function as a likelihood function as was done in Goldstein and Dalitz {{cite:0d0a890959fe5130dc31d5b42015898f23ab7d45}} and Kondo, Chikamatsu, Kim {{cite:e43ee0e28c2e94d1a77726eac16d5de674134f0d}} (GDKCK).
They used the parton distribution function to weight the different mass estimates of the top-quark mass ({{formula:0d6791a4-86fe-4686-8a55-6c66b42530fb}}  in our topology).
We found that such a weighting leads to a prediction for {{formula:f954c4b2-64a2-4d99-883f-e773711b6fc9}}  much smaller than the true value. This can be understood because the parton distributions make collisions with smaller center-of-mass energies (small {{formula:6b68e601-c582-4a6a-bcdf-e7b787b0a937}} ) more likely, therefore the posterior will prefer smaller values of {{formula:b4139afa-bba3-4b66-97ed-e8747919ace9}}  which are only possible for smaller values of {{formula:a5a53ff1-7bbb-436f-a8ce-3ec09aab68f7}} .
Only if one includes the cross-section for production, i.e. the likelihood of the event existing at all, in the Bayes likelihood function will we have the appropriate factor that suppresses small values of {{formula:0385959a-433e-4840-b73f-835d0ec56489}}  and therefore small values of {{formula:85057e64-1772-4b7d-a91d-269959c5f781}} . This balance therefore leads to the maximum likelihood (in the limit of infinite data) occurring at the correct {{formula:d20ce34c-b008-4bbd-97d7-e95b527d7d9d}} . Unfortunately, inclusion of the magnitude of the cross section introduces large model dependence.
In the case of the top-quarks mass determination, the GDKCK technique gives reasonable results. This is because they were not scanning the mass scale, but rather scanning {{formula:abeb2ea8-9038-41af-875d-845db709acd8}}  (the top quark mass) while assuming {{formula:14c53b78-3970-4bd7-8bc7-9687c6606492}}  and {{formula:3be418e4-3fa9-4ac4-9556-700fd3f6075c}} .
The likelihood of solutions as one scans {{formula:f92918a3-c8d9-428b-a9b3-1cf166757509}}  rapidly goes to zero below the true top-quark mass {{formula:e7206ef6-c24e-48c3-8f47-5ca2040ab734}} .
The parton distribution suppresses the likelihood above the true {{formula:90abb0e2-760d-467c-a9a7-a6699c22bf4d}} .
The net result gives the maximum likelihood near the true top-quark mass but suffers from a
systematic bias {{cite:deca71f35335f8f4682f5e4c3227ff30b8e7e125}}{{cite:bb8465bb11a9612adedbe43748871001ad34739c}} that must be removed by modeling {{cite:daae44da8d33d5be984a18e832e487a301ee1259}}.

One major advantage of using the {{formula:151e2390-2e1a-43b1-a0e7-f7c3f588185c}}  distribution (just as the {{formula:6384a265-4258-4976-9a7c-cef41b32ac81}}  distribution) is that the bulk of the relevant events are used to determine the mass
and not just those near the endpoint. To make the approach mostly model independent, we study on what factors the distributions shape depends.
We show that there is a strong dependence on upstream transverse momentum (UTM) which can be measured and used as an input and therefore does not increase the model dependency. We show there is no numerically significant dependence on the collision energy which is distributed according to the parton distribution functions.
This makes the distribution shape independent of the production cross section and the details of what happens upstream from the part of the decay chain that we are studying.
We model these effects with a simple Mathematica Monte Carlo event generator
assuming {{formula:26dc6555-36c6-4a47-940f-813ae9277ff4}}  GeV, {{formula:9178aa94-a787-4ec9-b769-d0e7f809bb61}}  GeV, and {{formula:6bd48a5a-8d89-4693-881c-442e1c6874c5}}  GeV.

Effect of Combinatorics Ambiguities

Just as in the topology in Fig REF  studied earlier, where {{formula:1b4e9f23-e4ae-49e6-ac2a-9ddaf6f7824c}}  decays via a three body decay, the branch assignments can be determined by either distinct OSSF pairs or by studying which OSSF pairs have both {{formula:a5a4f7f7-a153-4cbd-94fb-889b26579078}} .
In {{formula:0c849f6d-e5a5-42fd-99c2-a92252fd3d70}}  of the events, there is only one combination that satisfies this requirement. This allows us to know the branch assignment of {{formula:82bb5a6a-704e-4ab8-adbd-d208013cf879}}  of the four lepton events without ambiguity.

Unlike the three-body decay case, the order of the two leptons on each branch matters. The intermediate mass {{formula:0c1ca82c-aa25-4a17-8c67-c444cf2fbe64}}  depends on {{formula:4af19732-2000-4feb-8017-ebd206d7b6cf}}  and does not depend on {{formula:331e533e-aec5-41e7-aa9d-cba09ca7b4e7}} .
To resolve this ambiguity we consider the four combinations that preserve the branch assignment but differ in their ordering. The {{formula:95111afb-cd23-4c97-8289-1f9796db8366}}  for the event is the minimum of these combinations. Likewise the {{formula:77b2a937-a75f-404d-82bc-5a973f57c820}}  is the maximum of these combinations.
