Normally, a directory structure of a Java project corresponds
to the package naming; thus, the packages are named and
declared after the directories.
By the means of Java packages,
all the
classes within the project and external applications “know”
how to identify and import the classes they intend to use.
A fully-qualified
class name includes all the packages starting from the “root”
(the top-level directory of the hierarchy) all the way up to
the class itself, separated by a dot. The GIPSY Java packages
breakdown as of this writing corresponds to the Figure REF .
{{figure:b5022d8b-f119-4e68-963a-c213df5ab299}}

The logical breakdown was performed in accordance with the
original conceptual design primarily produced by Joey Paquet
and further by Aihua Wu and Bo Lu, has been the primary source
of the hierarchy plus any exceptions and extensions that
various team members come up with or have been forced to
during implementation were taken into account.

The basic structure is as follows. The top root hierarchy is
logically the gipsy package. The major non-utility packages
under it, which come from the conceptual design, are GIPC, GEE,
and RIPE. The major utility packages under gipsy that
are not present in the conceptual design are: interfaces
for most intermodule communication; wrappers for object
wrapping; storage for the serializable interface classes;
util for most common exceptions and utility modules (e.g. fast linked
list {{cite:851a2c591ee48620a77667232e5448d0afb357ef}}); and tests for the Unit and Regression Testing Suites.

Under the GIPC package the major modules (to be discussed later in
this chapter) include Preprocessing for general GIPSY program preprocessing,
intensional and imperative language compilers and their necessary
followers (GenericTranslator for the former and CommunicationProcedureGenerator
and SequentialThreadGenerator for the latter). Then the DFG package for
Lucid-to-data-flow-graph and back generation.

The GEE's main packages includes IDP for demand propagation and IVW
for caching and garbage collection.

Under RIPE we have interactive run-time editing and monitoring modules
that include textual editor, DFG editor, and the web-based editor.

GIPSY's major and minor modules are packaged
into a set of runnable .jar files and
distributed with wrapper scripts to be either
used as ordinary command line tools as a part
of GIPSY Development Kit or the WebEditor
web application. Different .jar files include
a subset of all GIPSY modules depending on the
need, e.g. GIPC includes GIPC-related classes
plus GEE as we allow to optionally invoke
GEE after successful compilation. RIPE, except itself,
needs both GIPC and GEE, whereas GEE does not at all
require presence of any other module. Thus, the GIPSY binary
distribution is broken down into five major .jar files
(notice, that these files do not include any external libraries GIPSY
references):

gipsy.jar simply includes almost all of GIPSY.

gipc.jar should be used/distributed as a part of
so-called “GIPSY Development Kit” if someone wants to be able to compile
intensional programs and optionally run them.

gee.jar represents GIPSY's non-interactive
run-time environment, the GEE. This can be distributed alone
to the hosts that only wish to run pre-compiled GIPSY programs
and have no development environment set up.

ripe.jar includes most of the interactive programming
environment of the GIPSY along with GIPC and GEE.

Regression.jar includes the Regression Testing application
plus all of GIPC and GEE as the most exercised modules for testing
as of this writing.

The Table REF  shows correspondence between the variety of modules and their
containment within a .jar file.
{{table:6fc24f54-281b-4338-b9e0-7f6af8c56b06}}

JLucid is limited only to GIPL-Java and Indexical Lucid-Java hybrids.

JLucid does not allow Java objects.

JLucid restricts the embed() mechanism only to itself and
its derivative – Objective Lucid.

Objective Lucid is primarily an experimental language to research on Java
objects in the intensional environment.

GICF addresses mostly the imperative compilers, but a similar approach
can be applied to the intensional and functional ones.

The future work to take on will focus in the following
areas to either address the limitations outlined in Section REF  or to introduce
new features, not necessarily all related to the topics of this
thesis.

Integration of the Demand Migration System (DMS) {{cite:b73a233bca6b91a2cca4526250ea5dd1f8d0e625}}.

Formal semantic verification from Indexical Lucid through Objective Lucid.

Placement of hybrid nodes into DFGs.

Security.

Trial C compiler with JNI.

Fully Explore Array Properties.

Genuine imperative compilers in GICF.

Introduction functional language compilers.

Visualization and control of communication patterns and load balancing.

Target Host Compilation.

Java wrapper for the DFG Editor of Yimin Ding.

The permanent is a scalar quantity computed from a matrix and has been
an active topic of research for well over a century. It plays a role
in cryptography and statistical physics where it is fundamental to
Ising and dimer models. While the determinant of an {{formula:6b942277-3a25-4e9f-af2f-a17c1e91d58d}} 
matrix can be evaluated exactly in sub-cubic time, efficient methods
for computing the permanent have remained elusive. Since the permanent
is {{formula:a31346a4-aed7-48b0-bffe-9456407ddbbc}} P-complete, efficient exact evaluations cannot be found in
general. The best exact methods improve over brute force ({{formula:218a84b0-53d4-40ef-a768-40d554bbd1c1}} ) and include Ryser's algorithm {{cite:cc8d78ab7665a77f804089eaf174083005ef69be}}, {{cite:44146120e9324af16608c73ee80407c6160371bd}} which
requires as many as {{formula:e2f8eda3-bbf7-41e1-afbe-52447e25ab35}}  arithmetic operations. Recently,
promising fully-polynomial randomized approximate schemes (FPRAS) have
emerged which provide arbitrarily close approximations. Many of these
methods build on initial results by Broder {{cite:137de20c643c04f93ecf69a0a0dd5ac072eb2f80}} who applied
Markov chain Monte Carlo (a popular tool in machine learning and
statistics) for sampling perfect matchings to approximate the
permanent. Recently, significant progress has produced an FPRAS that
can handle arbitrary {{formula:74c57040-489b-453d-ad4c-ae18983a08cf}}  matrices with non-negative entries
{{cite:1dce6b8001f05e652b5f12ceea15bbd2a6236bcb}}. The method uses Markov chain Monte Carlo and only
requires a polynomial order of samples.

However, while these methods have tight theoretical guarantees, they carry expensive constant factors, not to mention relatively high polynomial running times that discourage their usage in practical applications. In particular, we have experienced that the prominent algorithm in {{cite:1dce6b8001f05e652b5f12ceea15bbd2a6236bcb}} is slower than Ryser's exact algorithm for any feasible matrix size, and project that it only becomes faster around {{formula:3403d41b-d863-4309-9459-831aaced0327}} .

It remains to be seen if other approximate inference methods can be
brought to bear on the permanent. For instance, loopy belief
propagation has also recently gained prominence in the machine
learning community. The method is exact for singly-connected networks
such as trees. In certain special loopy graph cases, including graphs
with a single loop, bipartite matching graphs {{cite:62c3835f60a7d9d0455781936880ae6518e86115}} and
bipartite multi-matching graphs {{cite:fb4e51cff3f66ca5cfcd0497a27cc2d6a4d127b5}}, the convergence of BP
has been proven. In more general loopy graphs, loopy BP still
maintains some surprising empirical success. Theoretical
understanding of the convergence of loopy BP has recently been
improved by noting certain general conditions for its fixed points and
relating them to minima of Bethe free energy. This article proposes
belief propagation for computing the permanent and investigates some
theoretical and experimental properties.

In Section , we describe a probability distribution
parameterized by a matrix similar to those described in {{cite:62c3835f60a7d9d0455781936880ae6518e86115}}, {{cite:fb4e51cff3f66ca5cfcd0497a27cc2d6a4d127b5}} for which the partition function is exactly
the permanent. In Section , we discuss Bethe free
energy and introduce belief propagation as a method of finding a
suitable set of pseudo-marginals for the Bethe approximation. In
Section , we report results from experiments. We
then conclude with a brief discussion.

Given an {{formula:39293afb-de12-48d9-8a98-add0ef4cc199}}  non-negative matrix {{formula:bbd3bb02-9bb0-4ddd-81c8-43045714ab87}} , the matrix permanent is
{{formula:0ab88520-8c53-4cff-a46a-29166f365ad5}}

Here {{formula:ab695de4-6bc8-4bd8-a1ca-35301fd8d5bb}}  refers to the symmetric group on the set {{formula:ccba4614-94d0-48cd-b34e-d7371172acee}} , and can be thought of as the set of all permutations of the
columns of {{formula:6856ca4c-9d84-4163-8bdb-14665ee9d304}} . To gain some intuition toward the upcoming analysis,
we can think of the matrix {{formula:48f36840-2ce9-48da-acd0-72c28be77400}}  as defining some function {{formula:df734702-ec69-470a-a34c-82e0a181a03a}} 
over {{formula:aa5f8e65-13b2-4cdf-9b37-b2ace8e75c4a}} . In particular, the permanent can be rewritten as

function over the space of all permutations.

If we think of a permutation as a
perfect matching or assignment between a set of {{formula:11d6f223-b51d-4596-81f9-5572ade3746e}}  objects {{formula:0d4799c1-6dab-45c5-931d-f3364c83e6ed}}  and
another set of {{formula:fb9d0bb0-fbaf-45bd-926e-6ee01862f179}}  object {{formula:451b2dd4-f605-4302-ba41-34ee3ec634c9}} , we relax the domain by considering all
possible assignments of imperfect matchings for each item in the sets.

Consider the set of assignment variables {{formula:ebb0e5a9-5ed0-4714-8bf1-9d37cf442696}} ,
and the set of assignment variables {{formula:ea398fe9-bd29-4f19-808a-72a4a1754fb1}} , such
that {{formula:df41b495-4d4c-4b63-9afb-6f3444abf897}} . The value of the
variable {{formula:aac8c9df-e38b-4abe-8435-b98ceb67d68e}}  is the assignment for the {{formula:addabb4b-46b0-4db4-b6db-959df4793f73}} 'th object in {{formula:ee9d93b5-f175-4ac7-a560-3ae0d377eae0}} , in
other words the value of {{formula:54e68dd9-96b5-4f43-8453-fd2c8bc9be05}}  is the object in {{formula:edd03034-ae3e-47b7-bd9f-0c48f194f38a}}  being selected
(and vice versa for the variables {{formula:67eeae59-89a8-466c-885e-83b5ef65ee2d}} ).

We square-root the matrix entries because the factor formula
multiplies both potentials for the {{formula:5b00d84a-afd2-4c34-99b8-382789e29494}}  and {{formula:bc7d386f-b682-46f7-a6a8-d76c36eeb419}}  variables. We
use {{formula:2fe7577d-dba1-4fba-98ad-1e6041313c21}}  to refer to an indicator function such that
{{formula:7311c7de-ac65-4ad8-ae53-a5fa910bc609}}  and {{formula:ca0841a0-79f1-4058-8850-960fe6a20fcc}} . Then the {{formula:f44ba6be-72ed-4f53-a7ba-f1e7f717c8ee}}

the {{formula:3c20d002-2565-455c-aecb-4d745aa81209}} 'th object in {{formula:a09d658b-2486-4a8a-8239-1e69c37639a8}} , the {{formula:9a8b1a0c-4c2b-4577-a3dc-30b3daa5553e}} 'th object in {{formula:de13a847-9480-4958-aa0d-7c09d237903d}}  must be assigned to

goes to zero. Given these definitions, we can define the equivalent
density function that subsumes {{formula:68cbed74-b6d2-4ffa-93c6-f7d5cc93843d}}  as follows:

This permits us to write the following equivalent formulation of the permanent:

Finally, if we convert density function {{formula:18b8a51d-b9a3-4d53-9574-d7a93fb1b0a9}}  into a
valid probability, simply add a normalization constant to it, producing:
{{formula:d42820fe-10d8-42c9-b72c-44ddcd7707aa}}

The normalizer or partition function {{formula:55211067-58ef-4428-8f83-0437554e4354}}  is the sum of {{formula:c9f312c4-ec0c-4ddb-8232-1c648b97ac40}}  for
all possible inputs {{formula:06004138-57bc-46d0-95fd-ed748a574ca1}} . Therefore, the partition function
of this distribution is the matrix permanent of {{formula:c0dec33b-d15e-4af2-8e2a-33bd6c62205b}} .

To approximate the partition function, we use the Bethe free energy
approximation. The Bethe free energy of our distribution given
a belief state {{formula:6061a013-8e2a-4488-8f19-9990ae0de29b}}  is
{{formula:ca7d7dab-0927-4696-87c1-b90cfa0c040a}}

The belief state {{formula:11bdafa5-8b57-43fd-8799-9921eba00a24}}  is a set of pseudo-marginals that are only
locally consistent with each other, but need not necessarily achieve
global consistency and do not have to be true marginals of a single
global distribution. Thus, unlike the distributions evaluated by the
exact Gibbs free energy, the Bethe free energy involves pseudo-marginals
that do not necessarily agree with a true joint distribution over the
whole state-space. The only constraints pseudo-marginals of our
bipartite distribution obey (in addition to non-negativity) are the
linear local constraints:
{{formula:937821d5-4219-493f-8c87-a5a85dd03112}}

The class of true marginals is a subset of the class of
pseudo-marginals. In particular, true marginals also obey the
constraint {{formula:f2687ae6-dd5b-4a57-b2f9-57d4f1e57ace}} , which pseudo-marginals
are free to violate.

We will use the approximation
{{formula:8af4db03-a94d-4c5f-83b3-eeb691ec6eb4}}

The canonical algorithm for (locally) minimizing the Bethe free energy
is Belief Propagation. We use the dampened belief propagation
described in {{cite:c2888925a30ba4110d84027bc9087da88ee163b6}}, which the author derives as a (not
necessarily convex) minimization of Bethe free energy. Belief
Propagation is a message passing algorithm that iteratively updates
messages between variables that define the local beliefs. Let
{{formula:191ab23d-c300-4cc3-9fee-7a9c8cf37439}}  be the message from {{formula:895b75e9-4a4c-46b2-a099-a8334422f2ad}}  to {{formula:da408045-ebb1-4e72-b7d4-803951e9e8c0}} . Then the beliefs
are defined by the messages as follows:

{{formula:276d3ab4-c715-4265-b982-3bdfa1ff0537}}

In each iteration, the messages are updated according to the following
update formula:
{{formula:e6c31228-dfa4-4db0-81f3-8669a925c2f5}}

Finally, we dampen the messages to encourage a smoother optimization in log-space.
{{formula:9cf1b6ff-3ec6-4da4-bee8-15065cab3245}}

We use {{formula:afa87477-6b58-4567-9c43-6654f326d74d}}  as a dampening rate as in {{cite:c2888925a30ba4110d84027bc9087da88ee163b6}} and
dampen in log space because the messages of BP are
exponentiated Lagrange multipliers of Bethe optimization {{cite:c2888925a30ba4110d84027bc9087da88ee163b6}}, {{cite:5cc007a9f6e9841264390c5ca95b8715821996c4}}, {{cite:96b4f97cdcd63ef0cbe314e66b9f87f050594f6a}}. We next derive faster updates
of the messages (REF ) and the Bethe free energy
(REF ) with some careful algebraic tricks.

Computing sum-product belief propagation quickly for our distribution
is challenging since any one variable sends a message vector of length
{{formula:ba03371e-1bc2-4f2b-a21f-abab882cb063}}  to each of its {{formula:24968142-1d5e-4df4-8c7f-3e4955ac92a8}}  neighbors, so there are {{formula:f978d1c3-2367-40a9-bac7-920e51e7a47f}}  values to update
each iteration. One way to ease the computational load is to avoid
redundant computation. In Equation (REF ), the only
factor affected by the value of {{formula:e40ad15d-7930-4600-87d1-a9aef7feb8e8}}  is the {{formula:38a1e502-d512-43ba-80cd-68efa50240de}} 
function. Therefore, we can explicitly define the update rules based

fact that the computation for each setting of {{formula:daefe93b-5f99-4306-8486-e6ad0ac77fa5}}  is similar. When

We have reduced the full message vectors to only two possible values: {{formula:55afbce5-41ff-40c0-938b-743b39dcb256}}  is the message for when the variables are not matched and {{formula:23d0f4c9-4608-40c5-bfe3-e2c02eab4bb9}}  is for when they are matched. We further simplify the messages by dividing both values by {{formula:5238907a-d416-4a65-ac62-8ece7a1fa881}} . This gives us
{{formula:7935db71-9ce7-49a4-888e-6b823301b2f0}}

We can now define a fast message update rule that only needs to update one value between each variable.
{{formula:34491c3c-a50d-4ab9-bf19-f7305a94f1be}}

We can rewrite the belief update formulas using these new messages.
{{formula:0d1f324e-a090-4981-9434-c7bd2f53def7}}

With the simplified message updates, each iteration takes {{formula:a7e1b29f-defa-4fdf-a36f-f4e3c7910416}}  operations per node, resulting in an algorithm that takes {{formula:2fba6109-aa98-4028-afbe-32d10c605453}}  operations per iteration. We demonstrate experimentally that the algorithm converges to within a certain tolerance in a constant number of iterations with respect to {{formula:6c10f304-0431-4a98-8622-f35e1a140811}} , so in practice the {{formula:12240925-7cfb-47b8-b883-381fb5e3dd4a}}  operations it takes to compute Bethe free energy is the asymptotic bottleneck of our algorithm.

One important open question about this work is whether or not we can
guarantee convergence. Empirically, by initializing belief propagation to various random points in the feasible space, we found BP still converged to the same solution.
The max-product algorithm is guaranteed to
converge to the correct maximum matching {{cite:62c3835f60a7d9d0455781936880ae6518e86115}}, {{cite:fb4e51cff3f66ca5cfcd0497a27cc2d6a4d127b5}}
via arguments on the unwrapped computation tree of belief
propagation. The matching graphical model does not not meet the
sufficient conditions provided in {{cite:0de2fc4fa723c06e1a54315104d41e8b9768d839}} nor does our
distribution fit the criteria for non-convex convergence provided in
{{cite:b81ff7c45c69aa9347e5ff04054e1a3c96285951}} and {{cite:7b4e3d57565a28373aef1fc2c618e15f71bd0f94}}.

In our analysis, we have found that the Bethe free energy is certainly non-convex near the vertices of the distribution. That is, if we evaluate the Bethe free energy on pseudomarginals corresponding to exactly one matching, and take a tiny step in the direction of a non-adjacent matching vertex, Bethe free energy increases. On the other hand, when we initialize belief propagation such that the beliefs are at a vertex, BP moves away from the apparent local minimum and converges to the same solution as other initializations. This behavior implies that, while the Bethe free energy within the matching constraints is non-convex, it may still have a unique zero-gradient point despite not fitting the criteria in {{cite:7b4e3d57565a28373aef1fc2c618e15f71bd0f94}}, which exploit the strength of potentials.

Since all our empirical evidence implies that BP
always converges, we suspect that we have not yet correctly analyzed
the true space traversed during optimization. In particular, the
distribution described by Equation REF  is defined
over the set of all {{formula:264e57e9-3d6c-4175-abd1-420d3e9a495c}}  possible {{formula:381e759c-763f-4dda-8250-b0b3dd3f6937}}  states, while it is only
nonzero in {{formula:c1976eb7-309a-4ad5-bd75-a990c0b85a96}}  states. Any beliefs derived from belief propagation
obey similar constraints, so it is reasonable to suspect that careful
analysis of the optimization with special attention to the oddities of
the distribution could yield more promising theoretical
guarantees.

However, without being rigorous, we can note that the matching constraints created by the {{formula:0ece980e-471d-452d-bce3-14c7635573ac}}  functions enforce that the singleton beliefs are exactly the matched pairwise beliefs.
This means we can think of these as entries in a doubly-stochastic matrix {{formula:4fc8ad31-9ae0-4c8c-a5ca-dd01d7b39a0f}} .
{{formula:b6af2339-0100-4460-af98-40d5022cd266}}

Therefore it becomes clear that there is a strong connection to the Sinkhorn operation {{cite:62154ccc3407d19976000bd077255ec74f1e18e3}}, which iteratively scales rows and columns of a matrix until it converges to a doubly-stochastic matrix. It has been shown that the Sinkhorn operation effectively minimizes the pseudo-KL divergence between some matrix and the doubly-stochastic matrix{{cite:67846e2fc9555c9fedfc50d09c2be15766bf1d8b}}.
{{formula:13475dda-3e51-40de-aed9-2a451d4e52ab}}

Here the pseudo-KL divergence can be interpreted as the KL for each row and each column, each of which is an assignment distribution like in our matching setting. The Sinkhorn procedure is guaranteed to converge for indecomposable input matrices {{cite:62154ccc3407d19976000bd077255ec74f1e18e3}}, so the fact that the the procedure is reminiscent of ours is encouraging. However the two procedures differ enough that the guarantee does not directly translate.
{{figure:c3aec78d-d76f-490b-b44b-1e646689fcd8}}

In this section we evaluate the performance of this algorithm in
terms of running time and accuracy, and finally we exemplify a
possible usage of the approximate permanent as a kernel function.

We ran belief propagation to approximate the permanents of random
matrices of sizes {{formula:80d783ba-23a1-4530-bdc2-88a605ea62f2}} , recording the total running time and
the number of iterations to convergence. Surprisingly, the number of
iterations to convergence initially decreased as {{formula:39c7f417-5b47-4c08-a217-b90f8fb3b865}} 
grew, but appears to remain constant beyond {{formula:8c1097e0-ec3e-4ee0-9d38-974fedf2ec9b}}  or so.
Running time still increased because the cost of updating each
iteration well subsumes the decrease in iterations to convergence.

In our implementation, we checked for convergence by computing the
absolute change in all the messages from the previous iteration, and
considered the algorithm converged if the sum of all the changes of
all {{formula:5cf7e672-f15a-49fe-889e-edf9ba712a84}}  messages was less than {{formula:5875c1cc-0e9e-4c90-b2ee-308a414b3f35}} . In all cases, the resulting
beliefs were consistent with each other within comparable precision to
our convergence threshold. These experiments were run on a a 2.4 Ghz
Intel Core 2 Duo Apple Macintosh running Mac OS X 10.5. The code is in
{{formula:2cbfdfbc-a3ce-4bc3-94c3-f89c6b85695d}}  and compiled using gcc version 4.0.1.
{{table:87e16267-a670-4428-9292-b1778f8bf064}}{{figure:9d3a9ab8-800f-4799-9357-dd269667c479}}

We evaluate the accuracy of our algorithm by creating 1000 random
matrices of sizes 5, 8 and 200 matrices of size 10. The entries of each
of these matrices were randomly drawn from a uniform distribution in the interval {{formula:2efc2f57-4cca-4409-9204-b8ea016dc92b}} .
We computed the
true permanents of these matrices, then computed approximate
permanents using our Bethe approximation. We also computed an
approximate using a naive sampling method, where we sample by choosing
random permutations and storing a cumulative sum of each permutation's
corresponding product. We sampled for the same amount of actual time
our belief propagation algorithm took to converge. Finally we also
computed two weak approximations: the determinant and the scaled
product of the diagonal entries.

In order to be able to compare to the true permanent, we had to limit
this analysis to small matrices. However, since MCMC sampling methods
such as in {{cite:1dce6b8001f05e652b5f12ceea15bbd2a6236bcb}} take {{formula:4e3d27ea-1a04-4a95-8b78-0bef0f08ac0d}}  time to reach less
than some {{formula:b214eabe-3f94-40a1-9dd2-0865391c61a8}}  error, as matrix
size increases, the precision achievable in comparable time to our
algorithm would decrease. We scale the cumulative sum by
{{formula:b2c25d9d-69f1-4011-95e5-21c13d7755aa}} , where {{formula:eb25278b-e952-4373-87f3-6184ad2d5145}}  is the number of samples. This is the ratio
of the total possible permutations and the number of samples.

In our experiments, determinants and the products of diagonals are
neither accurate nor consistent approximations of the permanent. Sampling,
however, is accurate with respect to absolute distance to the
permanent, so for applications where that is most important, it may be
best to apply some sort of sampling method. Our Bethe approximation
seems the most consistent. While the approximations of the permanent are
off by a large amount, they seem to be consistently off by some
monotonic function of the true permanent. In many cases, this virtue
is more important than the absolute accuracy, since most applications
requiring a matrix permanent likely compare the permanents of
various matrices. These results are visualized for {{formula:aeefb267-4475-4a45-b919-ffe70ad420cc}}  in Figure
REF .

To measure the monotonicity and consistency of these approximations,
we consider the Kendall distance {{cite:cc78452174aa30624b711a6e08ed66f1c63300c8}} between the
ranking of the random matrices according to the true permanent and
their rankings according to the approximations. Kendall distance is a
popular way of measuring the distance between two permutations. The
Kendall distance between two permutations {{formula:94c1f335-93a1-4284-a780-76e5b939fe13}}  and {{formula:bad73d06-e2fb-4738-8c1f-a0aba4e0b324}}  is
{{formula:3ceb976b-f2f3-47df-94f9-79f6e5dc109f}}

In other words, it is the total number of pairs where {{formula:b3fce76c-0499-4438-a4de-52e5146e5ea6}}  and
{{formula:cc65afa0-240b-44c1-829c-e08c76d1b26a}}  disagree on the ordering. We normalize the Kendall distance by
dividing by {{formula:d39d4e59-a064-4f6c-ab4d-483041c22c20}} , the maximum possible distance between
permutations, so the distance will always be in the range
{{formula:a0cc95f1-0d46-46d7-9e01-68e4974ec2b6}} . Table REF  lists the Kendall distances between
the true permanent ranking and the four approximations. The Kendall
distance of the Bethe approximation is consistently less than that of
our sampler.
{{table:59542741-d677-4e03-8fdf-780488c8f3b7}}

To illustrate a possible usage of an efficient permanent
approximation, we use a recent result {{cite:ef049832dd7c3ee770f08ccf87bcd23b48025f3e}} proving that the
permanent of a valid kernel matrix between two sets of points is also
a valid kernel between point sets. Since the permanent is invariant to
permutation, we decided to try a few classification tasks using an
approximate permanent kernel. The permanent kernel is computed by
first computing a valid subkernel between a pairs of elements in two
sets, then the permanent of those subkernel evaluations is taken as
the kernel value between the data. Surprisingly, in experiments the kernel matrix
produced by our algorithm was a valid positive definite matrix. This
discovery opens up some intriguing questions to be explored later.

We ran a similar experiment to {{cite:b3d654abcf86f575275c29debbb96f0a979eed71}} where we took a the
first 200 examples of each of the Cleveland Heart Disease, Pima
Diabetes, and Ionosphere datasets from the UCI repository {{cite:64844765f58b41fead999752be6b4ae88face845}},
and randomly permuted the features of each example, then compare the
result of training an SVM on this shuffled data. We also provide the
performance of the kernels on the unshuffled data for
comparison. After normalizing the features of the data to the
{{formula:deae19ce-0a6e-478b-aad6-35dbb378d0bf}}  box, we chose three reasonable settings of {{formula:0299f2b4-13b1-41c7-b6e4-a0ac9a5ba833}}  for the
RBF kernels and cross validated over various settings of the
regularization parameter {{formula:c4276083-11ae-4487-8f16-3e2f30f7cd68}} . We used RBF kernels between pairs of
data as the permanent subkernel. Finally, we report the average error
over 50 random splits of 150 training points and 50 testing
points. Not surprisingly, the permanent kernel is robust to the
shuffling and outperforms the standard kernels.

We also tested the Bethe kernel on the pendigits dataset, also from
the UCI repository. The original pendigits data consists of
stylus coordinates of test subjects writing digits. We used the
preprocessed version that has been resampled spatially and
temporally. However, we omit the order information and treat the input
as a cloud of unordered points. Since there is a natural spatial
interpretation of this data, so we compare to sorting by distance from
origin, a simple method of handling unordered data. We chose slightly
different {{formula:da30cc48-573c-4452-8655-bcb28abaab0b}}  values for the RBF kernels. For this dataset, there
are 10 classes, one for each digit, so we used a one-versus-all
strategy for multi-class classification. Here we averaged over only 10
random splits of 300 training points and 300 testing points (see Table REF ).

Based on our experiments, the permanent kernel typically does not
outperform standard kernels when permutation invariance is not
inherently necessary in the data, but when we induce the necessity of
such invariance, its utility becomes clear.

We have described an algorithm based on BP over
a specific distribution that allows an efficient approximation of the
{{formula:960904c3-0671-4c40-80ab-2238efa5e121}}  matrix permanent operation. We write a probability distribution over matchings and use Bethe free energy to approximate the partition function of this distribution.
The algorithm is significantly faster than sampling methods, but attempts to minimize a function that approximates the permanent. Therefore it is limited by the quality of the Bethe approximation so it cannot be run longer to obtain a better approximation like sampling methods can. However, we have shown that even on small matrices where sampling methods can achieve extremely high accuracy of approximation, our method is more well behaved than sampling, which can approach the exact value from above or below.

In the future, we can try other methods of approximating the partition function such as generalized belief propagation {{cite:5cc007a9f6e9841264390c5ca95b8715821996c4}},
which takes advantage of higher order Kikuchi approximations of free
energy. Unfortunately the structure of our graphical model causes
higher order interactions to become expensive quickly, since each
variable has exactly {{formula:6266a6b0-ae45-4caa-8958-e3999462479e}}  neighbors. Similarly, the bounds on the
partition function in {{cite:e9be4ed745e64feeb1ac1c490ab9346fdf038e10}} are based on
spanning subtrees in the graph, and again the fully connected
bipartite structure makes it difficult to capture the true behavior of
the distribution with trees.

Finally, the positive definiteness of the kernels we
computed is surprising, and requires further analysis. The exact permanent of a valid kernel
forms a valid Mercer kernel {{cite:ef049832dd7c3ee770f08ccf87bcd23b48025f3e}} because it is a sum of positive products, but
since our algorithm outputs the results of an iterative approximation of the permanent, it
is not obvious why the resulting output would obey the positive definite constraints.

We have described an algorithm based on BP over
a specific distribution that allows an efficient approximation of the
{{formula:960904c3-0671-4c40-80ab-2238efa5e121}}  matrix permanent operation. We write a probability distribution over matchings and use Bethe free energy to approximate the partition function of this distribution.
The algorithm is significantly faster than sampling methods, but attempts to minimize a function that approximates the permanent. Therefore it is limited by the quality of the Bethe approximation so it cannot be run longer to obtain a better approximation like sampling methods can. However, we have shown that even on small matrices where sampling methods can achieve extremely high accuracy of approximation, our method is more well behaved than sampling, which can approach the exact value from above or below.

In the future, we can try other methods of approximating the partition function such as generalized belief propagation {{cite:5cc007a9f6e9841264390c5ca95b8715821996c4}},
which takes advantage of higher order Kikuchi approximations of free
energy. Unfortunately the structure of our graphical model causes
higher order interactions to become expensive quickly, since each
variable has exactly {{formula:6266a6b0-ae45-4caa-8958-e3999462479e}}  neighbors. Similarly, the bounds on the
partition function in {{cite:e9be4ed745e64feeb1ac1c490ab9346fdf038e10}} are based on
spanning subtrees in the graph, and again the fully connected
bipartite structure makes it difficult to capture the true behavior of
the distribution with trees.

Finally, the positive definiteness of the kernels we
computed is surprising, and requires further analysis. The exact permanent of a valid kernel
forms a valid Mercer kernel {{cite:ef049832dd7c3ee770f08ccf87bcd23b48025f3e}} because it is a sum of positive products, but
since our algorithm outputs the results of an iterative approximation of the permanent, it
is not obvious why the resulting output would obey the positive definite constraints.

In this paper we look at how a simple wall following system leads to chaos, when modeled as a mathematical system.
This shows the importance of understanding chaos in the creation of artificial intelligences for robots.
The model was originally described in the paper “Chaos in Wall Following Robots" by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler. A model for a simple wall following robot was described and it was shown that when following a sinusoidal wall the robot's behavior would undergo a transition to chaos via period doubling as the robot's field of view increased {{cite:2ba89510af0064903a36370068ca82b51867de57}}.
In this paper we extend this research by walls with discontinuous corners and show that the robot still experiences a transition into chaos.

The model for this simulation is small robot agent with an independent drive train and a simple forward pointing boundary sensor {{cite:2ba89510af0064903a36370068ca82b51867de57}}.
An independent drive train commonly found on tanks and the Mars Exploration Rovers allows the vehicle to turn in place by driving the wheels on each side in opposite directions.
The boundary sensor is only able to minimum distance to the boundary and not the shape or direction of the boundary.

Furthermore the sensor has field of view limited to {{formula:db0afe56-e962-4337-9c0a-9593b6c14626}} . Where {{formula:571e52c8-32a0-4646-885a-de6956deb545}}  is one of parameters varied in the experiment.

The most unrealistic part of this robot is that it can change its angular velocity (the rate at which it is turning)
instantaneously, allowing the robot to switch from a hard left turn to a hard right turn and back.
This can happen when the robot's sensor detects a wall at the edge of it's vision and then turns or moves away from the wall.
This is not physically possible but as long as the speed is low this approximates how real vehicles behave.
For the purpose of modeling the robot also maintains a constant velocity which we convivially set to one.

As such the robots position can be represented by an {{formula:7ee6c834-d8d9-46a5-bb57-16bf8a2a77c8}}  vector where {{formula:ec00b078-278d-48b7-a5dd-a00dadb7fbc3}}  is the counter-clockwise angle of the robot's direction of travel from the positive x-axis.
The velocity of the robot is represented by {{formula:33436b8d-b8ba-4c8c-8cf4-c2b64c34f6d8}}  and the angular velocity is {{formula:8af77d5a-f473-493a-9482-79a8c24730dc}} . (this makes the last equations somewhat trivial)

As the value of {{formula:f57c1f29-bee0-45d6-8919-5ef1632d9707}}  increases robot's path becomes slightly chaotic.
While the robot's path remains in a very narrow, and stable channel within that channel the path is chaotic.
With the sawtooth wave this behavior becomes most pronounced when {{formula:7e8fecfd-e52e-4390-8f49-f0ea7438bdb6}}  .
{{figure:7dc1062f-60b9-485b-a0e7-886442c9036a}}{{figure:90e3a006-be4f-4a09-9b58-e06975be38e6}}

Verhulst diagrams or more commonly cobweb plots were created of a single path to better view robot's behavior.
To do this a point from each period of the robot's path was selected.
For simplicity the points were when the x-coordinate was a multiple of the wavelength of the boundary.
Then either the {{formula:8d50fd6c-a843-400e-a4b2-d2cd8f832c60}}  or {{formula:3587617e-8767-4c32-a8d0-0994ed7e70b3}}  values could be used to make the Verhulst diagram.
The {{formula:148023ba-b82c-44a9-ad22-a1918b87dae5}}  value was chosen arbitrary.

In fact it was found that the robot tends to exhibit this chaotic behavior even at low {{formula:87736198-bd4c-4c09-a301-480458b8cdb5}}  where it appears stable.
This may be a property of having sharp corners in the boundary wave that are not present in a sinusoidal wave.
{{figure:3744874b-a7ff-4be3-ae45-04a7c3e96c12}}

For all three waves the chaotic patterns appeared to die down around {{formula:837e9670-623c-4abd-9a17-7dc86cf935e9}} .
Then after that all three waveforms undergo a transition to chaos.
To view the transition bifurcation diagrams were created for each type of wall.
Like the Verhulst diagrams the value of {{formula:8f605c6e-9fde-4972-a982-063f5c14e7a1}}  at the when {{formula:859dcdeb-999a-421d-ba66-1fe2f1ea5133}}  is a multiple of {{formula:b0fe8b94-0380-40bf-bcea-88c95aee1211}}  were taken from each simulation of the robot.
The first 30% of the values were discarded to ensure that the system and converged to it's attractor.

The sawtooth boundary produced an period doubling bifurcation diagram.
Where the full transition to chaos occurred when {{formula:4e6d3418-afce-46d1-b8db-49902cdf22da}} 
However an exception was also found when {{formula:4af7eff1-6dec-4687-8fff-09db9f6ab182}} .
The robot moved in the negative direction by turning counter clockwise in ellipses.
It may be that this is another attractor for the sawtooth boundary regardless of the {{formula:0c18598f-d73c-48cf-b5cf-ccaf45387c5d}}  value.
{{figure:c02164b1-7aaa-4598-91d5-737173f84827}}

When the robot was following a triangle wave it was found that the {{formula:cac45147-ee27-4026-8b73-73c5240d4596}}  values provided a better bifurcation diagram than the {{formula:ecac7d16-83a8-4a49-979d-ff33977cc8de}}  values.
The triangle wave boundary first cause chaotic behavior around {{formula:855005a2-3438-42d9-837c-cbff0b94cf8f}} 
The sharp disconnect when {{formula:c1d4cda6-025e-4db8-813a-6e071e4138fc}}  in the bifurcation diagram appears to be an indicator of a second attractor.
{{figure:a618337b-3c71-4b2d-be57-1cd85cc81b27}}

The square boundary gave results looking more similar to that of the triangle wave then the sawtooth wave.
It's first expression of chaos occurs around {{formula:59eb3c5c-fc64-45dd-aaa3-a417aeda785a}} 
Also around {{formula:bb686769-622b-48fb-b79e-835b47ccb82a}}  it too has a disconnect, with initial starting values of {{formula:ef18144e-93ad-4847-99ae-a4d4f629cf06}} .
In order to make the bifurcation diagram simulations were run for each {{formula:384b1bfc-b0ba-48f2-bce0-323160a3a977}}  value with a starting points at {{formula:676e586e-f240-4f0c-ad14-9ffc57b367e7}}  where for every half unit between {{formula:c76a9e37-9d3b-4784-bb90-d4527178ec47}}  and {{formula:f88f7e77-feac-40a6-8dd7-3b9782c40e87}} .
These two strange attractors actually curl around each other when visualized in 3d.
{{figure:2be28b5d-d1a3-4a60-8c2a-d7e27eae4254}}{{figure:f5f50376-5422-444f-8cce-484fa8ca71ca}}

In this work it was show that the behavior of a simple control system can under go a chaotic transition from a change in the environment.
A consistent pattern was still observable through out these changes.

Further improvements to the algorithm could be made by creating a spatial hash table of segments that maps the location of the robots to a list of segments that are with in the range of the robot.
This would reduce the number of tests the simulation performs by as much as 50%.

Further work beyond optimizations of the algorithm involve adding additional robot agents for make a swarm.
The swarm of wall following robots would interact with each other and the wall, which leads to a rich dynamical system.
Research on the conditions when the swarm behaved chaotically and when it did not would be done.

Valiant, in his celebrated work {{cite:07f28176ceaa5d58146dff759b6a02887421e5f4}} on circuit lower bounds for
computing linear transformations {{formula:9c36ab35-18f6-42f4-b981-e43ca39a95aa}}  for a
field {{formula:280bb4dd-8746-47d2-9c7f-08a03c3a1e37}} , initiated the study of rigid matrices. If explicit rigid
matrices of certain parameters can be constructed it would result in
superlinear lower bounds for logarithmic depth linear circuits over
{{formula:9b75efa5-dab6-401a-aa79-c7f13da93b2a}} . This problem and the construction of such rigid matrices has
remained elusive for over three decades.

Alon, Panigrahy and Yekhanin {{cite:7d30aca12cf92d864ffb309c2055e1badec9a1b3}} recently proposed a problem
that appears to be of intermediate difficulty. Given a subspace {{formula:cd3a363b-6190-4cd8-921d-4bb13ab76403}}  of
{{formula:2f43bafc-1af4-4738-adfc-ffda9bcf3513}}  by its basis and a number {{formula:c60f18e3-2dae-42d6-b3fd-fc1aadd8b2f6}}  as input, the problem is
to compute in deterministic polynomial time a point {{formula:15f92c38-94a1-47cd-b0b1-53d559358fb1}}  such
that {{formula:dab3a023-5d40-47a4-838d-2dc0f90b40a4}}  for all {{formula:3e694737-a376-40c8-9d70-4257db63af82}} , where {{formula:60f0cede-104c-43ac-8fe4-dd17e9fa0a3a}}  is the
Hamming distance. They call this the Remote Point Problem. The
point {{formula:aaea0dfb-5c93-4e23-86b3-e59a2fbc2bc5}}  is said to be {{formula:9a42093b-83a6-42e1-a425-974113aa0bde}} -far from the subspace {{formula:ce4ac455-876c-4a84-a722-a5652c40eca2}} .

Alon et al {{cite:7d30aca12cf92d864ffb309c2055e1badec9a1b3}} give a nice polynomial time-bounded (in {{formula:c80a40b9-b3a4-4eca-83c0-e2483e5953a9}} )
algorithm for computing a {{formula:90fd835f-74b5-416a-9042-1fccc15ddb6e}}  that is {{formula:3645ba0d-1045-4ba6-b781-559c7edae73c}} -far from a
given subspace {{formula:e9b4e55d-5ba1-43aa-88d5-6856541b8eb7}}  of dimension {{formula:3be8e1c6-ef3e-4536-93fd-e67cae267409}}  and {{formula:ff57da18-582c-41fb-b201-c22ca750416c}}  is a fixed constant. For
{{formula:a09643fc-9880-46fe-bed5-e5c52eeb0e79}}  such that {{formula:f94ec6ce-caa9-43ae-98bd-ccec65d5e753}}  they give a polynomial-time algorithm
for computing a point {{formula:3df393e2-aab5-49f5-9aee-ba4584fdb27e}}  that is {{formula:4392ded5-25c5-4451-93f1-acb458d24ad8}} -far
from {{formula:d6faed36-b518-4741-84d2-6ffef5ecf717}} .

In {{cite:758b9c174127d4edd8e5adf7a6fb5f7e73b5a924}} we recently investigated the problem of proving circuit
lower bounds in the presence of help functions. Specifically, one of
the problems we consider is proving lower bounds for constant-depth
Boolean circuits which can take a given set of (arbitrary) help
functions {{formula:3c4e953d-97c6-46e9-8f03-93414cd3bd70}}  at the input level, where
{{formula:c59deb98-7507-44ac-8d28-2a6955b3f5a1}}  for each {{formula:efcc1d84-f81f-467d-870e-e0a75979835e}} . Proving explicit
lower bounds for this model would allow us to separate EXP from the
polynomial-time many-one closure of nonuniform {{formula:7809debe-88f4-4aa9-8f37-915555c49582}} . We show that
it suffices to find a polynomial-time solution to the Remote Point
Problem for parameters {{formula:e70f02d8-01fb-4f0b-995b-1046fe289f4a}}  and
{{formula:ae4a3b59-ab58-496a-830a-9428d690d855}}  for all constants {{formula:262c7ce9-4b33-4833-b61b-7192deea7950}}  and {{formula:ec3482f1-ea45-4710-8113-5c38a49cb997}} .
Unfortunately, the parameters of the Alon et al algorithm are
inadequate for our application.

However, motivated by this connection, in the present paper we carry
out a more detailed study of the Remote Point Problem as an
algorithmic question. We briefly summarize our results.

1.   The first question we address is whether we can
give a deterministic parallel (i.e. NC) algorithm for the problem —
Alon et al's algorithm is inherently sequential as it is based on the
method of conditional probabilities and pessimistic estimators.

It turns out an element of an {{formula:fa6f180b-c4a6-4484-9c25-ae196abcd1c4}} -bias space for suitably
chosen {{formula:553a3477-6099-4ba4-9da1-8f2aea002767}}  is a solution to the Remote Point Problem which
gives us an NC algorithm quite easily.

2.   Since the RPP for {{formula:f1104aa3-6aaf-4d2b-a550-ee6c5b202c12}}  can be solved
using small bias spaces, it naturally leads us to address the problem
in a more general group-theoretic setting.

In the generalization we study we will replace {{formula:05e9a088-ca6b-4580-a372-968fa507c07c}}  with an
arbitrary fixed finite group {{formula:f3616bf4-65f1-43f2-ad43-3ca85e2309ba}}  such that {{formula:554964c8-75d4-49b7-b8d3-fd33c8b82bef}} . Hence we
will have the {{formula:42064092-b7ca-4375-9a23-23c77ca579f1}} -fold product group {{formula:fa5d2172-fae5-40b7-a24f-103530570c76}}  instead of the vector
space {{formula:a9235e48-5890-40d2-8f97-19861e8c4684}} .

A simple counting argument shows that there is a valid solution to the

We are also interested in a special case of this problem which we now

{{cite:7e61923ef17dc256799a4a9c7e0ef8676c412f2b}}. However, we are unable to compute a (good enough)

At low energy scale, interactions among electrons
largely determine the structure, phases, and stability of matter.
Although this fact is well known, pragmatic first-priniciples/quantum-mechanical
calculations to determine various properties of many-electron systems are often hindered by
two factors. First, in most condensed matter systems, the typical interaction energy between electrons
(the electric coupling constant {{formula:c3edfe6c-42bc-405c-b27f-ea90c9527ae8}}  divided by average electron-electron separation) is often larger
than the typical kinetic/Fermi energy of electrons. The results is that a perturbative expansion using
{{formula:a4161c7a-49fe-4c93-a59d-336b158b8afa}}  as the expansion parameter may not be fruitful. This is particularly true for
strongly correlated systems. Second, there is an exponential increase in the number of
degrees of freedom as the number of electrons involved
increases. When the number of electrons becomes large, according to Kohn,{{cite:d6ee4c1b0d81ca7a7dd6bccf32de2f4949d09a02}} calculations
based on constructing many-electron wave functions soon lose accuracy and
will be stopped by an “exponential wall".
It is thus imperative to have a method that goes beyond the conventional perturbative scheme
using {{formula:7c8a3eb3-fc3e-41df-a724-731fc1849532}}  as the expansion parameter and whose computational complexity does not
grow exponentially with the number of electrons involved.

In 1964, Hohenberg and Kohn {{cite:99afa81a68b8c78156bc8d1bd9ba5750e50fba07}} proved a theorem stating that there exists
a unique description of the ground state of a many-body system in terms of
the expectation value of the particle-density operator. This theorem started the
development of the density functional theory (DFT), which offers a possibility
of finding the ground state energy {{formula:688323ea-80d2-4436-8203-013d5e9687f4}}  by minimizing the energy functional {{formula:9409d51f-2750-43fa-940b-ecd6459bdc81}} 
that depends on the charge density {{formula:09dd7944-62b4-43b6-a2aa-37aba4e49a39}}  only:
{{formula:4e0abf46-f1d1-4713-8469-92ab3eb7bad3}}

with {{formula:aa1ddd50-7e03-40ac-9e98-207d3f787508}}  representing the external one-particle potential of the system. The electronic
density {{formula:815e403e-ad4d-45af-97cf-1f905fa02589}} , which minimizes the energy functional {{formula:317cc507-ca5e-45cf-a7a1-d3ee1ce27ecf}} , is the ground state electronic density.
Hohenberg and Kohn showed that the energy functional {{formula:7ef6c47a-962a-4cfc-940a-b3dfed841835}}  can be decomposed into
{{formula:99b4acbe-61d2-4bcf-8c61-6598fd1e58db}}

with {{formula:50bb13f0-48a6-4e51-b1e1-922c80a8346f}}  being a universal functional independent of the
external potential {{formula:7c127098-7f3a-4f50-95da-72cf01e74a6d}} . Mermin{{cite:f7df863e9ecaecadf21df3e0df392047b83d6d59}} extended this theorem to
finite temperature with {{formula:7f29f097-1a45-415f-86e6-18e8819bb75e}}  in (REF ) replaced by the grand potential,
and {{formula:53dae537-f7ef-4740-878e-73fec5555c16}}  replaced by a different
universal functional. The electron density {{formula:3a19b1df-7352-4a46-9ba1-b1332e2b6163}} , minimizing the grand potential functional,
corresponds to the electron density at thermal equilibrium.

To make practical use of the DFT, however, a recipe to compute the energy functional is needed.
Kohn and Sham{{cite:7bd42c6c991a25f09a0dcd49f710661083efbe2e}} proposed a decomposition scheme, aiming to
express the energy functional {{formula:235bd6d3-57f9-4bce-b709-b9ad18543b61}}  via an auxiliary, noninteracting
system that yields a particle density identical to that of the physical ground state.
For a typical nonrelativistic many-fermion system,
described by the Hamiltonian
{{formula:4aa78c64-e17f-4faf-8cdd-84f2a1c6fcbd}}

the Kohn-Sham decomposition takes the form
{{formula:4f1bb8c3-4011-42af-8baf-8dea7ae38d37}}

where the chemical potential {{formula:84fa6088-1c33-4e08-9224-265313c7ef09}}  is introduced to ensure {{formula:940f265f-ce1c-4d6e-bebd-17dd2ce01e8b}} , with {{formula:617c1bf3-f6c7-4bc4-ae10-babad87bcc13}}  being the
number of electrons.
Here {{formula:757d4aa4-d5e4-42fd-9968-942f98801fb7}}  is the kinetic energy of an auxiliary system of
noninteracting fermions that yields the electron density {{formula:45f0ff99-9b94-4b97-9a9e-4df979d90d7f}} ,
and the density functional {{formula:c7f9b8b0-106e-40a7-b240-40a948beea68}}  is the so-called exchange-correlation energy functional.
Given {{formula:6c587d27-1892-4d6b-b7fd-5e2dbec75680}}  and provided that it is differentiable, one may
minimize the functional {{formula:9eaef153-fd06-4390-8690-2ebb3e1a477e}}  to arrive at
the familiar Kohn-Sham single-particle equations{{cite:8f323e734444ef84b46d2ff459621db5e736fd12}}
{{formula:d2623782-8703-4d02-bb7d-62cf13d77e3e}}

All of the many-particle complexity
is now completely hidden in the exchange-correlation energy functional.

Although {{formula:70fef2bb-b919-42b1-9dc4-689f841da157}}  is universal,{{cite:99afa81a68b8c78156bc8d1bd9ba5750e50fba07}} there exists no
simple means thus far to obtain it. As a consequence, various ad hoc exchange-correlation density functionals
have been suggested/needed to yield acceptable results in different settings {{cite:1825d63d7d2c298f66bfa86862c87ae8c469b9d4}}, {{cite:a883e373efcae42ba3e3341342a9821828a4faaf}}, {{cite:09729c6c5c93d347d2f80b3842f1e53b2dd9e55b}}, {{cite:db9a138339d2219b2a0a06196ca44079cbca9f28}}
when employing the Kohn-Sham scheme.
Limitations of these approximate functionals have been discussed.{{cite:fa04979b02a726bc00cf13062256c125bf8faee1}}, {{cite:d0ddbe7d249460baa81754f78e970456c05dc0f7}}
Some of the failures while using ad hoc density functionals can be attributed to
misuse of the density-functional theory. For example,
it is sometimes neglected that the electron density {{formula:12eba9d4-f366-4376-87b6-671f27b10468}}  achievable
via introduction of a source potential
must obey {{formula:820a7f3f-6ba2-4f53-b947-d8896eeee7fa}}  and
does not cover the functional space {{formula:0e4ed58f-78f7-401a-8364-2cdcd2a8dd0a}} , a problem also known
as the {{formula:b6ec69ac-1f7f-4181-b6a3-67dca3954852}} -representability. {{cite:6644219b7019114936266b26cc0f9b2d1e00f8df}}, {{cite:dde0a5e4fef5bf2f21b05dccfbb27aec1a00a868}}, {{cite:d42d037fcaee3cac6dd3138eed26d4451d542336}}
As pointed out in reference VF95,
neglecting these constraints may lead to conclusions {{cite:bed127bd18ebaef0e537895d436796fde4ddff67}} that are
not always valid.

The main objective of the DFT is to
describe a many-body system in terms of the expectation value of the particle density operator.
In fact, the use of the expectation value of a suitable operator to describe a many-body system
via Legendre transformation, first introduced
into quantum field theory by Jona-Lasinio,{{cite:41c889c57ddac9da690af1c76b048668fb5666a2}} is known as the effective action formalism.
As the temperature approaches zero, the effective potential
becomes the ground state energy. This connection suggests that effective action formalism
can be used to achieve the general goal of the DFT: describing a many-particle system
in terms of the expectation value of the density operator. A number of publications {{cite:9c925e258bc1c445f01075e6da623a3b8e7acffe}}, {{cite:eb44fd7833f1dab909c7232a752dd560e64f9a05}}, {{cite:ef421621b47727be58c63f27da4c4004a5ad1bf3}}, {{cite:81fadf16ba4acd8a1e2a5c8416ea5af367d132c0}}
showed that at zero temperature the effective action plus {{formula:55b79339-1190-4cb1-9502-224390166941}}  is the ground state energy,
linking effective action to the DFT.

Existing methods of expressing DFT via effective action formalism
can be classified roughly into two categories: either (a) by introducing
an auxiliary field or (b) by using a perturbative scheme assuming the electric coupling
as a small parameter. The former category includes a method developed by Fukuda et al. {{cite:9c925e258bc1c445f01075e6da623a3b8e7acffe}}
and that developed by Polonyi and Sailer. {{cite:81fadf16ba4acd8a1e2a5c8416ea5af367d132c0}} The latter scheme is used by Valiev and Fernando{{cite:ef421621b47727be58c63f27da4c4004a5ad1bf3}}
and by Fukuda et al. {{cite:eb44fd7833f1dab909c7232a752dd560e64f9a05}}.

The strengths of the auxiliary field approach often come from the simplicity
of the effective action expression and from the fact that in principle each term already includes infinitely many
Feynman diagrams.{{cite:17d44636b2331c6dd4f1ce999e04305a3b32aecc}} However, as pointed out by Fukuda et al.,{{cite:9c925e258bc1c445f01075e6da623a3b8e7acffe}}
the auxiliary field approach seems to lack a direct connection to the Kohn-Sham scheme.
Valiev and Fernando {{cite:16b2442dc8dc321f1bf4847750a6388296be6854}} introduced an auxiliary field to compute
the exchange-correlation energy. However, the source term they introduced is coupled to the
auxiliary field instead of the electron density operator. Furthermore,
as pointed out by the authors themselves, {{cite:ef421621b47727be58c63f27da4c4004a5ad1bf3}}
an artificial decomposition of the auxiliary field into a sum of the Hartree potential,
the exchange correlation potential, and the remaining fluctuations is needed to write down the exchange-correlation energy.

There are two advantages when one uses electric coupling in the perturbative (diagrammatic) expansion
without introducing an auxiliary field. First, under the effective action formalism of this type,
a direct connection to the Kohn-Sham scheme can be made. {{cite:ef421621b47727be58c63f27da4c4004a5ad1bf3}}, {{cite:eb44fd7833f1dab909c7232a752dd560e64f9a05}}
Second, there exist other {{formula:ca2b3311-8887-40af-b4f1-c2decfe4ed11}}  expansion-based developments that can be used to
obtain {{formula:215ea8b4-e082-455c-9a7b-9b75fd766e10}} , the universal density functional (UDF).
For example, with increasingly complex incorporation of KS
orbitals and energies at each order of {{formula:18149479-99af-48ec-964c-b14061c0fa80}} ,
Görling and Levy {{cite:b46d254787b00098bc1dc47078f00b0a8872e716}} wrote {{formula:f2a6db85-f7c4-4784-9e34-8b4c776312b3}}  as a perturbation series.
Employing the Luttinger-Ward {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}} method that uses {{formula:10714d66-7bcf-4dfe-8cf1-e87e8b184544}}  as the
perturbative expansion parameter to calculate electron self-energy,
Sham and Schlüter expressed {{formula:b07081e6-a6ce-49bd-9e44-dee7cb44c8d2}}  as a rather convoluted implicit functional of
electron density.{{cite:758f4c139b872d77a345ad87a8f79f0a69ad4739}}, {{cite:085b279e5e83c0ed74dc964a1b66e866ecac28c0}} As shown by Tokatly and Pankratov,{{cite:d3ad5f3dedf73460bfcc3c585089c41a093b0c4a}} these methods mentioned above
can be expressed diagrammatically.
However, the problem associated with {{formula:9216f19e-4383-47ff-8764-e33777fb4280}}  based expansion remains.
As described in reference NegeleOrlandbook, the expansion
using {{formula:e3f8e822-776c-4d51-95c1-453d766a8ae9}}  is only good when
{{formula:f634cbc3-53c9-4758-8459-54714bedec69}}  is very small. Whether one can treat {{formula:060bfb4f-c203-416c-a1c6-997a9e798904}}  as a small parameter or not depends on the
kinetic/Fermi energy of the electrons and the strength as well as the magnitude of variation of
the single-particle potential involved. As a matter of fact,
the success {{cite:0bdcfd8ba557bc50dab69ea4c296373f2c9fb015}} in employing the GW approximation {{cite:0791a37c48e168339589190141d04b17a247972e}} indicates
that not treating {{formula:dc7d2c23-2d74-497c-851b-baf496914abf}}  as small may lead to results closer to experimental outcomes.

In principle, the problem associated with assuming {{formula:07bb30bd-ba53-4445-b17f-e41221d1ac17}}  small can be tamed by summing an
infinite subset of Feynman diagrams. However,
as pointed out by Hedin, {{cite:0791a37c48e168339589190141d04b17a247972e}} it is nontrivial to devise a systematic
resummation scheme where each new term is free from divergence even if {{formula:d0349d00-234f-43df-b661-0e1a1e457e64}}  and for which
the sum of the new terms, each containing an infinitely many Feynman diagrams,
accounts completely and non-redundantly for all conventional {{formula:fe4fe325-2d5f-4ee1-96af-bfb0e7c0f96c}}  expansion diagrams.
In this paper, without assuming {{formula:7b9f04da-9ba1-4970-bbb4-72517b5383a0}}  small we develop an auxiliary field method
that makes a direct connection to the Kohn-Sham scheme and at the same time provides equivalently
a systematic resummation scheme.

A commonly used approximation for
the density functional is the so-called
local density approximation (LDA) in which the exchange-correlation energy is
approximated by a linear functional {{formula:b635b4b8-de29-4cce-a08f-ee92642ba617}} , where
{{formula:92ea229d-7617-4aac-9dd9-38bd3b3e164d}}  is a function of the local density (not a functional of the density profile).
See reference Kohn99 for a nontechnical review.
This approximation ignores the nonlocal effect of the density profile, i.e., it assumes that {{formula:2c4f9565-67a4-4378-adf9-e2331fbf0434}} 
only depends on the value of {{formula:ca4f9a3b-f51f-475c-8a14-bbf6a51aba4c}}  at {{formula:0fccae9f-1fed-4973-b358-879561801f61}}  but not on the density {{formula:e761f661-b7d2-4b51-a55f-39e60379d20f}}  at
locations other than {{formula:dea47e99-d381-4bac-9076-154933d2b4d1}} . To complement the LDA by incorporating nonlocal
density dependence, Polonyi and Sailer {{cite:81fadf16ba4acd8a1e2a5c8416ea5af367d132c0}} proposed
the {{formula:9adb1258-de25-4618-93be-d38d08c338ea}} -local approximation for the density functional, based on an idea
very similar to the cluster expansion in statistical physics.
Using this method to obtain explicit expressions for the approximate functional
with {{formula:2c34a25f-ff50-4fd6-8caa-d3c71e42de57}} , however, becomes increasingly challenging due to the necessity of
going through the coupling constant integration
as required by the Hellmann-Feynman theorem.{{cite:526d2c8a6acb335802f1be21db7f098b8c118753}}, {{cite:656093dc3b12b6e3a6462688d747f2d1b3d50a5e}}

Another route to developing density functionals is via the so-called
optimal effective potential (OEP) methods. {{cite:39289ed58695db7103eb0aba4936e79ba79bde12}}, {{cite:076712cd4ca6493d01da03bce9261d525468300f}}, {{cite:ef99d8fe14a4da945af95913e58d397517179bb6}}
These methods typically start by introducing a priori an approximate, explicitly {{cite:c8108544b5095903450fd7d3e76b7aa62755d6c2}}
orbital-dependent functional. (The approximate functional can be either Hartree-Fock
or a more elaborated form.) The procedure then continues with
a minimization of the functional via varying single-particle
KS orbitals and associated energies. Recently, the definition of OEP methods has been
generalized {{cite:f2dc222ff7c5a85e8c8e61ce77175c393db0c5a5}}, {{cite:973b2d538766ef6685bc7d0e2637b78b821a881f}} to include
functionals dependent on either Green's function, the self-energy, or the KS potential.
Since our effective action based functional is based on self-consistently obtaining
the KS potential, it falls exactly in the latter category. The
generalized definition of OEP methods is probably becoming the standard definition now.
A general characteristic of OEP methods is that the functional arguments
–be they KS orbitals/energies, Green's functions, self energies, or KS potentials–
are obtained via self-consistent procedure. Therefore, even with correction terms derived from
pertrubative expansion, the self-consistency condition for OEP methods
distinguishes them from regular pertrubative methods. The important matter here is whether
an OEP functional can be systematically improved and possibly be asymptotically exact
or not.

Based on effective action formalism, the OEP functional proposed here is asymptotically exact
and can be shown to give rise to the desired UDF. Containing all the {{formula:e3bec729-9562-463d-88b2-c524b6872036}} -local interaction
vertices, our method can provide equivalent approximate functionals for {{formula:d2d0cce0-273c-43a5-ad8c-9db7579520a4}} 
without going through the Hellmann-Feynman theorem.
Since we focus on describing the proposed approach in a manner as self-contained as possible,
we have included a non-negligible amount of standard materials available in
existing literature/textbooks while keeping only a small portion of the existing literature
that we deem closely related to the present manuscript.
Readers interested in gaining a broad background are
referred to references KK08 and BdGdCetal01,Furnstahl07,JG89,BM07
for reviews on the extensive body of literature in the DFT and related many-body approaches.
Expert readers should note that new developments are mainly provided in sections IIIB-D.
Although section IV and end of section V also contain some
useful developments, they typically rederive/re-express known results
within our framework and/or provide contrast with existing methods.
Section VI contains some insight of problems shared in post Hartree corrections.

This paper is otherwise organized as follows. We first establish the notation in section ,
followed by the development of the general formalism in section .
The purpose of subsection REF  is to provide a computational recipe
and to give some perspectives on computational complexity: no novelty is claimed here.
In section , we discuss a number of case studies: the emergence
of the universal functional {{formula:854a1ab3-2c0c-435c-b6b5-f8290e5f6f1c}}  in Eq. (REF ) at arbitrary temperature,
the behavior of the effective potential and the single electron limit at zero temperature,
the screening effect, as well as the case of homogeneous electron gas.
In section , we then discuss the excitations of the system, and
make comparisons with existing studies along this direction.
An alternative formalism to obtain the effective action is then discussed in section .
We conclude with the discussion and future directions section, in which we also provide some more relations/comparisons
to other methods as well as some technical remarks.

have an exact correspondence to the Kohn-Sham decomposition, but has the advantage
that the correction terms may be obtained without further functional derivatives.
The first route, as will be described later in this section,
gives a recipe equivalent to the Kohn-Sham decomposition, together with a way
to calculate the exchange-correlation functional in a self-consistent manner.

This auxiliary field approach was pursued in an earlier publication, {{cite:9c925e258bc1c445f01075e6da623a3b8e7acffe}} but
there it was concluded that it seems infeasible to make a direct connection
to the Kohn-Sham scheme. Using the inversion method, {{cite:eb44fd7833f1dab909c7232a752dd560e64f9a05}} we show explicitly how
the connection to the Kohn-Sham scheme can be made. One advantage of the
auxiliary field method is that each Feynman diagram here corresponds to the sum of
infinitely many Feynman diagrams in standard perturbative field theory calculations {{cite:17d44636b2331c6dd4f1ce999e04305a3b32aecc}} such as
used in reference VF97arxiv. Subsections REF  through REF 
detail the proposed approach. Subsection REF  lays out the computational procedure
to give some perspectives on computational complexity.

When the system contains only one electron and when the energy difference
between the first excited state and the ground state is much larger than
{{formula:b8711843-3571-44d2-8c86-9a0fddf9c239}} , there will be no particle-hole pairs. Consequently, there should be no
exchange-correlation energy as well as the Hartree energy.
When one employs empirical density functionals, this feature
is unlikely to be preserved – an issue known as the self-interaction problem.
It is customary to define the exchange-correlation energy {{formula:cec408f6-d5f9-4d40-b821-bb29ff912b29}}  as the sum
of the Fock exchange energy {{formula:d34fc8b4-645a-4b6d-b5cf-7a88ae8c1c11}}  and the correlation energy {{formula:a95c9460-74a6-4150-a14c-4a4f753f6243}} .
Since it is easy to show that the exchange energy {{formula:ce7f3f0d-c00b-460e-87d6-c655582aea92}} 
exactly cancels the Hartree energy in the case of one electron, one easily concludes
that {{formula:05ee890a-38d7-4723-8f95-c4bb4b733cf3}}  for the one electron case. This argument has been used, for example, by
Perdew and Zunger.{{cite:e30f28e404796efa54980bce790dcf4d3da39d24}} However, from the diagrammatic expansion
point of view, the Hartree term and the Fock exchange term correspond only to the first
order (in terms of {{formula:87534aba-c528-43ba-9769-c1e60e997292}} ) diagrams. The cancellation of the first order terms does not imply
that the higher order diagrams, making up {{formula:937dc18b-823f-4d74-9908-cc088b1dd73f}} , will give no contribution.
That is, although the fact that {{formula:d7081ef6-18ec-4e5b-ba1c-77e298f82347}}  for one electron system can be argued,
a formal diagrammatic exposition incorporating all higher orders
is needed to justify the asymptotic exactness of the proposed functional.

The purpose of this section is to illustrate how

the self-interaction will remain if one truncate the series in eq. (REF ).
While the exchange-only functional will have no self-interaction problem, as we will
show below it is not because the exchange-only functional is an approach with more
correct physics, but because the simplification it makes is equivalent to
completely ignoring the correlation energy.

Except during the intermediate steps of computing the excitation spectrum, one deals with
the time independent system. Note that {{formula:f52514ea-1d4c-4b65-91b1-0346cce7ed07}}  plays the role of {{formula:e53c4dcd-0c7f-47ce-bfe8-58bc219d45a9}}

in the long wave length limit is a screened one instead of the bare Coulomb interaction.
It should be noted that the use of this screened propagator dates back half a century.
DuBois {{cite:a99fe440aa3c1048385a54251a9f74a889009943}} replaced the bare Coulomb interaction by the screened interaction
in his study of electron interactions. Hedin {{cite:0791a37c48e168339589190141d04b17a247972e}} also used it to replace the
bare Coulomb interaction in the expansion of the Luttinger-Ward functional, {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}}
resulting in the so-called GW approximation. The differences among the three mentioned approaches should
be described. In both DuBois's and Hedin's formalism, they use the full polarization of the
interacting system. The difference between their formalism is in the electron propagators employed.
In DuBois's approach, the free electron propagator is used, while in Hedin's method,
similar to the Luttinger-Ward functional, {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}} the full
electron propagator is employed. In our approach, it is the polarization of the KS system that
enters the calculation and the electron propagator entering the
diagrammatic calculation is the noninteracting KS Green's function.

Being the foundation for the LDA of the DFT,
the homogeneous electron gas (HEG) is also a simplified model
for a metal or a plasma. The HEG system is an interacting electron gas placed in
a uniformly distributed positive background chosen to ensure that the
total system is neutral. Due to the translational symmetry of the HEG system,
the one-particle propagator functions only depend on the coordinate difference between
two variables (space-time points) instead of on both variables.
Consequently, each propagator (Green's function) carries a definite momentum
even if the Coulomb interaction among electrons is fully taken into
consideration.

Investigation of the HEG system dates back to 1930s by
Wigner,{{cite:6900b191408bc1a0d7d5abb836e27c6dd861c5e6}} who coined the term “correlation energy" to represent the
ground state energy per electron after subtracting away the average kinetic
and exchange energy. (The Hartree energy is cancelled exactly by the interaction between
electrons and the positive background, and by the Coulomb energy among the uniform positive charges.)
Apparently, after choosing the Rydberg (the negative of the Hydrogen atom
ground state energy) as the energy unit, one may express either the correlation energy
or the ground state energy of the HEG system
in terms of the dimensionless quantity {{formula:20e30c09-a1b6-4d1f-872d-b83614b3f4c2}} ,
where {{formula:63bc7bc3-b27d-44fa-af08-d274793c892d}} , {{formula:96b8c942-5d3c-4ee3-ab21-8383f6674e56}}  being the volume of the system considered, {{formula:a4bebb68-7374-4251-9e0d-ab9b7537a647}} 
being the total number of electrons, and {{formula:edbac420-0b42-455e-8eff-f8d4e7e6252d}}  representing the Bohr radius.
In fact, efforts have been invested to express the correlation energy as a power
series in {{formula:17fd7f19-27ff-468c-88fb-ee50e952b0d2}}  (and {{formula:9eb76d75-a450-4274-b990-90d3f9037bcf}}  as well) at both the high density and low density limits.
Lacking real experimental results to compare with, however,
it is hard to assess how much improvement each increasing order of {{formula:747e4d68-9a3f-406f-82fa-fa5a9761e474}}  (or {{formula:a7a87537-36f0-4ba9-bde7-4659153e69f7}} ) can bring.

Since {{formula:73453016-874d-4d83-b7ba-203569593555}} , a small {{formula:2572c72d-3183-43d5-b654-0aad740fab3c}}  expansion is most naturally performed
by treating the Coulomb interaction as a perturbation.
Equivalent to the method of computing the
vacuum amplitude,{{cite:7ad337ba6e19ad6964c461f075086612847f9437}}, {{cite:2c1c3bcf3b516eb4172180d759085655d1d4ef60}}, {{cite:0ab64f8dfbbbb207daab38ac5a94f06f3879dc13}}
the time-ordered perturbative expansion developed by
Goldstone {{cite:3d444c104f65516733e497d4784d05c381eaeea0}} formalized the Brueckner theory {{cite:40ee9a7863785a3875d37886e4c473b2f8f02ef2}} and
made a direct connection to diagrammatic expansion in calculation of
the ground state energy. The electron propagator in diagrams under this formalism is
that of the noninteracting electrons.
An alternative formalism to compute the ground state energy (or the grand potential) is
to utilize the full propagator (i.e., the one with self-energy included)
in diagrammatic calculation. Under this alternative formalism,
only two-particle irreducible diagrams contribute.
Indeed, the work of Luttinger and Ward {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}} (as well as that of Klein {{cite:b3bd5e93bf6b42895ca3206adda324c7f8bafca8}})
was exactly along this line. Since the self-energy is not known a priori, this type of
energetic expression is a functional of the self-energy (or the full Green's function), which must be
determined via a stationary condition.{{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}}

An equivalent of the Brueckner-Goldstone formalism {{cite:3d444c104f65516733e497d4784d05c381eaeea0}}, {{cite:c2f44cc5e8d935a155aba339482f2a9ce94a80b5}}
was used by Gell-Mann and Brueckner {{cite:1449bd6167ed5de9bc0d56cf0bd9fd7c5dbccb2f}} to compute
the correlation energy of the HEG system. Given the long-range nature of the Coulomb interaction,
it is not surprising that Gell-Mann and Brueckner identified the occurrence of divergence as early as in
the second order of {{formula:7ef1db30-5559-46e2-8d81-b16effb0bf2f}} -based perturbative calculation. To circumvent this unphysical divergence,
they summed an infinite subset of diagrams to arrive at a contribution proportional to {{formula:4ee713c4-60d9-4802-88b6-2cb66290aacd}} .
To eliminate unphysical divergence, DuBois {{cite:a99fe440aa3c1048385a54251a9f74a889009943}} replaced the bare Coulomb interaction
by the screened one. Starting with calculating the vacuum amplitude,
he expressed the ground state energy in terms of integration of the full
electronic polarization over the Coulomb coupling strength, using a version of the Feynman-Hellmann theorem.
While the full polarization is used, the electron propagator entering DuBois's formalism
is the free electron propagator instead of the full propagator.
Unfortunately, DuBois made a mistake in extracting the higher order terms
of the ground state energy at the high density (small {{formula:da1d949e-274c-4e69-9f64-bbfe0e3dc227}} ) limit.
Although this error was later corrected by Carr and Maradudin,{{cite:ddc29033a141c22311caf69e3158da2e6f3bc0ba}} according to
Hedin,{{cite:0791a37c48e168339589190141d04b17a247972e}} this high density expansion violated
at moderate {{formula:11a58dea-3f06-4e9e-80a4-901cd3fd0a92}}  values Ferrell's condition,{{cite:0f2af298f8c0a315fe8e6a76f35542a7f640bd8e}} which is based on the simple
fact that the second order perturbation contribution
to the ground state energy is always negative.

Except for using the screened Coulomb interaction to replace the bare one and working directly
at zero temperature, Hedin's approach is largely similar to the finite-temperature formalism
of Luttinger and Ward {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}} in the sense that the full electron propagator is used
as the fundamental variable. As a consequence, the higher order diagrams contributing to the full
polarization appear different in DuBois's work and in Hedin's formalism.
Instead of solving his own self-consistent equations, however, Hedin approximated the
full Green's function within his formalism by the non-interacting Green's function
to compute the energetics of the HEG system. Nevertheless, it is still possible to
maintain the exactness within Hedin's approach if two-particle reducible diagrams are
properly included.
We will provide an example of such a two-particle reducible diagram
that would not be included in Hedin's approximate calculation but should be incorporated
for theoretical soundness.

Another important issue in obtaining the ground state energy of a many-electron system
has to do with whether the finite temperature formalism (setting {{formula:f99772f5-e868-44a5-b987-def5eef6c57e}}  first followed by {{formula:2730cb8c-32e1-4453-bcb5-c52b1ab861fa}} )
or the zero temperature formalism (setting {{formula:01bd7950-c57d-4be9-9528-e6f63c7fdd7a}}  and then followed by {{formula:140e6a22-8bf9-453d-8de9-1cbf8e16d01b}} ) is used.
In terms of diagrammatic expansion, there exist diagrams (termed anomalous diagrams
by Luttinger et al.{{cite:7d00d176f5127f322a56a3902ee783420f57ae18}}, {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}}) that are present (giving finite contribution)
within the finite temperature formalism but are
absent (giving zero contribution) within the zero temperature formalism.
To be specific, a diagram is anomalous if within it
there exist two electron propagators linking
two different times (say {{formula:33395e81-170c-4b7d-b4ad-d96cc405be7e}} , {{formula:79932685-205c-426d-8e78-6ec796de3da4}}  and of course {{formula:794baf1d-efed-4df3-bdcd-c1bc958f94fd}} )
in the opposite orders: {{formula:3124e521-0449-4aba-9b3c-0564c92e5acc}} .

Zero temperature methods typically rely on the Gell-Mann and Low theorem, {{cite:e6c6568085262eef6364aef591744c1e0acee992}} which assures that
adiabatic transformation of the noninteracting ground state by gradually switching on the
interaction leads to an eigenstate of the interacting system.{{cite:7ad337ba6e19ad6964c461f075086612847f9437}}, {{cite:0ab64f8dfbbbb207daab38ac5a94f06f3879dc13}}
The energetic difference of this eigenstate and the noninteracting ground state is what
the zero temperature formalism obtains. This approach therefore makes sense only if
the adiabatically transformed state is the ground state of the interacting system, which
occurs only if the noninteracting Fermi surface is identical to that of the interacting system. {{cite:2c1c3bcf3b516eb4172180d759085655d1d4ef60}}
For the HEG system, the perturbed Fermi surface remains spherical (identical to that of
the unperturbed one) since the Coulomb interaction respects spherical symmetry and
the background positive charge distribution also has spherical symmetry.
Consequently, for the HEG system, the anomalous diagrams should end up giving no contribution. Indeed,
Luttinger et al. {{cite:7d00d176f5127f322a56a3902ee783420f57ae18}}, {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}} illustrated how the contributions
from the anomalous diagrams in this case are cancelled by the chemical potential shift.
Luttinger and Ward {{cite:75b8221295133f712b0e64e803fc1317fe2d5eff}} also showed how one may avoid anomalous contributions from appearing
by expressing the grand potential as a sum of all possible linked diagrams (including two-particle reducible ones).
The key step there is to subtract from each self-energy part a number, which is given by
that self-energy part evaluated at the Fermi surface.
As we will illustrate later, under our finite temperature formalism it is not necessary to implement
such an elaborate subtraction scheme because each two-particle reducible diagram is automatically
accompanied by another appropriate diagrammatic subtraction.

What sets our self-consistent equation (REF ) apart from that of Luttinger and Ward
and of Hedin is the variable to be solved for.
It is the KS potential, instead of the physical Green's function, that enters
our exact, self-consistent equation. In general, one needs to first solve {{formula:93fc1046-02fd-42e8-9fb5-2d955a619fec}} 
self-consistently using eq. (REF ) prior to the evaluation of the
grand potential (or the ground state energy).
When limiting to a homogeneous system with constant electron density, however,
{{formula:dea1b862-fa84-4d8c-96e3-5e16b00195ea}}  becomes the only possibility. Whether or not such a choice
satisfies the self-consistent equation (REF ) depends on whether
a uniform electron density truly represent the lowest energy configuration.
For the present purpose of considering a high density HEG,
we assume a constant {{formula:705dd709-d0a4-4986-be2d-ba0f27a4f1b5}}  to proceed.
Because a constant {{formula:adf9506f-28bd-4ba8-a6b8-a757ce519fd3}}  can be easily absorbed into the chemical potential,
the resulting KS Green's function carries a corresponding
energy that consists of kinetic energy only. That is, rather than being an approximation as in Hedin's case,
the single-particle Green's function carrying only kinetic energy represents exactly the self-consistent
KS Green's function under our formalism. Consequently, for the HEG system, the
grand potential (or the ground state energy) may be calculated using eq. (REF ).
