We now prove Theorem REF . Let us first notice that
Theorem REF  immediately implies the first claim in Theorem REF ,
namely that approximating the ground state and ground energy of a
commuting Hamiltonian in 1D to within polynomially good accuracy can
be done efficiently. This follows from the well known fact that the
ground state of a commuting Hamiltonian in 1D can be described by an
MPS of constant bond dimension. We can therefore apply
Theorem REF  to the problem, and hence approximate both the ground
state and ground energy efficiently.

For completeness, here is a sketch of a proof of this fact: assume
we have a 2-local commuting Hamiltonian in 1D. If the Hamiltonian
is {{formula:47a07211-104f-41cf-ad27-428aad642a90}} -local for {{formula:1bca10ed-f284-46ea-8a6e-e3755851055b}} , just combine adjacent particles together.
To see that there is a ground state which is described by an MPS of
constant bond dimension, notice that for any commuting Hamiltonian,
there is a ground state {{formula:43a5db9d-1628-4f1b-b738-e159c9071668}}  which is an eigenvector of each
of the terms in the Hamiltonian, with some well defined eigenvalue
for each term. For each term, consider the projection onto the
eigenspace corresponding to that eigenvalue. For any state with
non-zero projection on the ground state, applying these projections
(no matter the order) would result in a ground state. Since there is
always a computational basis state {{formula:5b123f35-4cbd-4bb3-aaa5-a6f7eb60e2d0}}  that has a non-zero
projection on the ground state, we can express a ground state as the
projection of all these local terms applied to {{formula:0e57bf36-e952-40ed-85cf-be20f2746316}} . We first
apply the projections which interact the pairs of particles {{formula:5cd36a62-69ca-447e-adb8-5dee2738d693}} ,
{{formula:00f6aee6-b1b5-4a4f-8c4e-661dfe01ed00}} , etc; we then apply the projections that interact the pairs
of particles {{formula:9374368e-c132-46e1-8137-4db308c8ccc9}} , {{formula:0e3b4dfe-3ccb-4deb-bf26-1d741cf5846a}} , etc. This sequence of operations can
be viewed as a tensor network of depth 2. We can thus represent
the ground state as the contraction of a tensor network of depth
2. It can be easily seen that such a state must have a constant
Schmidt rank along any cut between the left and right sides; to move
to an MPS of a constant bond dimension, use Vidal's result
{{cite:d5d018fbfc14958f8349b2867ef4053e61385ef8}}.

subspaces {{formula:c9f37a54-eef9-416d-961d-47b6c921345f}}  invariant, and moreover, when
restricted to such a subspace, {{formula:1aad2ab9-2d68-4cca-8f50-91bbb9befa83}}  acts non-trivially only
on {{formula:a2f69c0d-c45f-4624-b869-af901f8958ed}}  (the right part of {{formula:69c61f32-24f3-4b4d-87b4-b66667235f20}}  and the left part of {{formula:e69ad797-d76c-44c8-ad93-5f42863479c2}} ).
Consequently, there exists a ground state which resides in some
subspace {{formula:5687ffb0-b46e-4a24-9bb4-a8233382452b}} , for
some choice of {{formula:dc3fe0ed-722a-487c-8d41-07fdd75479a3}} . Moreover, within the
subspace {{formula:1d54cdb6-8de7-4871-99e7-5ef7d49f72b9}}  the state can be written as a tensor
product of 2 particle states living in the spaces of the form {{formula:86a741c4-e958-46a1-8752-5f563202a0d0}} ,
tensored with some arbitrary single particle states living in the
{{formula:cf682c33-b5ec-413b-87a6-b0c06d7ff086}}  spaces.

If the algorithm knows the correct choice of indices
{{formula:5c5fe5fc-860d-4dcb-9d18-535fc4dcfa9a}} , it can find such a ground state
efficiently, as follows. Note that the descriptions of both the
spaces {{formula:bb57196c-1417-42b9-9820-0add0a038b35}}  and their divisions {{formula:7f77584b-638a-496e-9277-a9e494d28ba7}}  are derived from
local properties of {{formula:fedc57cd-1099-4519-b753-810316ed6659}}  imposed by the two local Hamiltonians
{{formula:ce30a67c-47ca-4507-ac61-89e9402d56de}}  and {{formula:fbabbffe-17a0-46d8-ab11-051f3d9557fb}} . The subdivision of {{formula:8f53a6ae-d7ff-4e78-963d-fc27128e50c5}}  in this
way can be expressed as a solution to a set of quadratic homogeneous
constraints. Since the dimension of {{formula:20a7544a-966b-404e-af7c-4453c67f5acf}}  and hence the number
of variables is constant, it can be efficiently computed. If the
algorithm knows the {{formula:76a94584-62d0-47ce-9998-6b49a646530c}} 's, it therefore knows the description
of the subspaces {{formula:2c3e077f-25be-462a-8acf-8f5101c17fa6}} , and the
restriction of the {{formula:d23dba6a-d8f7-46ee-8421-c539edde09ae}}  to those spaces; it therefore just
needs to find a ground state of linearly many 2-particle
Hamiltonians, which is an easy task. It is therefore enough for the
algorithm to find the correct {{formula:5b57ae23-5c96-4b7c-aa07-d405a68f01c4}}  indices.

We will do this using dynamic programming. The critical point in
using dynamic programming here is that the energy contribution of
{{formula:1817a4ee-fc18-4dd5-9d86-877e47824799}}  depends only on the choice of {{formula:a36d48d0-00bd-45cb-aa04-3e5a5f2b20b0}}  and
{{formula:5c9b9265-5fe2-45a6-8b13-6498d0f5578b}} , so the choice of {{formula:b4c61656-92e7-49b6-badf-481ffa597435}}  for {{formula:267b1ca5-ac71-4d05-9b99-b3818e34d80a}} 
does not affect the energy of the {{formula:e4b90c08-db00-42ef-a82d-c8a18cb34852}}  terms for any {{formula:59e97252-a543-4cd6-a8de-1959029332d2}} . Using this observation, the algorithm proceeds from left to
right as follows. For the first term {{formula:6944c54b-7ed0-4f97-84ab-04264fe77bd2}} , the algorithm finds
the division into a direct sum of subspaces for particles 1 and
2. The algorithm keeps an optimal state (choice of {{formula:addac5d7-736a-4753-b14d-59fe68649fdd}} ) and
energy for each possible {{formula:89a238b7-00d1-4626-8cc5-8cd1cfb3a8af}} .

Then, in a general step, we assume at particle {{formula:a4b5eda3-a792-4db1-8348-1e85465e155c}}  we have the
following information for each index {{formula:9f7d5677-f632-4df5-8698-240f4eec668c}} : a list of indices
{{formula:7cd1537b-38c6-41e6-8549-1e2f65f5bcae}}  such that the ground energy of the
Hamiltonian of particles {{formula:75c0a7d8-84b5-4305-838f-80f1c09903e9}}  restricted to the subspaces
{{formula:be999b84-e900-430f-9814-ee6bf577f8b6}}  is
minimal. To continue to the next particle, we first compute the
division into subspaces for particle {{formula:9e4089a0-de7b-4850-88a3-81d543b16bdd}} , indexed by
{{formula:dfa55805-9735-420c-bd41-7f227aecec94}} , and optimize for each subspace in turn. For each
subspace, we consider all items in the previous list; for each item,
we have a list of subspaces, one for each particle. We compute the
minimal energy for each such restriction, including now the
{{formula:2b7ce545-e87c-4f6a-9411-f5278cbdc7ea}}  term in the calculation of the energy, restricted
according to subspaces {{formula:810bf9a6-daf7-46b7-b758-b231b1344608}}  and {{formula:eb7494a1-0a6b-4b0a-8797-2824ea21706b}} , the last
choice coming from the list. We pick the tail of the subspace of
the {{formula:16c4ef06-450b-4419-8fe7-e8201012995a}}  particle to be the one which minimizes the terms up to
that point.

Notice that in each step the dynamic program compares partial
energies emerging from restricting the state to a different sector
in the Hilbert space. These energies can be computed efficiently with
polynomially many bits, namely up to exponentially good precision.
Thus, this second algorithm achieves exact results for a somewhat
larger set of Hamiltonians than our first algorithm, namely those
for which
the partial energies will not be confused if the computations are
done with exponentially good precision.

Note that even with
this extremely good resolution, it might be the case that the ground
energy is confused with a slightly excited energy which is, say,
doubly exponentially close. We do not know of a good
condition which would rule out the possibility of such very close
energies, except for some very trivial assumptions such as requiring
that all eigenvalues are integer numbers. For example,
even if we require that the different entries in the terms in the
Hamiltonian are all rationals smaller than 1 with denominator
upper bounded by a constant, it is still not known how to rule out
the possibility that two eigenvalues of the overall Hamiltonian are
doubly exponentially close. This issue touches upon an open question
in number theory related to sums of algebraic numbers – see the
open problem described in Ref. {{cite:875bccf7235e6f0a98b7b5f7d197d946f98c942e}}, which can be traced back to
Ref. {{cite:d271cd63a6cfa4f9fd5233815d259eabd68ea6b8}} (if not earlier), and also Ref. {{cite:70be07dc4440b63f1f563739a768bd7517119ab7}} and references
therein.

gold_section_text:
It is natural to ask how much the results in this article can be
improved. By Ref. {{cite:31c393f3562373f7cb2fdfbbffbde51df0987987}}, we know that no polynomial algorithm
exists for finding optimal approximations of polynomial bond
dimension (unless P=NP). However, the difficult instances of
Ref. {{cite:31c393f3562373f7cb2fdfbbffbde51df0987987}} have a spectral gap of {{formula:4921fd0f-0d24-4978-acb7-002315317358}} . Hastings has
shown that ground state of 1D quantum system with a constant gap
can be approximated by a MPS with polynomial bond dimension
{{cite:efd85deefa25d1c8b9b0c119d2f50222eda99c61}}. However, this is too large to immediately yield an
efficient algorithm from our result. It may still be true, however,
that under the additional restriction that the Hamiltonian has a
constant gap, a polynomial time algorithm exists, even when the bond
dimension is as large as polynomial.

It is very likely that the efficiency of our algorithm can be
significantly improved even for the general case. In particular, a
factor of {{formula:9a1d64cd-f663-4d76-9455-9b6383c1265b}}  would be shaved from the error in Theorem REF 
if we could use an {{formula:ea4fd508-7282-4a16-8866-2fa127de3bdc}} -net which is both exactly canonical
and enables perfect overlap between matrices at neighboring
particles, as we later explain. Unfortunately, even if this can be
done, the running time for this general algorithm is still quite
large.

As mentioned earlier, we leave for further research the question of
how this algorithm can be used in combination with DMRG, and how
certain symmetries in the problem can be utilized to enhance its
performance time for specific interesting cases.

We note that very similar results to those presented in this
article were derived independently by Schuch and Cirac {{cite:a3f672ea23b64347f83065c14a70549c876a6d78}}.

The dynamic path-planning problem consists in finding a suitable
plan for each new configuration of the environment by recomputing a
collision-free path using the new information available at each time step {{cite:354229ecda290760072f769cdb9d667a1e349beb}}.
This kind of problem has to be solved for example by a robot trying to navigate
through an area crowded with people, such as a shopping mall or supermarket.
The problem has been widely addressed in its several flavors,
such as cellular decomposition of the configuration space {{cite:6ab09399e5c2058e4433494474376aeecd91bb5c}},
partial environmental knowledge {{cite:416266c7ec89437a08fa42057a79a27cf73196b8}},
high-dimensional configuration spaces {{cite:dfd53cd5efc682718fe1c6fa2ae9060ccc36f793}}
or planning with non-holonomic constraints {{cite:6c1a7e72d4d8c92937ef31adfaffd946ab0e5540}}.
However, even simpler variations of this problem are complex enough
that they can not be solved
with deterministic techniques, and therefore are worthy of study.

This thesis is focused on algorithms for
finding and traversing a collision-free path in
two dimensional space, for a
holonomic robotA holonomic robot is a robot in
which the controllable degrees of freedom is equal to the total degrees of
freedom.,
without kinodynamic restrictionsKinodynamic planning is a problem in which velocity and acceleration
bounds must be satisfied, in a highly dynamic environment, but for comparison
purposes three different scenarios will be tested:

Several unpredictably moving obstacles or adversaries.

Partially known environment, where some obstacles become visible when the
robot approaches each one of them.

Totally unknown environment, where every obstacle is initially invisible
to the planner, and only becomes visible when the robot approaches it.

Besides the obstacles in the second and third scenario we assume
that we have perfect information of the environment at all times.

We will focus on continuous space algorithms and
will not consider algorithms that use a discretized representation of the
configuration spacethe space of possible positions that a physical
system may attain, such
as D* {{cite:6ab09399e5c2058e4433494474376aeecd91bb5c}},
because for high dimensional problems the
configuration space becomes intractable in terms of both memory and computation
time, and there is the extra difficulty of calculating the discretization size,
trading off accuracy versus computational cost.
Only single agent algorithms will be considered here.
On-line as well as off-line algorithms will be studied. An on-line algorithm is
one that is permanently adjusting its solution as the environment changes, while
an off-line algorithm computes a solution only once (however, it can be executed
many times).

The offline Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree (RRT) is efficient at finding solutions, but the results are far from
optimal, and must be post-processed for shortening, smoothing or other qualities
that might be desirable in each particular problem. Furthermore, replanning RRTs
are costly in terms of computation time, as are evolutionary and cell-decomposition
approaches. Therefore, the novelty of this work is
the mixture of the feasibility benefits of the RRTs, the repairing capabilities
of local search, and the computational inexpensiveness of greedy algorithms,
into our lightweight multi-stage algorithm. Our working hypothesis will be that
a multi-stage algorithm, using different techniques for initial planning and
navigation,
outperforms current probabilistic sampling techniques in highly dynamic
environments

At each time-step, the problem could be defined as
an optimization problem with satisfiability constraints.
Therefore, given a path our objective is to minimize an evaluation function
(i.e., distance, time, or path-points), with the {{formula:4b5d7bcd-9190-411f-9ad3-4a0e0062559a}}  constraint.
Formally, let the path {{formula:31102e91-e414-413f-b113-fcb5eb5fd0c6}} be a sequence of points, where
{{formula:752432bf-02c2-4ca0-918f-e4c32029e031}} is a {{formula:248fa4f4-b7ba-49ab-a4f2-e09b4eb8da61}} -dimensional point ({{formula:aa3db2cb-7891-4771-a79d-5c02f1c7d2c3}}),
{{formula:3fa84b48-4f79-4275-b78a-5208cf9ce1c9}}  the set of obstacles positions
at time {{formula:fd63fe4b-cdce-4173-ac6e-02a02bede137}} , and {{formula:504f2827-2d17-4141-92ab-d8386cdc3813}}
an evaluation function of the path depending on the object positions.
Our ideal objective is to obtain the optimum {{formula:16aa5668-d1d2-4038-9d9d-1fe949084dc1}}  path that
minimizes our {{formula:d18633b4-581d-4a67-8705-8f81a4364fdd}}  function within a feasibility restriction in the form
{{formula:7136c55b-61df-4c18-9fc9-579d479f85a0}}

where {{formula:ac8246e7-41e0-4fdf-8123-df131ac813e8}}  is a feasibility function that equals
{{formula:858aceed-667c-4be4-9d42-ac11e2afb1a6}} 
if the path {{formula:0667c173-e176-40c9-8818-237f48dc720d}}  is collision free for the obstacles {{formula:f13fbca2-5f79-4f6b-a535-2637e66744b3}} .
For simplicity, we use very naive {{formula:1d7d1953-fb16-47dd-8f41-e24f34308302}}  and
{{formula:7f39faa8-f786-41f2-a456-73dc91db14fe}} 
functions, but our approach could be extended easily to more complex evaluation and
feasibility functions.
The {{formula:863228ab-60e0-4a06-96a5-a7c73f30ecab}}  function used assumes that the robot is a point
object in space, and therefore if no segments
{{formula:5a4f1309-ce08-490a-8d9f-b2c136e02d81}} 
of the path collide with any object {{formula:01b11c48-6e7b-4ee9-9d6d-e4e705c25da1}} , we say that the path

The {{formula:35f512eb-2b54-4daa-84a2-f1ce1e5c4f8c}}  function is the length of the path, i.e., the sum of the distances between
consecutive points. This could be easily changed to any other metric such as the time
it would take to traverse this path, accounting for smoothness,
clearness or several other optimization criteria.

In the following sections we present several path planning methods that can be
applied to the problem described above. In section REF  we review
the basic offline, single-query RRT, a probabilistic method that builds a
tree along the free configuration space until it reaches the goal state.
Afterwards, we introduce the most popular replanning variants of
RRT: Execution Extended RRT (ERRT) in section REF , Dynamic RRT (DRRT) in
section REF  and Multipartite RRT (MP-RRT) in section REF .
The Evolutionary Planner/Navigator (EP/N), along with some variants, is presented
in section REF .
Then, in section REF  we present a mixed approach, using a RRT to
find an initial solution and the EP/N to navigate, and finally, in section REF  we
present our new hybrid multi-stage algorithm, that uses RRT for initial
planning and informed local search for navigation, plus a simple greedy
heuristic for optimization. Experimental results and
comparisons that show that this combination of simple techniques provides better
responses to highly dynamic environments than the standard RRT extensions are
presented in section REF . The
conclusions and further work are discussed in section .

In this chapter we present several path planning methods that can be
applied to the problem described above. First we will introduce variations of
the Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree (RRT), a probabilistic method that builds a
tree along the free configuration space until it reaches the goal state. This
family of planners is fast at finding solutions, but the solutions are far from
optimal, and must be post-processed for shortening, smoothing or other qualities
that might be desirable in each particular problem. Furthermore, replanning RRTs
are costly in terms of computation time. We then introduce an
evolutionary planner with somewhat opposite qualities: It is slow in finding
feasible solutions in difficult maps, but efficient at replanning when a
feasible solution has already been found. It can also optimize the solution
according to any given fitness function without the need for a post-processing
step.

One of the most successful probabilistic methods for offline path planning
currently in use is the Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree (RRT), a single-query planner for
static environments, first introduced in {{cite:5445a03032dc516fec7fe7f57e2e74a3b918c13b}}. RRTs works towards finding a continuous path from a state
{{formula:579734b6-968f-4baa-b46a-6a626bcb7a70}}  to a state {{formula:01d8416d-8b05-4443-a1c3-e8891a4fd6d4}}  in the free configuration
space {{formula:fb738f02-86f0-4d32-8469-0a797715a772}}  by
building a tree rooted at {{formula:fa551f8e-d4f7-4be1-b1c8-331c14add523}} . A new state {{formula:4f7e59f8-1c47-4ba7-8a76-5ef60b49e697}}  is uniformly
sampled at random from the configuration space {{formula:127d68b9-82dc-4416-947e-7f3e07ee9522}} . Then the nearest node,
{{formula:5115fbfc-3b3b-4111-8ea9-bad22bee2925}} , in
the tree is located, and if {{formula:9bb469fc-c0ba-466a-ad60-bf1f579817aa}}  and the shortest path from
{{formula:fc2b7f79-b19c-490d-ac9e-350759223e4b}}  to
{{formula:6437e187-4f2f-4338-9ef6-752c930c5cb4}}  are in {{formula:22203b12-e991-46b4-b66f-2e1d8ff48d00}} , then {{formula:3924aee7-fc62-4ab3-9aaa-9911b97958d3}}  is added to the tree (algorithm REF ). The tree
growth is stopped when a node is found near {{formula:bde510af-ff2f-4e50-9929-519cc33bbb1c}} . To speed up convergence,
the search is usually biased to {{formula:ff83c145-63ff-4fe7-82d9-5ad6ae3d7745}}  with a small probability.

In {{cite:44d3d82479c5b7bc86eae2b0e9650b0da45218aa}}, two new features are added to RRT. First, the EXTEND
function (algorithm REF ) is introduced, which instead of trying
to add {{formula:dcc92448-6196-41b2-9b49-b30612b89aef}}  directly to
the tree, makes a motion towards {{formula:8afc4aaa-6cc1-4e8c-8b2d-e7717bc7439b}}  and tests for collisions.

The Retraction-based RRT Planner presented in {{cite:d3adbed7820f0e66ff7e6f7a182de56f601fc92f}} aims at
improving the performance of the standard offline RRT in static
environments with narrow passages. The basic idea of the
{{formula:3a30f324-34c0-488f-a84f-1c158f41992f}} 
function in algorithm REF  is to iteratively retract a randomly generated
configuration
that is in {{formula:938047f9-1b2a-4968-8037-75f8e9fc521d}}  to the closest boundary point in
{{formula:474680ef-9574-4dff-970a-8974b0cbb2ef}} . So, instead of

{{formula:d61d76a8-c325-42d1-867d-ea60380b1d37}}  to {{formula:3807b41b-26ac-4651-a6a4-9de2f00b1681}} , it extends from {{formula:580ad911-310e-432c-b6ce-6a945b818647}}  to the closest point in
{{formula:04acb0b6-5f81-4192-9b9e-089e6af9f6e0}}  to {{formula:8f954493-fb68-4237-9ad8-7906e8b2eefa}} . This gives more samples in narrow passages. This
technique could easily be applied to on-line RRT planners.

The Execution Extended RRT presented in {{cite:8a9e04e10a71e10d415f99d85011eb419aa700aa}} introduces two
extensions to RRT to build an on-line planner, the waypoint cache and adaptive
cost penalty search, which
improve re-planning efficiency and the quality of generated paths. ERRT uses
a kd-tree (see section REF ) to speed nearest neighbor look-up, and does not use
bidirectional search. The waypoint cache is implemented by keeping a constant
size array of states, and whenever a plan is found, all the states in the plan
are placed in the cache with random replacement. Then, when the tree is no
longer valid, a new tree must be grown, and there are three
possibilities for choosing a new target state, as shown in algorithm
REF , which is used instead of
{{formula:113dd676-38a3-4245-8388-fca25b6797ec}}  in previous
algorithms. With probability
P[goal], the goal is chosen as the target; with probability
P[waypoint], a random waypoint is chosen, and with the remaining
probability a uniform state is chosen as before. In {{cite:8a9e04e10a71e10d415f99d85011eb419aa700aa}} the values used
are P[goal]{{formula:a035cd41-cff2-4d07-a6c7-609b179fe6be}}  and P[waypoint]{{formula:ad67d28e-6a4e-49c8-af2f-2c93727db611}} .

Another extension is adaptive cost penalty search, where the planner adaptively
modified a parameter to help it find shorter paths. A value of 1 for beta will
always extend from the root node, while a value of 0 is equivalent to the
original algorithm. However, the paper {{cite:8a9e04e10a71e10d415f99d85011eb419aa700aa}} lacks
implementation details and experimental results on this extension.

The Dynamic Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree described in {{cite:0f44dafaf1a885ff1e8e2474a76ea7c49b952d09}} is a
probabilistic analog to the widely used D* family of algorithms. It works by
growing a tree from {{formula:64c46d7f-7bac-48d8-93ad-9a900e80f991}}  to {{formula:3f6e698d-a41f-4e5b-8ce4-ee19352162c5}} , as shown in algorithm
REF . This has the advantage that the
root of the tree does not have to be moved during the lifetime of the planning
and execution. In some problem classes the robot has limited range
sensors, thus moving or newly appearing obstacles will be near the robot, not
near the goal. In general this strategy attempts to trim smaller branches that are
farther away from the root. When new information concerning the configuration space is
received, the algorithm removes the newly-invalid branches of the
tree (algorithms REF  and REF ), and
grows the remaining tree, focusing, with a certain probability (empirically tuned
to {{formula:88eeaf7b-93bf-433a-8251-9c29f68c8618}}  in {{cite:0f44dafaf1a885ff1e8e2474a76ea7c49b952d09}}) to a vicinity of the recently trimmed branches,
by using the waypoint
cache of the ERRT (algorithm REF ). In experiments presented
in {{cite:0f44dafaf1a885ff1e8e2474a76ea7c49b952d09}} DRRT vastly outperforms ERRT.

Multipartite RRT presented in {{cite:5905f9665e8742b19e43150390b2bb4938b89cb0}} is another RRT variant which
supports planning in unknown or dynamic environments. MP-RRT maintains a
forest {{formula:1cf71ee3-5a7d-42dd-8e16-b8b850f912e7}}  of disconnected sub-trees which lie in {{formula:6192575b-16e1-4d43-ad04-4450d80c3918}} , but which are not
connected to the root node {{formula:9b5b2bf6-bd21-4c0b-80d5-96fed885dabb}}  of {{formula:52770ed1-ce30-4028-8dda-d3275aa00500}} , the main tree. At the start of a
given planning iteration, any nodes of {{formula:c7fb20ea-1249-49d4-89f2-e93daca27c2d}}  and {{formula:2adb2699-6353-409e-a0d2-754c639e3ccd}}  which are no longer valid are
deleted, and any disconnected sub-trees which are created as a result are placed
into {{formula:bc5add25-b54a-4e71-9def-3aff9971a877}}  (as seen in algorithms REF  and REF ).
With given probabilities,
the algorithm tries to connect {{formula:f015349b-a4c2-4998-9fe5-77660fe957a0}}  to a
new random state, to the goal state, or to the root of a tree in {{formula:8d16bb00-7691-4e05-9870-f1aaf99fc5f3}}  (algorithm REF ). In {{cite:5905f9665e8742b19e43150390b2bb4938b89cb0}}, a simple greedy smoothing heuristic is used, that tries to
shorten paths by skipping intermediate nodes. The MP-RRT
is compared to an iterated RRT, ERRT and DRRT, in 2D, 3D and 4D problems, with
and without smoothing. For most of the experiments, MP-RRT modestly outperforms
the other algorithms, but in the 4D case with smoothing, the performance gap in
favor of MP-RRT is much larger. The authors explained this fact due to MP-RRT
being able to construct much more robust plans in the face of dynamic obstacle
motion. Another algorithm that utilizes the concept of forests is
Reconfigurable Random Forests (RRF) presented in {{cite:fc783850e7a862c59bf072eb7cc47826e5a25065}}, but without the
success of MP-RRT.

The Rapidly Exploring Evolutionary Tree, introduced in {{cite:dac057944633c02d98bfb451584dea52169dbe29}} uses a
bidirectional RRT and a kd-tree (see section REF ) for efficient
nearest neighbor search. The
modifications to the {{formula:29288180-316c-41e8-a625-b78ec6e84f70}}  function are shown in algorithm
REF . The
re-balancing of a kd-tree is costly, and in this paper a simple threshold on the
number of nodes added before re-balancing was used. The authors suggest using the
method described in {{cite:6ad1ed07e4aeb8ebaa2547e1d752119cbf97a919}} and used in {{cite:8a9e04e10a71e10d415f99d85011eb419aa700aa}} to improve
the search speed. The novelty in this algorithm comes from the introduction of
an evolutionary algorithm {{cite:a6443e77219dbb68e4fa1b86b359836b7b9aadaa}} that builds a population of biases for the RRTs. The
genotype of the evolutionary algorithm consists of a single robot configuration for each tree. This
configuration is sampled instead of the uniform distribution. To balance
exploration and exploitation, the evolutionary algorithm was designed with 50% elitism. The fitness
function is related to the number of left and right branches traversed during
the insertion of a new node in the kd-tree. The goal is to introduce a bias to
the RRT algorithm which shows preference to nodes created away from the center
of the tree. The authors suggest combining RET with DRRT or MP-RRT.

The kd-tree, first introduced in {{cite:3e418e388210d607c36e5d3d04021b741fef99db}}, is a binary tree in which every
node is a k-dimensional point. Every
non-leaf node generates a splitting hyperplane that divides the space into two
subspaces. In the RRT algorithm, the number of points grows incrementally,
unbalancing the tree, thus slowing nearest-neighbor queries. Re-balancing a kd-tree
is costly, so in {{cite:6ad1ed07e4aeb8ebaa2547e1d752119cbf97a919}} the authors present another approach:
A vector of trees is constructed, where for {{formula:585ce032-22e5-46c6-bf93-11655d426fe3}}  points there is a tree that
contains {{formula:c77eac61-dbd5-48da-a45e-2503bb18d8ac}}  points for each {{formula:0da2ce62-2d23-488e-aa8f-7f7b7b5bc316}}  in the {{formula:225171f7-fc8e-48d7-9d4e-a98d01a3549c}}  place of the binary
representation of {{formula:6cc55495-0f2f-4504-b038-fb959c29d3b4}} . As bits are cleared in the representation due to
increasing {{formula:468c5827-043a-4784-9dc8-a12896e7a6d5}} , the trees are deleted, and the points are included in a tree
that corresponds to the higher-order bit which is changed to {{formula:87d67dd9-a118-40cd-88b4-7bf514a70b35}} . This general
scheme incurs in logarithmic-time overhead, regardless of dimension. Experiments
show a substantial performance increase compared to a naive brute-force approach.

An evolutionary algorithm {{cite:a6443e77219dbb68e4fa1b86b359836b7b9aadaa}} is a generic population-based meta-heuristic
optimization algorithm. It is inspired in biological evolution, using methods
such as individual selection, reproduction and mutation. The population is
composed of candidate solutions and they are evaluated according to a fitness
function.

The Evolutionary Planner/Navigator presented in {{cite:8d245cdf9a43bd9ac7efba22b666192cf0e52998}}, {{cite:b49111413a01d57eb455f63cb8b6c47ab1449a1d}}, and 
{{cite:2cd00d1d9f1c2eeb8b56437748d413ad7578ec24}} is an evolutionary
algorithm for path finding in dynamic environments. A high level description is
shown in algorithm REF . A difference with RRT is
that it can optimize the path according to any fitness function
defined (length, smoothness, etc), without the need for a post-processing step.
Experimental tests have shown it has
good performance for sparse maps, but no so much for difficult maps with narrow
passages or too crowded with obstacles. However, when a feasible path is found,
it is very efficient at optimizing it and adapting to the dynamic obstacles.

Every individual in the population is a sequence of nodes, representing
nodes in a path consisting of straight-line segments. Each node consists of an
{{formula:1cae2104-1bac-447e-8ba1-7bd1b0c7bd23}}  pair and a state variable {{formula:49446302-47d3-4b28-b124-c9c7917b4795}}  with information about the feasibility of
the point and the path segment connecting it to the next point. Individuals have
variable length.

Since a path {{formula:31e73f94-71f0-4367-bf00-4306271348af}}  can be either feasible or unfeasible, two evaluation functions
are used. For feasible paths (equation REF ), the goal is to minimize distance traveled,
maintain a smooth trajectory and satisfy a clearance requirement (the robot
should not approach the obstacles too closely). For unfeasible paths, we use
equation REF , taken from {{cite:4cee723d478959242220954ccf2100016981db6a}}, where {{formula:88e7a789-d7ff-472d-94a6-fc8e92d42e46}}  is the number
of intersections of a whole path with obstacles and {{formula:7496ea7f-7d2d-48cb-8ae3-d3db9ff0cfb0}}  is the average number
of intersections per unfeasible segment.
{{formula:cc28a241-35f3-45af-9705-b0ec55a183c0}}

EP/N uses eight different operators, as shown in figure REF  (description taken from {{cite:8d245cdf9a43bd9ac7efba22b666192cf0e52998}}):

Crossover: Recombines two (parent) paths into two new paths. The
parent paths are divided randomly into two parts respectively and recombined:
The first part of the first path with the second part of the second path, and
the first part of the second path with the second part of the first path. Note
that there can be different numbers of nodes in the two parent paths.

Mutate_1: Used to fine tune node coordinates in a
feasible path for shape adjustment. This operator randomly adjusts node
coordinates within some local clearance of the path so that the path remains
feasible afterwards.

Mutate_2: Used for large random changes of node coordinates in
a path, which can be either feasible or unfeasible.

Insert-Delete: Operates on an unfeasible path by inserting
randomly generated new nodes into unfeasible path segments and deleting
unfeasible nodes (i.e., path nodes that are inside obstacles).

Delete: Deletes nodes from a path, which can be
either feasible or unfeasible. If the path is unfeasible,
the deletion is done randomly. Otherwise, the operator
decides whether a node should definitely be deleted
based on some heuristic knowledge, and if a node is
not definitely deletable, its deletion will be random.

Swap: Swaps the coordinates of randomly selected
adjacent nodes in a path, which can be either feasible
or unfeasible.

Smooth: Smoothens turns of a feasible path by “cutting corners,”
i.e., for a selected node, the operator
inserts two new nodes on the two path segments connected to that node
respectively and deletes that selected node. The nodes with sharper turns are
more likely to be selected.

Repair: Repairs a randomly selected unfeasible segment
in a path by “pulling” the segment around its
intersecting obstacle.

The probabilities of using each operator is set randomly at the beginning, and
then are updated according to the success ratio of each operator, so more
successful operators are used more often, and automatically chosen according to
the instance of the problem, eliminating the difficult problem of hand tuning
the probabilities.

In {{cite:2cd00d1d9f1c2eeb8b56437748d413ad7578ec24}}, the authors include a memory buffer for each
individual to store good paths from its ancestors, which gave a small performance
gain.

In {{cite:befe6ecb6dd5ff5fd25c59859924eef6be942ad8}}, the authors propose strategies for improving the
stability
and controlling population diversity for a simplified version of the EP/N.
An improvement proposed by the authors in {{cite:b49111413a01d57eb455f63cb8b6c47ab1449a1d}} is using heuristics for the initial
population, instead of random initialization. We will consider this improvement
in section REF .

Other evolutionary algorithms have also been proposed for similar problems, in {{cite:ad6b7df78d218be850892c11fdf315c5db342e70}} a binary genetic algorithm is used for an offline planner, and {{cite:5df701afaae20facef3f47ff70951eeb3ae73451}} presents an algorithm to generate curved trajectories in 3D
space for an unmanned aerial vehicle.

EP/N has been adapted to an 8-connected grid model in {{cite:ac673bab1b5503487fee69b20a697bce1af67ce6}} (with previous work in {{cite:3223d731c39beb3245a78c7213b7a5a5cef144b0}} and {{cite:4c34d8f1dfbab49bb13b101a1cdd6687821b56b6}}).
The authors study two different crossover operators and four asexual operators.
Experimental results for this new algorithm (EvP) in static unknown environments
show that it is faster than EP/N.

As mentioned in section , RRT variants produce
suboptimal solutions, which must later be post-processed for shortening,
smoothing or other desired characteristics. On the other hand, EP/N,
presented in section REF , can optimize a solution according to any
given fitness function. However, this algorithm is slower at finding a first
feasible solution. In this section we propose a combined approach, that uses
RRT to find an initial solution to be used as starting point for EP/N,
taking advantage of the strong points of both algorithms.

EP/N as presented in section REF  can not find feasible paths in a
reasonable amount of time in any but very sparse maps. For this reason, RRT
will be used to generate a first initial solution, ignoring the effects produced
by dynamic objects. This solution will be in the initial population of the
evolutionary algorithm, along with random solutions.

EP/N is the responsible of regaining feasibility when it is lost due to a
moving obstacle or a new obstacle found in a partially known or totally unknown
environment. If a feasible solution can not be found in a given amount of time,
the algorithm is restarted, keeping its old population, but adding a new
individual
generated by RRT.

In highly dynamic environments, with many (or a few but fast) relatively small
moving obstacles, regrowing trees are pruned too fast, cutting away important
parts of the trees before they can be replaced. This dramatically reduces
the performance of the algorithms, making them unsuitable for these classes
of problems.
We believe that better performance could be obtained
by slightly modifying a RRT solution using simple obstacle-avoidance
operations on the new colliding points of the path by informed local search.
The path could be greedily optimized if the path has reached the feasibility
condition.

If solving equation REF  is not a simple task in static environments,
solving dynamic versions turns out to be even more difficult. In dynamic path planning
we cannot wait until reaching the optimal solution because we must deliver
a “good enough” plan within some time restriction. Thus, a heuristic approach
must be developed to tackle the on-line nature of the problem. The heuristic
algorithms presented in sections REF , REF  and REF 
extend a method developed for static environments, which produces poor response
to highly dynamic environments and unwanted complexity of the algorithms.

We propose a multi-stage combination of simple heuristic and probabilistic techniques
to solve each part of the problem: Feasibility, initial solution and optimization.
{{figure:dda88efd-06b6-4e2d-822d-5b1aac61cc97}}

The key point in this problem is the hard constraint in equation REF 
which must be met before even thinking about optimizing. The problem is that in
highly dynamic environments a path turns rapidly from feasible to unfeasible
— and the other way around — even if our path does not change.
We propose a simple informed local search to obtain paths in
{{formula:0b05097f-ed7d-4b5d-87e2-28ff0366add2}} .
The idea is to randomly search for a {{formula:f941f48e-5e59-4721-a85c-96651c8f983d}}  path by modifying the nearest colliding
segment of the path. As we include in the search some knowledge of the problem,
the informed term is coined to distinguish it from blind local search.
The details of the operators used for the modification of the path are described in
section REF . If a feasible solution can not be found in a
given amount of time, the algorithm is restarted, with a new starting point generated by a RRT variant.

The problem with local search algorithms is that they repair a solution that it is
assumed to be near the feasibility condition.
Trying to produce feasible paths from scratch with local search (or even
with evolutionary algorithms {{cite:b49111413a01d57eb455f63cb8b6c47ab1449a1d}}) is not a good idea due the randomness of the
initial solution. Therefore, we propose feeding the informed local search with a standard RRT solution
at the start of the planning, as can be seen in figure REF .

Without an optimization criterion, the path could grow infinitely large in time or
size. Therefore, the {{formula:b9810caa-06fe-4864-9d56-46217c113507}}  function must be minimized when a
(temporary) feasible path is obtained. A simple greedy technique is used
here: We test each point in the solution to check if it can be removed
maintaining feasibility; if so, we remove it and check the following point,
continuing until reaching the last one.

The second stage is the informed local search,
which is a two step function composed by the arc and mutate operators

The first one tries to build a square arc around an

The second step in the function is a mutation
operator that moves a point close to an obstacle to a
random point in the vicinity, as explained graphically in figure REF .
The mutation operator is inspired by the ones used in the Adaptive Evolutionary

Although the algorithms developed in this thesis are aimed at dynamic
environments, for the sake of completeness they will also be compared in
partially known environments and in totally unknown environments, where some or
all of the obstacles become visible to the planner as the robot approaches each
one of them, simulating a robot with limited sensor range.

The first environment for our experiments consists on two maps with 30 moving
obstacles the same size of the robot, with a random speed between 10% and 55%
the speed of the robot. Good performance in this environment is the main focus
of this thesis. This dynamic environments are illustrated in figures REF  and REF .
{{figure:86c11ccd-e995-492d-8e5a-9bb29c084e44}}{{figure:c0bb3a3b-e5a6-4863-a896-5832cd8f8b8e}}

The second environment uses the same maps, but with a few obstacles, three to four
times the size of the robot, that become visible when the robot approaches each
one of them. This is the kind of environment that most dynamic RRT variants were designed
for. The
partially known environments are illustrated in figure REF 
and REF .
{{figure:281d3384-b279-46cf-8ab1-0934004fff7f}}{{figure:142ec489-c6b9-4c02-a74a-a0c77322f8de}}

For completeness sake, we will compare the different technique in a third
environment, were we use one of the maps presented before, but
all the obstacles will initially be unknown to the
planners, and will become visible as the robot approaches them, forcing several
re-plans. This unknown environment is illustrated in figure REF .
{{figure:77082c35-4920-49ab-9175-7a682d667e34}}

The algorithms where implemented in C++ using the MoPa frameworkMoPa homepage:
https://csrg.inf.utfsm.cl/twiki4/bin/view/CSRG/MoPa
partly developed by the author. This framework features exact collision
detection, three different map formats (including .pbm images from any
graphic editor), dynamic, unknown
and partially known environments and support for easily adding new planners.
One of the biggest downsides is that it only supports rectangular objects, so
several objects must be used to represent other geometrical shapes, as in
figure REF , composed of 1588 rectangular objects.

There are several variations that can be found in the literature when
implementing RRT. For all our RRT variants, the following are the details on
where we departed from the basics:

We always use two trees rooted at {{formula:e005213d-b9a8-43c3-9a77-f011d7aa1553}}  and {{formula:a82f06eb-ecf3-4eeb-bf73-387b18c2b18d}} .

Our EXTEND function, if the point cannot be added without collisions to a
tree, adds the mid point between the nearest tree node and the nearest collision
point to it.

In each iteration, we try to add the new randomly generated point to both
trees, and if successful in both, the trees are merged, as proposed in {{cite:44d3d82479c5b7bc86eae2b0e9650b0da45218aa}}.

 We believe that there might be significant performance
differences between allowing or not allowing the robot to
advance towards the node nearest to the goal when the trees are disconnected, as
proposed in {{cite:5905f9665e8742b19e43150390b2bb4938b89cb0}}.

In point REF  above, the problem is that the robot would become stuck
if it enters a small concave zone of the environment (like a room in a building)
while there are moving obstacles inside that zone, but otherwise it can lead to
better performance. Therefore we present results for both kinds of behavior:
DRRT-adv and MP-RRT-adv move even when the trees are disconnected, while
DRRT-noadv and MP-RRT-noadv only
move when the trees are connected.

In MP-RRT, the forest was handled by simply replacing the oldest tree in it if the
forest had reached the maximum allowed size.

Concerning the parameter selection, the probability for selecting a point in the
vicinity of a point in the waypoint cache in DRRT was set to 0.4 as suggested in {{cite:0f44dafaf1a885ff1e8e2474a76ea7c49b952d09}}. The probability for trying to reuse a subtree in
MP-RRT was set to 0.1 as suggested in {{cite:5905f9665e8742b19e43150390b2bb4938b89cb0}}.
Also, the forest size was set to 25 and the minimum size of a
tree to be saved in the forest was set to 5 nodes.

For the combined RRT-EP/N, it was considered the planner was stuck after two
seconds without a feasible solution in the population, at which point a
new solution from a RRT variant is inserted into the population. For the simple
multi-stage probabilistic algorithm, the restart is made after one second of
encountering the same obstacle along the planned path. This second approach,
which seems better, cannot be applied to the RRT-EP/N, because there is no
single path to check for collisions, but instead a population of paths. The
restart times where manually tuned.

The three algorithms were run a hundred times in each
environment and map combination.
The cutoff time was five minutes for all tests, after which the robot was
considered not to have reached the goal. Results are presented concerning:

Success rate (S.R.): The percentage of times the robot arrived at the goal,
before reaching the five minutes cutoff time. This does not account for
collisions or time the robot was stopped waiting for a plan.

Number of nearest neighbor lookups performed by each algorithm (N.N.): One of the
possible bottlenecks for tree-based algorithms

Number of collision checks performed (C.C.), which in our specific
implementation takes a significant percentage of
the running time

Time it took the robot to reach the goal, {{formula:2773e644-1b37-43dc-9fdb-b1397b27ccd1}}  the standard
deviation.

The results in tables REF  and REF  show that
the multi-stage algorithm takes considerably less time than the DRRT
and MP-RRT to reach
the goal, with far less collision checks. The combined RRT-EP/N is a close
second. It was expected that nearest neighbor
lookups would be much lower in both combined algorithms than in the RRT variants,
because they are only performed in the initial phase and restarts,
not during navigation.
The combined algorithms produce more consistent results
within a map,
as shown by their smaller standard deviations, but also across different
maps. An interesting fact is that in map 1 DRRT is slightly faster than MP-RRT, and
in map 2 MP-RRT is faster than DRRT. However the differences are too small to
draw any conclusions.
Figures REF  and REF  show the times and
success rates of the different algorithms, when changing the number of dynamic
obstacles in map 1. The simple multi-stage algorithm and the mixed RRT-EP/N
clearly show the best performance, while the DRRT-adv and MP-RRT-adv
significantly reduce their success rate when confronted to more than 30 moving
obstacles.
{{table:bc52d313-1c0b-41a3-8edb-41daaadadf3d}}{{table:51a25ef8-cc49-4ba2-a91d-8405a88f2489}}{{figure:19cd0c65-05d1-4156-bee3-ce55529948d9}}{{figure:2f6f93e4-b325-4535-bec0-b2b88ebf4124}}

Taking both maps into consideration, the results in tables REF 
and REF 
show that both combined algorithms are faster and more consistent than the RRT
variants, with the simple multi-stage algorithm being faster in both.
These results were unexpected, as the combined algorithms were designed
for dynamic environments.
It is
worth to notice though, that
in map 1 DRRT-adv is a close second, but in map 2 it is a close last, so its
lack of reliability does not make it a good choice in this scenario. In this
environment, as in the dynamic environment, in map 1 DRRT is faster than MP-RRT,
while the opposite happens in map 2.
{{table:fec82596-6cb9-4191-bc24-37fbdd15207d}}{{table:f5b726f2-6ab2-47b9-b1f8-c165c7af6dbb}}

Results in table REF  present the combined RRT-EP/N clearly as
the faster algorithm in unknown environments, with the multi-stage algorithm in
second place. In contrast to dynamic and partially known environments in this
same map, MP-RRT is faster than DRRT.
{{table:bf268cfa-9680-4290-9ab4-1b41aa99b4b2}}

The new multi-stage algorithm proposed here has good performance in
very dynamic environments. It behaves particularly well when several small
obstacles are moving around at random. This is explained by the fact
that if the obstacles are constantly moving, they will sometimes move out of the
way by themselves, which our algorithm takes advantage of, while RRT based
ones do not, they just drop branches of the tree that could prove useful
again just a few moments later. The combined RRT-EP/N, although having more
operators, and automatic adjustment of the operator probabilities according to
their effectiveness, is still better than the RRT variants, but about 55%
slower than the
simple multi-stage algorithm. This is explained by the number of collision
checks performed, more than twice than the multi-stage algorithm, because
collision checks must be performed for the entire population, not just a single
path.

In the partially known environment, even though the difference in collision checks
is even greater than in dynamic environments, the RRT-EP/N performance is
about 25% worse than the multi-stage algorithm. Overall, the RRT variants
are closer to the performance of both combined algorithms.

In the totally unknown environment, the combined RRT-EP/N is about 30% faster
than the simple multi-stage algorithm, and both outperform the RRT variants,
with much smaller times and standard deviations.

All things considered, the simple multi-stage algorithm is the best choice in
most situations, with
faster and more predictable planning times, a higher success
rate, fewer collision checks performed and, above all, a much simpler
implementation than all the other algorithms compared.

This thesis shows that a multi-stage approach, using different techniques for
initial plannning and navigation, outperforms current probabilistic sampling
techniques in dynamic, partially known and unknown environments.

Part of the results presented in this thesis are published in {{cite:9ebf9e02288705b03074ebfed7da8465ca7af14e}}.

We propose several areas of improvement for the work presented in this thesis.

The most promising area of improvement seems to be to experiment with different on-line planners
such as a version of the
EvP ({{cite:3223d731c39beb3245a78c7213b7a5a5cef144b0}} and {{cite:ac673bab1b5503487fee69b20a697bce1af67ce6}}) modified to work in
continuous configuration space or a potential field navigator. Also, the local
search presented here could benefit from the use of more sophisticated
operators and the parameters for the RRT variants (such as forest size for
MP-RRT),
and the EP/N (such as population size) could benefit from being tuned specifically for this
implementation, and not simply reusing the parameters found in previous work.

Another area of research that could be tackled is extending this algorithm to
higher dimensional problems, as RRT variants
are known to work well in higher dimensions.

Finally, as RRT variants are suitable for kinodynamic planning, we only need to adapt
the on-line stage of the algorithm to have a new multi-stage planner for problems
with kinodynamic constraints.

The MoPa framework could benefit from the integration of a third party logic
layer, with support for arbitrary geometrical shapes, a spatial scene graph and
hierarchical maps. Some candidates would be
OgreODE {{cite:26187a799436f78d4bcb554547d4a3a84dafc279}}, Spring
RTS {{cite:16eaad8b443f1c01fb238804eaa6920111e56c53}} and
ORTS {{cite:74a95b269834a96602f8aa464f593fab50a8ce38}}.

Other possible improvements are adding support for other map formats, including
discrimination of static and moving obstacles, limited
sensor range simulation and integration with external hardware such as the Lego
NXT {{cite:806e3adc7aff0bf51c96b6c0643c0a00201563b6}}, to run experiments in a more
realistic scenario.

The problem of computing the minimum-cut in a weighted graph has been
classically studied in literature
as the dual of the well known max-flow problem for networks
{{cite:af971373749d2c43068f14726f7500066c0d456c}} and classical solutions to the max-flow problem were used to solve the
min-cut problem. These algorithms could be classified as those based on augmenting paths
{{cite:af971373749d2c43068f14726f7500066c0d456c}}, {{cite:0874cd78b4517c30f90f843b9dc66a250e0fd8c5}}, improvements to the augmenting path
approach based on blocking flows{{cite:28b9b679209676ee2e3a3d66a9977a05b3ca6c88}}, {{cite:cced8c6dc804b8019da711409398d97786d4465f}} and those based on
pre-flow method introduced by Goldberg and Tarjan{{cite:355b08f2005289e90969ca7b9415efacab96eb51}}. The best known algorithms for the max-flow
problem are based on the preflow approach{{cite:66876b8e1450cb6109970f05622f82acc2842e11}}, {{cite:babef0f42aba01f07ef694abf807294b63937d2f}}, {{cite:601a740dc584444b2a139570e18649af2f68099b}}. The max-flow
problem also has been recently studied in a distributed setting in {{cite:774371722a015412fae236ba505b599874c2b2bd}}.

Further investigations revealed that there are more efficient direct
solutions to the min-cut problem (without solving max-flow and taking the dual).
Nagamochi and Ibaraki{{cite:87712ec1e251d134feb3a6ebc897758e053c45bf}} published the first deterministic
global minimum cut algorithm that is not based on flow, but was rather
complicated. Stoer and Wagner{{cite:8ace0fb3ca453c95631bd911a5b5db4cfa8c77ae}} presented a simple
deterministic global minimum cut algorithm which runs in {{formula:62536803-2827-4962-9b93-6934378012f4}} .

Karger{{cite:71caf217c0b2b5fa9acfdd1cd1707ac739ba40b5}} presented the first randomized global min-cut
algorithm which runs in {{formula:6f93dac2-a2c3-45d9-8529-39b3d819892f}} . The running time of a
single trial of the algorithm is {{formula:27083db4-00aa-4558-b24f-9daf24c3aac6}} . The algorithm has to
be repeated {{formula:0b3e2deb-2d91-4661-b1aa-d27f1c9f9cff}}  times to achieve a high success probability
of {{formula:c27967fe-8fd0-49eb-a756-dab63c79b18c}} . Karger and Stein{{cite:96dd56f3386bd6a5e2cd5921af7362475fc26816}} further improved its
running time to {{formula:dac6f106-b3c4-4a31-9049-dff9a0804b6b}}  for the same probability.

Recently there has been revived interest in the min-cut problem
owing to its applications to network coding and wireless sensor networks
{{cite:696e7a320fa7f921fc83b2c1f3655c6c959c741b}}, {{cite:63f86ce2194c874e1fb015101e066b6e0f66d026}}, {{cite:708c372b5a76b823fbc7acf148c16919feb62cae}}. Sensor networks operate in a
distributed setting and motivates a solution to the problem in a
distributed setting.

In this paper, we show how Karger's algorithm{{cite:71caf217c0b2b5fa9acfdd1cd1707ac739ba40b5}} can be
adapted to efficiently solve the min-cut problem in a distributed
setting. We assume a very general model of a graph where each node
knows only information about its neigbours. It is assumed that the
storage capacity of a node is bounded linearly in the size of the
number of its neigbours and the computing capacity of a node is
bounded polynomially in the number of its neighbours. The assumption
is reasonable as each node must have storage and processing
capacity sufficient to keep track of communication with its neighbours.
The nodes can perform local computations and can communicate only with
its neighbours along the edges of the graph. Our objective is to find
the value of the global min-cut and communicate the same to all the
nodes. Moreover, each node must know which among the edges incident
on it are present in the min-cut computed. While the correctness proof follows directly from Karger's algorithm, the complexity analysis differs significantly. We show that for a graph
of {{formula:b199b711-d529-4e79-b118-3c65da7ab089}}  vertices and {{formula:9310b349-6eef-4b1a-bdf1-ca13a4630bd2}}  edges, the algorithm computes the global
min-cut with probability atleast {{formula:19ef76b8-ca68-48f8-9dfe-11668373e2de}} 
with {{formula:405f1b86-9ad1-4267-b1d6-220e11037e00}}  message complexity and {{formula:5eb21406-1b7b-42c3-8f8e-4573d022a85a}}  time complexity when
there is a global clock for synchronization. We note that although
the assumption of a global clock may be impractical in applications
like sensor networks, there are standard techniques for converting
synchronous distributed algorithms to asynchronous algorithms, with
some loss in computational efficiency{{cite:ba9445905591d774256d685982c9e0a87675aa2f}}. We pursue the simpler synchronous setting here
as it allows a less cumbersome presentation of the algorithm and a
simple analysis.

Assume that given a weighted graph {{formula:153c2c5a-b547-4536-9a84-a1fc31df66c9}}  where {{formula:08cdee5e-b73b-4a17-8155-3e6545fc4ccd}}  and {{formula:da14da62-7746-4cbf-9a29-e44a20eb7bab}}  is given(We use the terms network and graph interchangeably). In our algorithm {{formula:9ea23006-0dd7-4c93-91d0-2ec8e2188b28}}  represents the neighbourhood of vertex {{formula:206ed955-4908-4476-8915-d5b6296a1888}} , {{formula:df0fb72c-a9ef-4df8-ac68-97e9da5ccb0f}}  represents the present edge weights of {{formula:144e089c-3228-4e3c-b9ac-15c0f438ea16}} , that is, for each {{formula:bb5d843f-fd6f-4b09-b782-a5fc9d2707a6}}  indicates the weight of edge {{formula:64f9875b-bcbe-4569-9a91-77d329b0f747}} . {{formula:1919915d-ce81-496e-9cfb-04dc34ae231d}}  is the rank of edge {{formula:1928015f-c02f-4c86-91a6-6015a628b47c}} , a random number which is uniformly chosen between 1 and {{formula:dccacaef-82a3-4d5c-aa5b-0f484510076c}} (for some fixed {{formula:9e813b94-4842-4c77-a558-43e82a9f2841}} ), on each trial. {{formula:b428b91d-5506-4a5f-a0c8-18cf59347e63}}  represents the maximum value of rank among all the edges. We call an edge active if at least one of its end points is active.

The algorithm proceeds by simulating edge contractions as in{{cite:71caf217c0b2b5fa9acfdd1cd1707ac739ba40b5}}, by collecting vertices joined together by contraction into vertex groups. Edges within a group are inactive as they cannot be further contracted. At each step, an active edge of maximum rank is chosen for contraction. Since edge ranks are assigned uniformly at random, each active edge has equal probability for getting contracted. The algorithm continues contractions till only two vertex groups remain and the set of edges across the two groups is chosen as the mincut for that trial. The smallest cut found in {{formula:8eec160a-d70d-4af4-94fa-f5410ddef5fa}}  trials will be the mincut with probability {{formula:0f09a8b3-4133-41f7-847b-f25f9e59851b}} .

The variable {{formula:6c1ca326-88cf-4eab-8802-4e633be8bbb0}}  stores the last message received at vertex {{formula:d467eb85-b6fc-4251-9696-52ab6fe50387}} (used to reduce message flooding) and the boolean variable {{formula:1b70b948-20a1-40ae-b04c-c88a59d87ffe}}  is set to {{formula:d533f265-b7c5-4b5c-89b7-97b7c88caf92}}  when only two vertex groups are remaining and no more contraction can be made, and set to {{formula:de2a9591-ed19-4c59-b1de-03ab18a1b0e1}}  otherwise.

The variable {{formula:16f65bb5-2292-47b9-a31d-ff7d9a6cce8c}}  represents the present group id of vertex {{formula:f5a95c3b-7f62-48fa-9ff4-7c8e2688e3dd}} , initially {{formula:ae2d1bf1-9cae-4834-8877-d929988303e9}} . Initially there are {{formula:ef58724a-364b-40ad-8531-db6662c66907}}  groups, one for each vertex. As contractions progress, the number of groups reduces and we set {{formula:1d03ce82-c322-4e04-ad88-550a9aa14bb0}}  if {{formula:7d2a1dfb-f9e1-421e-ba5d-d702ad0f0c27}}  and {{formula:2898e879-9cfc-4002-b858-3988e5871c29}}  otherwise. {{formula:63f511c9-c01e-4c82-bee2-d1a20aafe423}} .
Now choose {{formula:f0afc1df-aa75-4e81-a4da-54d30b7470dc}} . Then, {{formula:d4ecfa37-5c01-406f-9a8f-98d7de284abd}} .

The following Lemma proceeds exactly as in {{cite:71caf217c0b2b5fa9acfdd1cd1707ac739ba40b5}}.

Lemma 3.2 A particular min-cut in G is produced by the contraction algorithm with probability {{formula:6590a4af-9806-4164-b3a4-4532e637f26d}} .

Let {{formula:6f517fd0-0de4-465f-a222-1b694bcfd34a}}  be the value of the mincut in {{formula:2007ceb9-86c8-4fb0-b0e0-e0afde69f79a}} . Each contraction reduces the number of vertices in the graph by one. Consider the contraction executed when the graph has {{formula:b1f8e550-e917-4bb0-84ca-5e85a099f888}}  vertices. Since the contracted graph has a min-cut of at least {{formula:76cc00bb-fb2d-4356-865c-a6ad2824055b}} , it must have minimum degree {{formula:2ea957dd-1d82-444a-b73b-1213f4156b59}} , and thus atleast {{formula:5e79e702-9f1a-4575-b0c4-10f076190dd7}}  edges. However, only {{formula:5225dd0f-9537-4128-bff2-fee7a6983b1c}}  of these edges are in min-cut. Thus, a randomly chosen edge is in the min-cut with probability at most {{formula:1cb5c51a-2119-4e6b-a780-39ac2061a77e}} . The probability that we never contract a min-cut edge through all {{formula:90f4f174-b103-47e4-813d-15700ff6e00a}}  contractions is atleast
{{formula:0647c7c0-9aa9-40fa-809b-40e82749e8e1}}

Theorem 4.1 The Karger's distributed algorithm uses {{formula:734bb21b-e58c-44df-ab72-dcbf4e47f029}}  messages, in a single trial.

It is not hard to see that the most expensive steps in a trial are those of determination of {{formula:0f279028-17cf-4618-89ae-2e61ca547383}}  from local maxranks(find-global-maxrank()) and that of computing the mincut at the end(find-global-mincut()). In find-global-maxrank(), each node sends its local maxrank value to its neighbours and this is repeated atmost {{formula:d2b3aa32-2572-4a0a-9a8c-a370a0b538e7}}  times(number of times equal to the diameter of the graph sufficies). Hence the total number of messages is bounded by {{formula:021afade-de52-4b2a-add1-a133c4c8989d}} . Thus the message complexity for {{formula:9fca2b24-b5d7-4f08-a9e2-03f8388008c9}}  iterations per trial is {{formula:f9d23f20-2ec8-4d43-a4e9-f61ab8805198}} . Finally, in step {{formula:1d0ea785-35f8-4756-abf8-49cbdac418cb}}  of find-global-mincut(), {{formula:38d64d4f-ca81-4782-ac4a-6121b7e5f546}}  nodes send messages to its neighbours. The total number of messages sent at each step is bounded by {{formula:efdd89db-3467-4096-9f42-07265ef95a4d}} . Thus, the total number of messages is {{formula:a5c59ecc-cb8c-4491-ae92-74874ab972c7}} . Hence the overall message complexity is {{formula:446b14e9-43b9-44de-acca-75bb0353e83a}} .

Theorem 4.2 The Karger's distributed algorithm computes mincut in {{formula:e5b85085-658c-424f-93ca-b9d71aa4f1b4}}  time, in a single trial.

Before contraction, the algorithm assigns a rank (random number) to each edge and finds the max-rank among all the vertices in the graph. This requires atmost {{formula:cf6b0e75-6d84-45f2-bc61-2e6f6390b432}}  steps(strictly, number of steps equal to the diameter of the graph). For contraction, a message is sent from a vertex within one group to other group and the message is propagated to all the vertices within the second group and the neighbouring vertices of that group, which also takes atmost {{formula:2d4510f6-320c-49bf-9a20-7273d67ca633}}  pulses. Since only one contraction can take place at any time and there are {{formula:31343565-2b4e-49bf-8694-76e08c938808}}  such contractions, the running time is {{formula:c2f55877-09f1-4a1c-9d4f-999740ca9269}} . To estimate time for computing the mincut, the function find-global-mincut() runs {{formula:382dbcd9-4f0d-4023-8c7a-dea3a1c2359f}}  steps and in step {{formula:455a10a5-17d4-473f-9139-2f6b16f837ef}} , {{formula:2e8d28b0-f991-4b8a-b54c-97f1ab71131b}}  nodes flood the network. Thus the time per step is {{formula:5acfb40a-50d4-4fd5-89da-1557f1d3ee3b}} . Hence the total complexity is {{formula:0645cf28-97c0-45e6-ab46-77798df5208e}} .

A synchronous distributed version of the Karger's randomized algorithm under network setting is presented in this paper with a proof of correctness and complexity analysis. The present algorithm appears not to make use of the full power of parallelism available. It is interesting to look at how to efficiently reduce time and message complexity by conducting edge contractions in parallel.

Every infinite graph has an infinite clique or an infinite anticlique
– this is the paradigmatic formulation of Ramsey's theorem
{{cite:2e045494bf5cb0fa84bb41eaf9c3e9dcd05c6138}}. But this theorem is highly non-constructive since there
are recursive infinite graphs whose infinite cliques and anticliques
are all non-recursive (not even in {{formula:1f1ff055-142f-485e-83e6-1075f7311805}} , {{cite:323b09f218755f1ed78087e358aa245e6aa27862}}, cf. {{cite:9dc30d1bbfb6fcfc33e2c96741875cf22469cdbf}}). Recall that a graph is recursive if both its
set of nodes and its set of edges can be decided by a Turing
machine. Replacing these Turing machines by finite automata, one
obtains the more restrictive notion of an automatic graph: the
set of nodes is a regular set and whether a pair of nodes forms an
edge can be decided by a synchronous two-tape automaton (this concept
is known since the beginning of automata theory, a systematic study
started with {{cite:7c0a04ccea71a1f09908b90f779604988be3198d}}, {{cite:b4b039eab4c76a0578b9cb4d2a5d94f93398a8f1}}, see {{cite:6db33a0f7cd99de03f15f2274c60f186f93e9151}} for a recent
overview). In this context, the situation is much more favourable:
every infinite automatic graph contains an infinite regular clique or
an infinite regular anticlique (cf. {{cite:6db33a0f7cd99de03f15f2274c60f186f93e9151}}).

Soon after Ramsey's paper from 1930, authors got interested in a
quantitative analysis. For finite graphs, one can ask for the minimal
number of nodes that guarantee the existence of a clique or anticlique
of some prescribed size. This also makes sense in the infinite: how
many nodes are necessary and sufficient to obtain a clique or
anticlique of size {{formula:8aaebe7e-4788-4ca7-aefa-70823bc4dc48}}  (Ramsey's theorem tells us: {{formula:cfb60f7a-ef68-44cf-9769-efd6ec90fb01}} ) or
{{formula:bbc9cc69-d4c4-419b-a4d3-bad512648d8f}}  (here one needs more than {{formula:7e1d2605-4ec1-42ef-954b-27f2d51af97a}} 
nodes {{cite:fb61af920ebc7d8d372e355fc608a8c5bb3d495d}}, {{cite:a95d0b80c446b13b622a855f184cfdb4bce83be8}}).

Since automatic graphs contain at most {{formula:7e48eab2-6a52-436c-8cb9-a772196ab4f0}}  nodes, we need a more
general notion for a recursion-theoretic analysis of this
situation. For this, we use Blumensath & Grädel's {{cite:b4b039eab4c76a0578b9cb4d2a5d94f93398a8f1}}
{{formula:bca741c4-2f64-4d5d-a7b0-31b520d6edec}} -automatic graphs: the names of nodes form a regular
{{formula:2bde5c03-c551-439a-8412-4d7849bd0c36}} -language and the edge relation (on names) as well as the
relation “these two names denote the same node” can be decided by a
synchronous 2-tape Büchi-automaton. In this paper, we answer the
question whether these {{formula:02e75918-6dbe-465f-b266-5958ef1f97cf}} -automatic graphs are more like
automatic graphs (i.e., large cliques or anticliques with nice
properties exist) or like general graphs (large cliques need not
exist).

Our answer to this question is a clear “somewhere in between”: We
show that every {{formula:8f667b5d-eb89-4799-a036-e68192235bbb}} -automatic graph of size {{formula:d76367a5-e5c9-423b-9e47-6b04e4f98655}}  contains a
clique or anticlique of size {{formula:0a675f70-63fe-470f-bda4-492e6b8e64dd}}  (Theorem REF ) –
this is in contrast to the case of arbitrary graphs where such a
subgraph need not exist {{cite:fb61af920ebc7d8d372e355fc608a8c5bb3d495d}}. But in general, there is no
regular clique or anticlique (Theorem REF ) – this is in
contrast with the case of automatic graphs where we always find a
large regular clique or anticlique. Finally, we also provide an
{{formula:1f05de15-7dd3-4c4b-8560-fce39a1a950c}} -automatic “ternary hypergraph” of size {{formula:71a17bb9-be70-45dc-9f86-dd970cc126fb}}  without any
clique or anticlique of size {{formula:ae2306af-72e7-40bb-ae15-e0b89bc3e79a}} , let alone {{formula:4a981e7a-8bdd-45b4-a487-50fb16ed3f4c}} 
(Theorem REF ).

For Theorem REF , we re-use the proof
from {{cite:72f1508287df2f948ac481b44d1429fe77701fff}} that was originally constructed to deal with
infinity quantifiers in {{formula:57e90dd3-d554-47e0-9b50-21c7286721b0}} -automatic structures. The proof of
Theorem REF  makes use of the “ultimately equal”
relation. This relation was also crucial in the separation of
injectively from general {{formula:04deaf2e-2738-415c-abe9-673d30207e8f}} -automatic structures {{cite:94c08825470b70c229a8645d638f3bd150ea1177}}
as well as in the handling of infinity quantifiers in {{cite:8f98238ccdc4bf5c80ca3463f45a5e309983d94c}}
and {{cite:72f1508287df2f948ac481b44d1429fe77701fff}}. In the ternary hypergraph from Theorem REF ,
a 3-set {{formula:fb2881e4-1178-49bc-8701-19a44c41a486}}  of infinite words with {{formula:4a90f74a-bcb3-4cf7-8006-9b34f878995d}}  forms
an undirected hyperedge iff the longest common prefix of {{formula:13da3499-7f25-4faa-97d0-8c03adbbbd59}}  and {{formula:e1b3f242-54e7-457b-aefd-446cd57a6bcf}} 
is shorter than the longest common prefix of {{formula:4585685e-c2ce-4eed-8745-c814c4939385}}  and {{formula:43918832-c6e5-480a-b51f-911fb03c2eb6}} .

>From Theorem REF  (i.e., the existence of large cliques
or anticliques in {{formula:e3dc764d-8930-4638-ab86-6de3684db9ab}} -automatic graphs), we derive that any
{{formula:1abf46e1-e36e-432e-890f-0d3d3189cba8}} -automatic partial order of size {{formula:5bf0a409-4d42-495d-8418-6fdfa40e5b59}}  contains an antichain
of size {{formula:e1c1e771-91d7-4295-8864-46c133dae72d}}  or a copy of the real line.

For a set {{formula:455a7af4-22f1-465e-941f-60e2c86ed985}}  and a natural number {{formula:2552b63d-5c1d-4cba-b850-b4014df1b877}} , let {{formula:1812fdb5-2bd5-4150-8c75-7bb7646a1ce4}}  denote the set

special: any {{formula:a057bfdd-b29d-402c-b36a-e7139e8e6cb3}} -partition {{formula:af2151fb-3cc9-41d1-bd73-9ccdef11250c}}  can be considered as an
(undirected loop-free) graph {{formula:4a9c8b3c-4d52-4b73-8eec-70c6fff23a2c}} . Homogeneous sets in {{formula:3fadf257-e6b8-4589-beab-4d124fa92dd3}}  are

homogeneous set of size {{formula:449ce6b3-b168-4b50-8a3f-af9e93be1a73}}  (where {{formula:fcc24f60-68a8-4512-b29d-5c4769721db3}}  and {{formula:d2d16773-dce7-49e4-8c93-c9274a55c51b}}  are

To reasoning the correctness of programs, C.A.R. Hoare presented an axiomatic system for specifying and verifying programs{{cite:2edf30e4613f061ac51b9bc062499691ebdcf36e}}{{cite:73be4372a099086a7c6e95cdec43f2be136cdd5b}}.
However, this logic can not deal with pointer programs because of pointer alias, i.e. many pointers may refer to the same location.
A few extensions to Hoare logic have been made to deal with pointers or shared mutable data structures {{cite:09bdf990a7060fe33aef6e5bb45be36f020dc886}}{{cite:1bd58fcff5e5aadd0d47dee0f63c4243bbed19fc}}{{cite:a987ab9ccae5075c8eaaf4fd9370252dda0c2785}}.
Among them, separation logic {{cite:bbf8e2ce60093bf1ed110116befd502c4ba340e5}} is one of the most successful extensions.
That logic uses a memory model which consists of two parts: the stack and the heap. Pointers can only refer to data objects in the heap. Separation logic extends
the predicate calculus with the separation operator, which can separate the heap into different disjoint parts.
Then the Hoare logic is extended with a set of proof rules for heap lookup, heap mutation and variable assignment. Though a few programs have been used to demonstrate the
potential of local reasoning for scalability{{cite:bd9b8b5e4cc36b65a48cccee57a83708654fa2ff}}, verifying programs using separation logic is still very difficult.

This paper presents an extension to Hoare logic for verification of pointer programs. This logic uses an extension of the Logic for Partial Functions (LPF) {{cite:180370c394bed7246ac6538ca57bc174b9a5a115}} to describe pre- and post-conditions of code fragments. Three type constructors are introduced to construct composite types and pointer types used in programs. Several kinds of function symbols associated with these types, together with a set of proof rules, are introduced to model and specify the memory layout/access in pointer programs.

In this logic, people can define recursive functions to retrieve abstract values from interconnected concrete data objects. These functions are called data-retrieve functions (DRFs). DRFs are recursively defined based on basic function symbols and the memory access/layout function symbols.
For each DRF {{formula:fdae8b3b-9e86-4fbf-8833-9d8defcdad64}} , there is a memory-scope function {{formula:8c69f15a-a16f-4938-a55d-a7e193201706}}  of which the definition can be constructed syntactically from the definition of {{formula:b23a1fdf-1098-4d3a-b87a-1c24022f19ad}} . If an application of {{formula:fa2c5fef-0db1-4f03-880e-d3234432f49c}}  results in an abstract value, then an application of {{formula:1e2bb95a-afb3-48b2-a06b-53937beb8126}}  to same arguments results in the set of memory units accessed during the application of {{formula:61f0a407-564a-46d8-b2db-50c0a045f0c8}} . During program executions, the application of {{formula:04c0cd1c-6f55-45fe-8f09-3bcb8df19dab}}  to same arguments results in same abstract value as long as no memory unit in this set is modified.

In this logic, program specifications are of the form {{formula:06c85a31-f4fe-4def-95a2-d0bffa48ca59}} , where {{formula:b3619bd7-3240-45ac-94a4-762e1d3accea}}  is a set of LPF formulae (usually a set of function definitions), {{formula:e9df56d9-1112-4fec-bb9b-e0e52d6dd741}}  is a fragment of code, and {{formula:4aab8ff5-53c6-4b19-9e18-9faca5f7a8c5}}  are the pre-condition and post-condition respectively. Such a specification means that if all the formulae in {{formula:a8ce031e-4058-4fb0-a57a-4bdefc2465e3}}  hold for arbitrary program states, and {{formula:5121b20b-97f7-4895-9e07-568a45ba23a8}}  starts its execution from a program state satisfying {{formula:a6f49f6c-c524-4196-9c10-50f634275c09}} ; then the state must satisfy {{formula:9d0d4f3d-1aee-4136-8461-ed67c8e5a2a1}}  when {{formula:c237192d-b443-49e5-a68d-ac0b51f22fb8}}  stops.

This paper is organized as follows. An extension to LPF is presented in Section . To model memory access and layout in pointer programs, several kinds of new function symbols and constants are introduced into LPF. A set of proof rules are introduced to specify these function symbols and constants. In Section , the concept `memory scope forms' of terms and `memory scope functions' (MSFs) are introduced. A proof rule is introduced to specify how definitions of MSFs can be constructed. A property about memory scope forms is also given in this section. The syntax of a small program language is given in Section . The semantic of this program language is also briefly described in this section. The syntax and meaning of program specifications are given in Section . The extension to Hoare logic is presented in Section .
The proof rule for assignment statements is modified to dealing with the pointer alias problem. Another proof rule is introduced for memory allocation statements.
Section  presents a formal verification of the running example in this paper. Section  gives some heuristics on program verifications using our logic. Section  concludes this paper.

In Appendix , we verify another program which inserts a new node to a binary search tree. In Appendix , we use a simplified version of the Schorre-Waite algorithm
to show that our logic can help people think about program verification in different abstract levels.

The logic for partial functions (LPF) used in Vienna Development Method (VDM) can reason about undefinedness, (abstract) types, and recursive partial function definitions.
The syntax of LPF terms and formulae is briefly described here. A term of LPF can be one of the following forms:

a variable symbol;

{{formula:a0d89699-f81d-4617-9966-758bd749764f}}  if {{formula:cbd2f1c1-49c5-492c-ad0d-80cf45fba7fe}}  is a function symbol, {{formula:9ef486c1-a3da-4a46-9e27-35e6bcd193ab}}  and {{formula:76e07376-26dd-4add-9326-29860e458e25}}  are terms,

{{formula:e1e05c40-faa9-4973-a0ef-aff4b3a26389}} , where {{formula:06efaee4-7b36-49c6-8d8e-32b7f216dafb}}  is a formula.

A formula of LPF can be one of the following forms:

a boolean-typed term,

It is originally represented by the symbol {{formula:19cfd2a4-2e03-4d95-a698-6779f296f0a7}}  in LPF papers, but {{formula:9288b550-2851-4a23-af62-e46e1d257c77}}  is used to denote the memory access function in this paper.)

{{formula:d663da9f-4ae9-484a-bc3f-8e350792f274}} , if {{formula:fe132e92-4e8b-4457-912f-5d25c5eea7f7}}  is a predicate symbol and {{formula:7ea30fa5-279f-40fa-9655-afa4b1e26437}} , and {{formula:2fd83784-a364-4ef8-b4e6-f9d9c785c6b3}}  are terms. In this paper, we view a predicate symbol as a boolean-typed function symbol.

{{formula:8c9eed4e-a8b2-4a13-87de-86b6a0a90d86}} , where {{formula:debd2dc1-fe93-4f5c-b493-ce091409ceef}}  are terms,

{{formula:fde98218-c227-428d-be79-bbfb121c83fa}} , where {{formula:47274d5a-2d3a-4b3b-84a2-f13c3cd11ac6}}  is a term and {{formula:aa8d597f-9963-4a44-b36d-9cca4fb5c135}}  is a type symbol.

{{formula:886356e6-ed5c-42af-ad54-f88dfd3aee53}} , {{formula:1e03b7d6-c2dc-4a91-b87c-ed2e29666a63}} , {{formula:96ced833-f7ed-4570-9744-fbb8ec11619f}}  are formulae if {{formula:1da0f303-756d-43fe-821f-941155c5db4d}}  are formulae.

{{formula:5195f023-764f-49ad-9b1a-4c74ed86ae05}} , where {{formula:23acbd55-9b05-4d39-a4a2-1ef54ab74e5d}}  is a variable, {{formula:66d6a646-02cc-4a3c-a38f-4b6b8a724c33}}  is a type symbol, and {{formula:31e73063-12ba-408a-99ed-556e762b83e0}}  is a formula.

{{formula:66b86fe3-4a7a-446a-9fdc-4b3169c4cb2d}} , where {{formula:cd8c52c2-8d6c-4032-8459-8d545ee9fa0f}}  is a term, and all the free variables in {{formula:d22de05c-adcf-41ce-ba78-ad91a8c6ccef}}  are in the set {{formula:e108b651-5bc1-40f6-8df5-0fe5735ab9c8}} .

For the proof rules, semantics and other detail information of LPF, we refer readers to {{cite:180370c394bed7246ac6538ca57bc174b9a5a115}}.

The LPF formulae used in our logic have a constraint: the logical connectives, {{formula:fd394dd1-5552-4404-8b53-c5c50a254d7c}} , {{formula:c4f4e4fa-9f7e-401c-a586-50ed9ae4ef13}}  and quantifiers can not occur in a term. Specifically, in a conditional form {{formula:7a83a343-c235-44a0-837b-d5b29e0c9f31}} , {{formula:c9418fa6-0909-4b0a-a605-8128504a6bc0}}  contains no logical connective and quantifier. However, we can use some operators like cand, cor, {{formula:db76c710-a7ae-4dc6-b3eb-1c87e03cf72f}} , in terms. These operators can be defined using conditional forms. This constraint makes it possible to define the memory scope form of terms.

In this paper, LPF is extended to deal with issues about memory access/layout, composite and pointer program types, data-retrieve functions and memory-scope functions. Now we first extend LPF with program types and associated function symbols.

In LPF, a type can be either a basic type such as {{formula:8849d8f2-684a-460e-93eb-efcd66555bf4}}  and {{formula:6a67d350-72e9-4067-bf08-025cd481a5cc}} , or a type constructed using type constructors such as
SetOf, SeqOf and Map. However, the abstract types constructed using these type constructors can not be used directly in imperative programs.
To deal with types appeared in programs, we introduce three new type constructors into LPF: pointer (P), array (ARR), and record (REC). We call the types that can appear in programs as P-types.

{{formula:1e51a0d8-a069-4a93-bd17-a34498de36ea}}  and {{formula:6f6ab56c-ed5e-4e3e-90f6-2e96db9dd71e}}  are P-types;
