We design experiments parameterized on:
the total number of input points {{formula:3bcefa83-da8f-4a62-8aaa-6e8ed4254341}} ,
the dimension {{formula:0fadca27-2636-425c-969d-96ee9b2683f5}}  of pointsets {{formula:722289de-c1a2-4493-8de6-f4185f6ac55b}} , and the dimension of projection {{formula:194ecdd4-a86e-4329-95f0-bcd5a01731f9}} .
First, we examine our algorithm on random inputs for implicitization and
{{formula:453c9ba8-e8b5-452e-97b3-6dc32629d037}} -resultants, where {{formula:d920137c-ceb7-4883-86b9-02dd27974f7a}} , while varying {{formula:201ba0fa-b916-4fd3-b92a-8d44f82c8e00}} .
We fix {{formula:89800204-3f68-41de-81f0-dd8e546e5fff}}  and select random points on the {{formula:6aed2359-376e-4aa7-b770-820ea81e272c}} -simplex
to generate dense inputs, and points on the {{formula:64c0a53a-07f7-4759-89ed-c9b9cef27024}} -cube
to generate sparse inputs.
For implicitization the projection coordinates correspond to
point {{formula:32f4a4b9-1531-4a9c-af45-d615ebb4fcb2}} .
For {{formula:32718443-ce7a-4761-bfcb-14099dd1e288}}  the problem corresponds to implicitizing surfaces:
when {{formula:09717e77-9e41-4866-b9e5-086ce4da8462}} , we compute the polytopes in {{formula:5bb10aba-5a37-416e-8cbe-e3a8d4e3cd60}} sec
(Figure REF ).
When computing the {{formula:9a3c8134-b626-4488-85f7-2c733acbcf6b}} -resultant polytope,
the projection coordinates correspond to
{{formula:70fba45a-fda7-4723-88b8-dc34bf778c4d}} .
For {{formula:15485a15-99ed-44aa-a63d-4de693e2d6a1}} ,
when {{formula:77d453b2-cd65-4257-ae49-6ad4dd936ce7}} , we compute the polytopes in {{formula:9a09b850-9a88-45e8-9b1a-2df0e4990db9}} sec
(Figure REF ).

By using the hashing determinants scheme we gain a {{formula:3a076ee6-a7cd-42ac-a4ad-c5ee2cc57468}}  speedup
when {{formula:1c40c803-55bb-4b5e-abfe-9b027b1089b1}} .
For {{formula:30939f1f-6630-49d6-936f-e89b2367476f}}  we gain a larger speedup; we computed in {{formula:e17df229-1917-430b-86c7-182a0277cf08}} min an
instance where {{formula:c3b34ec8-3313-4e0d-9fcb-75e7d250ede2}}  and would take {{formula:fd10dcfe-3720-489f-8664-ead653539f1c}} hr to compute
otherwise.
Thus, when the dimension and {{formula:81925893-1c0e-43ea-b222-232e47aba0ac}}  becomes larger, this method allows our
algorithm to compute instances of the problem that would be intractable
otherwise, as shown for {{formula:46d9f65b-5b15-4eff-9259-1d2a32ba8f83}} 
(Figure REF ).

We confirm experimentally the output-sensitivity of our algorithm.
First, our algorithm always computes vertices of {{formula:10e29ae6-063b-4c0a-8149-81ab651b6b94}}  either to extend
{{formula:fd0b103e-4e31-45d2-a082-208c29223d52}}  or to legalize a facet.
We experimentally show that our algorithm has, for fixed {{formula:f87e76f8-1d73-4b53-96c7-8b0d61737959}} , a
subexponential behaviour with respect to both input and output
(Figure REF , REF ) and its output is
subexponential with respect to the input.
{{table:a5b097e6-b27b-4ce1-b604-0e01b77e8d7a}}{{figure:924603b4-1f03-456c-a85d-e0e3aba8bd0b}}

As the complexity analysis (Theorem )
indicates, the runtime of the algorithm depends on the
size of the constructed placing triangulation of {{formula:6dae6f84-42bd-456f-9362-65e189de5ef9}} . The size
of the placing triangulation depends on the ordering of the inserted points. We
perform experiments on the effect of the inserting order to the size of the
triangulation as well as the running time of the computation of the
triangulation (Table REF ). These sizes as well as the
runtimes vary in a very narrow range. Thus, the insertion order is not crucial
in both the runtime and the space of our algorithm.
Further experiments in 4-dimensional {{formula:24b26ba7-53f7-44a9-94d9-4a8673c8b7a8}}  show
that the size of the input bounds polynomially the
size of the triangulation of the output (Figure REF ) which explains
the efficiency of our algorithm in this dimension.

We explore the limits of our implementation. By bounding
runtime to {{formula:57e4e486-c7d4-4712-b5e5-57acb9003276}} hr, we compute instances of 5-, 6-, 7-dimensional
{{formula:d9bdda62-716b-4cfe-b15e-0942d55b2ce9}}  with 35K, 23K, 500 vertices,
respectively (Table REF ).

We also compare with the implementation of Ref. {{cite:f2b3c0746cc6abf08d4f8dcdc0b8bb40f2fdc1de}}, which
is based on Gfan library.
They develop two algorithms to compute projections of {{formula:88e1518f-418b-48bc-b5d6-7c16b9a0a233}} .
Assuming {{formula:82979992-ee4a-4546-b50c-f6b476dbdcd3}}  defines a hypersurface, their methods compute
a union of (possibly overlapping) cones, along with their
multiplicities, see Theorem 2.9 of Ref. {{cite:f2b3c0746cc6abf08d4f8dcdc0b8bb40f2fdc1de}}.
From this intermediate result they construct the normal cones to the resultant
vertices.
{{table:0efc6419-1dba-47dd-baf8-07ef7f6fdce2}}

We compare with the best timings of Gfan methods using the examples
and timings of Ref. {{cite:f2b3c0746cc6abf08d4f8dcdc0b8bb40f2fdc1de}} (Table REF ).
Our method is faster in examples (d), (e), (g), (h) where {{formula:ec3b19dc-54c7-432f-8f74-a1f5013a6e0d}} , is
competitive (up to 2 times slower) in (a) where {{formula:f9246be5-cf2c-44c7-927f-1e86af3f796c}}  and (i) where
{{formula:bd29bd61-1eb6-4ec3-b7ac-01da3734c4b0}}  and slower in (b), (c), (f) where {{formula:a489e37f-c7a2-42b6-aba7-40943683a7d6}} . The bottleneck of our
implementation, that makes it slower when the dimension of the projection {{formula:84c74b2c-8485-4cdd-9c3a-f57c9a6c53aa}}  is
high, is the incremental convex hull construction in {{formula:f9d61ff6-abdb-4681-9691-bddac6263b1f}} .
Moreover, since our implementation considers that {{formula:53252df0-1df4-4f88-af07-b3f715c11b01}}  lies in
{{formula:4ccbf626-d36b-4d58-bcf5-c5712648a281}}  instead of {{formula:62a2acfa-464a-4fae-b92a-f3bf7af80ab4}} , (see also the discussion on the
homogeneities of {{formula:7c0c2691-662f-4e93-929c-bb395789a5e8}}  in Section ),
it cannot take advantage of the fact that
{{formula:fe368540-3678-472b-a0a4-17f6f8cc6b63}}  could be less than {{formula:d56d0940-7249-47d0-930c-40fc0995c137}}  when {{formula:331b3668-fa79-4814-a187-fc43b727b23f}} .
This is the case in examples (b), (c) and
(f).
On the other hand, we run extensive experiments for {{formula:5ed33ccf-eb2b-4056-bbdf-1bab6558d9f5}} , considering
implicitization, where {{formula:fd902a7e-b892-4bbb-92b3-8a32b847a196}}  and
our method, with and without using hashing, is much faster than
any of the two algorithms based on Gfan (Figure REF ).
However, for {{formula:8d068712-6d5e-4513-8546-c95016f435a4}}  the beta version of Gfan used in our experiments was not
stable and always crashed when {{formula:6b91cf13-00d5-4753-a021-99c8a8a9b812}} .
{{table:d51de594-374e-477f-a64a-587ee88bc979}}

We analyze the computation of inner and
outer approximations {{formula:18c0a785-22c3-4d07-af66-8fa10b2d859a}}  and {{formula:dc3ed4cf-9133-4ca6-bcdd-bbbac35f9831}} .
We test the variant of Section  by
stopping it when {{formula:5ce5f0d0-dea9-4d44-bfe4-dbfc0a453dca}} . In the
experiments, the number of {{formula:5c053cfd-9024-4b03-8406-68fa9cfbb674}}  vertices is {{formula:2f0159e9-5bf7-4fd9-9b06-c93af5394b8f}}  of the
{{formula:b2d61bd5-0e19-48d6-9760-8feb97b5c73f}}  vertices, thus there is a speedup of up to 25 times over
the exact algorithm at the largest instances.
The approximation of the volume is very satisfactory:
{{formula:bb6263ff-15c5-430e-a276-5f4416517ad4}}  and
{{formula:c8fbe000-d6f6-4f16-b042-ddd044058b13}} 
for the tested instances (Table REF ).
The bottleneck here is the computation of
vol{{formula:ab25e226-b006-4410-bbdd-7488c9cb0ec7}} , where
{{formula:f3e6eafb-0082-45c9-aa72-09f005a4da6d}}  is given in H-representation: the runtime explodes for {{formula:f27cc22b-3c69-4f2d-b43e-08180d4385bc}} .
We use
polymake in every step to
compute vol{{formula:efa09423-d56f-43a0-918d-c88b369f794b}}  because we are lacking of an implementation that, given a
polytope {{formula:a10d18f8-0448-49f9-8686-f50010dabbf7}}  in H-representation, its volume and a halfspace {{formula:51cc0c4c-0ba0-4704-831e-a2f9a0845767}} , computes the
volume of the intersection of {{formula:14dcae55-0ed5-451e-af13-c00ec561d6d7}}  and {{formula:b3fa0430-e1c8-4b6c-8c97-2442380d266b}} .
Note that we do not include this computation time in the reported time.
Our current work considers ways to extend these observations to a polynomial
time approximation algorithm for the volume and the polytope itself when the
latter is given by an optimization oracle, as is the case here.

Next, we study procedures that compute only the V-representation of
{{formula:4fdb9f44-3002-4a49-b75f-bb33d811187a}} .
For this, we count
how many random vectors uniformly distributed on the
{{formula:16472968-5ca9-47f6-a61a-63e9498b6551}} -dimensional sphere are needed to obtain
{{formula:73c1428d-3a5e-46a7-b3d7-ee84e3889a79}} .
This procedure runs up to 10 times faster than the exact algorithm
(Table REF ).
Figure REF  illustrates the convergence of
{{formula:2739cc46-abed-4757-af48-b1ae8c324357}}  to the threshold value {{formula:d2987ca2-d74d-46b1-83aa-bc59ad158faf}}  in
typical {{formula:bc5ae6e8-ecf3-4995-88c0-b26bb6aed12b}} -dimensional examples.
The basic drawback of this method is that it does not provide guarantees for
{{formula:adf68f81-b479-4b45-b92d-2a76f7ab32a0}}  because we do not have sufficient
a priori information on {{formula:3f6f1ebd-d0bb-473c-ac2c-621f2281870c}} .
These experiments also illustrate the extent in which
the normal vectors required to deterministically construct {{formula:bc0632f7-7bc6-427a-a810-fe207fdcf4c2}} 
are uniformly distributed over the sphere.

One algorithm that should be experimentally evaluated is the following.
We perform a search over the vertices of {{formula:7143b7f3-fce8-49b6-bbe1-b3f73f071f64}} , that is, we build a search
tree with flips as edges. We keep a set with the extreme vertices with respect
to a given projection. Each computed vertex that is not extreme in the above set is
discarded and no flips are executed on it, i.e. the search tree is pruned in
this vertex. The search procedure could be the algorithm of TOPCOM or the one
presented in Ref. {{cite:b68fe42c2ae8da5785ac966b64ee0621039d191b}} which builds a search
tree in some equivalence classes of {{formula:111fa37f-ec19-487e-a1d8-7f39cc08d698}} . The main advantage of this
algorithm is that it does not involve a convex hull computation. On the other
hand, it is not output-sensitive with respect to
the number of vertices of the resultant polytope;
its complexity depends on the number of vertices on the silhouette
of {{formula:1f8f2b14-1b5d-4e70-867d-5bdbf283723e}} , with respect to a given projection and those that
are connected by an edge with them.

As shown, polymake's convex hull algorithm is competitive,
thus one may use it for implementing our algorithm.
On the other hand, triangulation is expected to include fast
enumeration of all regular triangulations for a given (non generic)
lifting, in which case {{formula:2ade4f19-e5a9-46ca-8104-443a3d9ea35d}}  may be extended by more
than one (coplanar) vertices.

Our proposed algorithm uses an incremental convex hull algorithm and it is
known that any such algorithm has a worst-case super-polynomial total time
complexity {{cite:ece43dff68b2d483ee4738fba1542d081c2ba783}} in
the number of input points and output facets.
The basic open question that this paper raises is whether there is a polynomial
total time algorithm for {{formula:439ccf85-5805-408f-8147-024e7cb75400}}  or even for the set of its vertices.

All authors were partially supported from project
“Computational Geometric Learning”, which acknowledges the
financial support of the Future and Emerging Technologies (FET)
programme within the 7th Framework Programme for research of
the European Commission, under FET-Open grant number: 255827.
Most of the work was done while C. Konaxis and L. Peñaranda
were at the University of Athens.
C. Konaxis' research leading to these results has also received
funding from the European Union's
Seventh Framework Programme (FP7-REGPOT-2009-1) under grant agreement no 245749.
We thank O. Devillers and S. Hornus for discussions on
triangulation, and A. Jensen and J. Yu for discussions
and for sending us a beta version of their code.

Dissipative dynamical systems, with a low dimensional phase space, present
an important class of simple non-linear physical systems
with intrinsic complex behavior (homoclinic bifurcations, period doubling,
onset of chaos, turbulence), which generated
intense experimental, theoretical
and numerical work in the last few decades
{{cite:84e5170ceee00bca6d97baaf3501498fd467ae01}}, {{cite:69208d75ef372e600936b31b00b082a920428cf1}}.

Recently {{cite:e766d4ae42b21a0e88cf5e51ecf775230c416db1}} we have reexamined dissipative dynamical
systems with a 3-dimensional phase space from the perspective of Nambu-Hamiltonian
Mechanics(NHM) {{cite:8b5eae309e35f2f6251642bc8ceb6e33e9014dc6}}, {{cite:2b6d78ccec361041ac50a08cd89edb4848de24f0}}. The latter represents a generalization of
Classical Hamiltonian Mechanics, mostly appropriate for the study of odd-dimensional
phase-space volume preserving flows( Liouville's theorem). As such and
in order to make it directly applicable
to the dynamics of dissipative systems in {{formula:5f6977bc-d90f-442f-987a-b49133529893}}  we must associate it to a volume
preserving dynamics sector.
We have done so by introducing a flow decomposition to
their equations of motion and therefore isolate
in their flow vector field its rotational(solenoidal) part.
It is manifestly volume preserving, non-dissipative and hence directly describable
in terms of the intersecting surfaces of NHM. Along with the remaing irrotational component to the flow
the decomposition fully
recovers the dissipative dynamics of the system in question, presenting itself as an
equivalent formulation of the odd-dimensional dynamical system.

We have applied the above recipe to the famous examples of Lorenz{{cite:bf90c38cdc7021283b28dc59e5aca30fc3d74787}}
and Rössler
{{cite:9dac0252945817ce89740884efdd7623ffd89683}}
chaotic attractors
which represent the prototype models for the onset of turbulence.{{cite:69208d75ef372e600936b31b00b082a920428cf1}}.

In sect. 2 we start off with a discussion of flow decompostion for the most elementary and
familiar of all dissipative systems in {{formula:30646537-92c2-41d6-9dc1-61065456b2cb}}  without chaotic behavior :
the dissipative harmonic oscillator (DHO).
In this case the existence of a Hamiltonian formalism identifies for its "closed" nondissipative sector
the harmonic oscilator (HO) with a well defined integrable classical and quantum
evolution.

The presence of chaotic flows for dissipative systems in {{formula:3db0f77d-7139-42dd-8ef3-1a80fecaa2cf}}  is argued, by analogy,
to nescessitate intersecting Nambu Surfaces which define rerspectively "closed" physical systems
with integrable {{formula:fcd3b0bc-40ee-4bff-9f54-17396ae5996f}}  periodic orbits and simultaneously a well
defined classical and quantum behaviour.

In sect. 3 we apply the framework for the cases of the
Lorenz and Rössler strange attractors.
We isolate their non-dissipative sector parametrized by
two intersecting surfaces: a cylinder and a paraboid for the Lorenz attractor
as well as a helicoid with a cylinder for the Rössler system.
They account, amazingly, for the double scroll topology of the full " butterfly"
Lorenz attractor. and the single scroll topology for the Rössler case.
We end our presentation with Conclusions and open problems.

Dissipation is a necessary condition for dynamical systems to exhibit chaos. Yet it is not suficient. This is enunciated through a powerful No-go theorem . Indeed the Poincare-Bendixon alows for
only fixed points and limits cycles in two dimensions. Chaotic Flows need space to emerge. At the
minimal level they emerge with dissipative systems in {{formula:18755661-ffe1-496b-9213-5597d083dbc5}}  . They are typically associated with
Strange Attractors such as the famous ones of Lorenz and Rössler. They belong to a large class of dynamical systems whose dynamics is governed by continuous set of 1st order ordinary differental
flow equations
{{formula:341bf244-2da3-4ecf-b915-ee9703c462e0}}

where {{formula:9ffb81b5-6224-44a8-a5c4-1dfa73f36684}}  is a velocity field flow with {{formula:cfee3a47-99aa-4298-8c05-a2effcf54f91}}  some control external parameter. Their
phase space dynamics, depending on whether they exchange energy with their environment or not,
can be either open-dissipative or closed (conservative-Hamiltonian) .
This is reflected on their velocity flow field being divergenceless or not.
Let us see all these issues for the simple case of the Dissipative Harmonic Oscillator (DHO) whose phase space equations of motion are well known to be for {{formula:debc19d3-e506-456c-a5ba-7acce272fd91}}  and {{formula:9f949c91-8035-4058-a34a-4bbe7eb0a28c}} :
{{formula:a7bd07a5-fb27-4100-9cd6-16228bba82e7}}

The velocity flow is given by {{formula:19c71c8a-d651-416e-ba36-d1ba97b3cf21}}  for appropriate values
{{formula:f8248de5-3f2e-4293-949e-c86ddb66abb7}}  with a net outflow

Segmentation problem of branching tubular
objects in 2D and 3D images arises in many
applications, for examples, extracting roads in aerial photography,
and anatomical surfaces of blood vessels in
medical images. In this paper, we are concerned with identifying
tube-like structures in Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA)
images. Because of the necessity to
obtain as much fine details as possible in real time, automatic, robust
and efficient methods are needed. However, due to the low contrast,
intensity inhomogeneity, partial occlusions and intersections, and the
presence of noise and possible blur in the images, this segmentation
problem is very challenging.

There are many different approaches for vessel segmentation, see
for example {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}}, {{cite:79b92d23e3d762f5af8df282ac2c4c94d38f13fb}}, {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}, {{cite:61f9c0188a268a176f8366ded2d59cec5c64a57e}}, {{cite:b367cec1327e6c0306e9e3c89fd2c83fb2754c2b}}, {{cite:40e9de0cef316650d84bf71428cb48209f574905}}, {{cite:5024c45c99b9ad737707cf1600a09b8a533c5c9d}} and the extended reviews
{{cite:0cc8c1c2f9905eda73cb90b9126a29560296e6e1}}, {{cite:79bf47abcdb18dd7a8019bdca15a3112767befc9}}. In the following, we concentrate on two approaches
that are related to our approach:
the active contour approach and the partial
differential equation (PDE) approach.
For the vessel segmentation algorithms
that are based on deformable models {{cite:d63f0815bdddcab03daa81af2a2beabe7b13cae9}}, because
the explicit deformable model representation is usually impractical,
level set techniques to evolve a deformable model have been introduced,
and they provide implicit representation of the deformable model.
However, the level set segmentation
approach is computationally more expensive as it needs to cover
the entire domain of interest, which is generally one dimension
higher than the original one. Interested readers can refer
to recent literature on the level set segmentation strategy for
tubular structures {{cite:61f9c0188a268a176f8366ded2d59cec5c64a57e}}, {{cite:6ed1948ddfb7e766a16db7dc3efd5581982d74fe}}, {{cite:b993ef1eb81902ef43663c01e051b5fbc86f2ddd}}.

Based on the curve evolution techniques,
Mumford-Shah functional and level sets,
a new model for active contours to detect objects
in a given image was proposed in {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}}.
Unlike the classical active contour models, this model does
not depend on the gradient of the image.
In {{cite:7d3fdb1ed083e172b7f704e92f3b353243467b88}}, a generalization of the active contour
without edges model was proposed for object detection using logic operations.
However, both the active contour model {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}} and the logic framework
{{cite:7d3fdb1ed083e172b7f704e92f3b353243467b88}} are not suitable for detecting tubular structures with low
contrast and intensity inhomogeneity, see numerical results in Section .

In {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}, a geometric deformable model
for the segmentation of tubular-like structures was
proposed. The model is characterized mainly by two
components by using a suitable diffusion tensor:
the mean curvature flow and the
directionality of the tubular structures. The major
advantage of this technique is the ability to segment
twisted, convoluted and occluded structures without
user interactions; and it can follow the branching of different
layers, from thinner to larger structures. The
dependence on the grid resolution chosen to solve
the discretized PDE model is still an open problem.
The authors in {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}} have also applied a variant
of the proposed PDE model to the challenging problem
of composed segmentation in {{cite:d4334c529ddac329280f99511c9290f94e7746ef}}.

Besides the methods above,
there were some initial work by using wavelets or tight-frames
to do texture classification and segmentation {{cite:42b58bb11fa8b766d4a924236f1ac5df2f5e437d}}, {{cite:f2b75031666b49934baebd14ec5d7d3128460b62}}.
The tight-frame
approach is a versatile and effective tool for many different
applications in image processing, see
{{cite:5702dafd3c859f0128138034c4e2ecf2ecb280f6}}, {{cite:c3921281419bec53d71201994bd4ffdeef21c52f}}, {{cite:52e1d42d34d3ce272813a5e78faf51c69222140f}}, {{cite:d134f2fc66ccbb7e5664a8520d4004276f8ac7df}}, {{cite:b75f78edc782507d8b985fa6f2740f87178d68f8}}, {{cite:dc54c5a30fec1f0f0b5d72da2a194451da8dd39d}}, {{cite:0855442387036cdd47405a922ccef2918b44d04c}}.
There are many kinds of tight-frame systems, such as
those from framelets {{cite:5bfa6619471683f29816ea5c861289c8d0129f71}}, contourlets {{cite:8ff8202cf06b7348d6d72420dfb0bf22fe632453}} and curvelets
{{cite:8f872a5bd21d4470ec8181c72715bbad65010e81}}, {{cite:f28c2661ddecc60ae1e2dbed090d143b09c5e77f}}, etc.
Recently, the authors in {{cite:79b92d23e3d762f5af8df282ac2c4c94d38f13fb}} proposed to combine
the tight-frame image restoration model of {{cite:2da2b8fecfd98d13baf833e0c5db08f229676e2d}}
and the total variation based segmentation model
of {{cite:589470fed1a4c2e1a7675f01ec7134c7d81f82b4}}, {{cite:42c112594b7c749dae038d77e6c40423994783fb}}, {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}} to do segmentation. Their
approach results in a minimization problem. In this paper,
we also derive a segmentation algorithm that uses the
tight-frames. However our method is not based
on minimizing any variational model and hence it is
different from the method in {{cite:79b92d23e3d762f5af8df282ac2c4c94d38f13fb}}. In fact, our algorithm
iteratively updates the set of possible boundary pixels
to change the given image into a binary image. Like the method in {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}},
our method also has the ability to segment twisted, convoluted
and occluded structures. We will show that our algorithm is convergent.
In fact, numerical results show that it converges within 10
iterations for 2D as well as 3D Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) images.
We will see that our method can
extract much more details from the given image than the
method in {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}}, {{cite:79b92d23e3d762f5af8df282ac2c4c94d38f13fb}} and {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}.
We remark that a preliminary version of our segmentation algorithm
has been given in our proceeding paper {{cite:e59fe9ec00ba1d4f46a5686ac323fe32710c66e8}}. The main
contributions in this paper are: (1) a simpler strategy to initialize
and refine the regions enclosing the possible boundary
of the vessels, (2) the new strategy leads to a simple proof of
convergence and easier choice of parameters, (3) a different tight-frame
with better directionally selective property is used to
obtain more details in the image, (4) a new 3D result with higher noise
and more complicated vessel is added.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section ,
we recall some basic facts about tight-frame and
tight-frame algorithms. Our segmentation algorithm is given in
Section . In Section  we test our algorithm
on various real 2D and 3D MRA images and compare it
with those representative algorithms from different approaches:
PDE-based {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}, tight-frame {{cite:79b92d23e3d762f5af8df282ac2c4c94d38f13fb}} and active contour
models {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}}. Conclusions are given in Section .

The technology of Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) imaging is based
on detection of signals from flowing blood and suppression of signals
from other static tissues, so that the blood vessels appear as
high intensity regions in the
image, see Fig. REF (a). The structures to be segmented are
vessels of variable diameters which are close to each
other. In general in medical images, speckle noise and weak edges make it
difficult to identify the structures in the image. Fortunately, the MRA
images contain some properties that can be exploited
to derive a good segmentation algorithm. From Fig. REF (a),
we see that the pixels near the boundary of the vessels
are not exactly of one value, but they are in some range, whereas
the values of the pixels in other parts are far from this range. Thus
the main idea of our algorithm is to approximate this range accurately.
We will obtain the range iteratively by a tight-frame algorithm.
The main steps are as follows. Suppose in the beginning
of the {{formula:966ab99f-980b-4998-bc4c-87bb4c004306}} th iteration, we are given an approximate image {{formula:c9b671cb-7583-4082-80bb-6d8e47ea4109}} 
and a set {{formula:5d4cb209-4a33-49c5-9a54-176576b96185}}  that contains all possible boundary pixels.
Then we (i) use {{formula:2db983ce-ab7d-4dae-ae92-f976c99daf61}}  to estimate an appropriate range
{{formula:40b3b57c-6dc1-45bd-9296-3fd20e4854b3}}  that contains the pixel values of possible
boundary pixels; (ii) use the range to separate the image into
three parts—those below the range (background pixels), inside
the range (possible boundary pixels), and above the
range (pixels in the vessels);
(iii) denoise and smooth the inside part by the tight-frame
algorithm to get a new image {{formula:f3cab75e-de6c-426e-8997-6216d9105a1e}} .
We stop when the image becomes binary and this
happens within 10 iterations for the real MRA images
we tested, see Table REF 
in Section .
In the followings, we elaborate each of the steps.
Without loss of generality, we assume that the given image {{formula:c1f9100c-57e4-4d71-949b-ea0ab9180ba6}} 
has dynamic range in [0, 1].

image with {{formula:8f4c70ac-72ca-4172-b09d-b9f8209e0d31}}  pixels. Since the costs of computing {{formula:9419612b-f8d3-47ac-a4eb-eedd53af74d8}} ,
{{formula:daab8fa1-c346-4569-84fd-ef55e29cb94d}} , {{formula:9d9749b1-64b8-4b20-b0a2-fce8a5abfa25}} , and {{formula:5df75bdc-95f4-485f-8a97-7f4d13105935}} 
are all of {{formula:609125df-d490-495f-8485-6cfcafb4a62d}}  operations, see (REF )–(REF ); and the cost of
a tight-frame transform is also linear with respect to {{formula:85869300-1a8e-4aef-bb33-61721af6a0a9}} 
(see e.g. (REF ) where {{formula:2077b7ac-a94e-4700-b379-1ab73b7d2d5b}}  are all tri-diagonal matrices),
we see that the complexity of our algorithm is {{formula:30f003ab-d8b1-47a8-a741-d15568470c00}} 
per iteration.
In fact, one can speed up the computation tremendously
as all computations can be done only on pixels around {{formula:2b8b45a9-d5d4-48fe-a39d-9814fbdfe2c9}} 
and there is no need to carry out the computations in {{formula:0f826ec2-810f-4eee-96cd-145ad1a7c117}} —though
in the numerical tests, we did not optimize
the code and we just carried out the computations in {{formula:07cce43a-2aff-48bb-8305-bb4bf2b8ca04}} .
According to Table REF , after just 3 iterations, the set
{{formula:85698c86-8bed-4100-b2c0-67326369b654}}  contains
only a hundred pixels in the 2D case and just two thousand pixels in
the 3D case.

In this section, we try our tight-frame segmentation algorithm
(Algorithm 1) on 2D and 3D real MRA images tested in {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}
and {{cite:d4334c529ddac329280f99511c9290f94e7746ef}}. Our algorithm is written in Matlab.
The thresholding parameters {{formula:d7b9c4c2-01bc-4ef2-b8bf-cacc0187c068}}  used in (REF ) are
all chosen to be {{formula:b1746ded-b1db-453e-95c8-5ff6d5f4c6eb}} ; and
we choose {{formula:ac4fcf54-54e1-42cd-ab94-56b51578da4b}}  and 0.06 for 2D
and respectively 3D images in (REF ).
To display the boundary and the surface in the binary images visually,
we use the Matlab commands “contour” and “isosurface”
for 2D and 3D images respectively. The
tight-frame we used is the D{{formula:7f53e4d7-3e53-4324-8a0f-a414c1f8215e}} WT downloaded from
{{cite:87947011d92878f14944a7a8e604b010dad73b6d}} where all parameters in the code are chosen to be the
default values. In particular, the number of wavelet levels
used in the code is 4.
The 2D images are tested in a MacBook with 2.4 GHz processor
and 4GB RAM, while the 3D images, because of their sizes,
are tested on a node with 120GB RAM in a PC-cluster.
We compare our method with those representative
algorithms from different approaches:
PDE-based {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}, tight-frame {{cite:79b92d23e3d762f5af8df282ac2c4c94d38f13fb}} and active contour
models {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}}, where the programs are provided by the authors.

Example 1.
The test image is a {{formula:ab97e548-fe09-459b-a354-e75ee33fa683}}  MRA image of a carotid
vascular system, see Fig. REF (a). The blood
vessels contain regions with high and low intensities,
including some very thin vessels in the middle with intensities as
low as the intensity of the background. Intersections of partial structures
even increase the difficulty of the segmentation. The segmentation
results by different methods are given in Fig. REF 
where the given image is overlaid so that we can compare
the accuracy of the methods.
Clearly, the results of Figs. REF (b) and (c) are not satisfactory
since the vessels obtained in Fig. REF (b) are
disconnected and some vessels in Fig. REF (c) are not detected.
By comparing the parts inside the rectangles in Fig. REF (d)
with those in Fig. REF (e), we see that our method can extract
clearer boundary than the method in {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}, especially for
handling the artifacts near the boundary.
We also see that the noise in the image has been removed because
of the denoising property of formula () as
explained in Section . Our method converges
in 5 iterations and requires 0.64 seconds. The first column of
Table REF  gives {{formula:71d7430b-2f70-4e44-a233-c6f0d63af9f0}}  at each iteration.
{{figure:1131d720-0060-4a9a-bc3c-c55d7dfb995d}}{{table:8781783f-16b7-4f36-b721-f13090aaa48f}}

Example 2. The test image is a {{formula:08038f73-e42d-4659-9ae4-00599cf93aa5}}  MRA image
of a kidney vascular system as shown in Fig. REF (a). This
example shows the ability of our method to reconstruct structures
which present small occlusions along the coherence direction.
Our method converges in 6 iterations with 0.78 seconds;
and the second column in
Table REF  gives {{formula:48a2f596-d82c-4095-8934-4d8bf9c645d5}}  at each iteration.
The results by the method in {{cite:c247ca6d406f947b396a9e425f67b421c9e99860}} (Fig. REF (b))
and by the method in {{cite:79b92d23e3d762f5af8df282ac2c4c94d38f13fb}} (Fig. REF (c)) are not
good since they can not recover the small occlusions along the
coherence direction, while this can be done by our method and
the method in {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}, see Figs. REF (d) and (e).
Furthermore, our method is better than the method in {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}}
by comparing the rectangular parts of Fig. REF (d)
with those in Fig. REF (e), since our method can detect
smoother edges; see Figs. REF (f)–(k)
which are the results of zooming in the
rectangular parts of Figs. REF (d) and (e) respectively.
The results also show that our method is very effective in removing artifacts.
{{figure:b2d8fbf8-b25f-4119-842c-9952b4038ff9}}

Example 3. This is a 3D example where we extracted
a volumetric data set of size {{formula:391d2de0-baff-403b-93e7-c3d5498a2314}} 
from a {{formula:94c21368-c4f3-4a1c-afda-f5765eaa4dd9}}  CTA
(Computed Tomographic Angiography) image of the kidney
vasculature system, see Fig. REF (a).
Because of different curvatures, diameters, bifurcations, and weak
surfaces impaired by noise, it is hard to detect
the tips of the thin vessels.
Figs. REF (b) and (c) give the results by
using the method in {{cite:d4334c529ddac329280f99511c9290f94e7746ef}} and our proposed method
respectively. The figure shows that our method
can give much more details. A visual comparison of the given
image with our result shows that almost all the vessels
are correctly segmented. We note that our method converges in 9 iterations,
see the third column in Table REF .
{{figure:760e1b8d-8aed-4127-be58-19de68621eda}}

Example 4. Our second 3D example is
an MRA data set of a brain aneurysms (vessel wall dilatations).
The {{formula:73eb1907-b4ce-460b-b124-319da7c34d9f}}  volumetric data set
has been extracted from a {{formula:29f96c37-5117-4956-b657-51dfee9e8a37}}  MRA
image of the brain-neck vasculature system, see
Fig. REF (a). As in Example 3, the different
curvatures, diameters and bifurcations of the vessels
make it a difficult problem. In addition, the high noise
makes the thin vessels hard to see even by the naked eyes.
For this topological complex tubular structures,
Figs. REF (b) and (c) give the results by the method
in {{cite:ccc6eed5adc050000ac3302498ce54acd48c4f02}} and our method respectively. Obviously, our method
can segment many more thin vessels, especially those corrupted
by the high noise. The results reflect that our new method is very
effective in handling the noise spread on the surface of the vessels.
For this complicated example, our method converges in 9
iterations only, see the fourth column of Table REF .
Our segmentation technique can be used to compute vessel radii
and other clinically useful measurements in case of aneurysms.
In Fig. REF (c), one may argue that there are some small isolated
points in the image and the surface of the vessels is not
smooth. This can easily be remedied by smoothing our final binary image
by the tight-frame formula () one time before we show the image,
since () has the denoising property
as we explained in Section .
See Fig. REF (d)
for the denoised-and-smoothed image after one iteration of ().
{{figure:ddd85f32-50c5-4c2f-ac5c-899eda06a847}}

In this paper, we introduced a new and
efficient segmentation method based on the tight-frame approach.
The numerical results demonstrate
the ability of our method in segmenting tubular structures.
The method can be implemented fast and give very accurate,
smooth boundaries or surfaces. In addition, since the pixel values
of more and more pixels will be set to either 0 or 1 during the iterations,
by taking advantage of this, one can construct a sparse
data structure to accelerate the method. Moreover, one
can use different tight-frame systems such as those from
contourlets, curvelets or steerable-wavelet {{cite:8ff8202cf06b7348d6d72420dfb0bf22fe632453}}, {{cite:f28c2661ddecc60ae1e2dbed090d143b09c5e77f}}, {{cite:0f95a0fb0e378d8f648bc1c49c5b6a13e4fc9731}}
to capture more directions along the boundary.
Though we have proved that our algorithm will always
converge to a binary image, it will be interesting to
see what functional the binary image is minimizing.
The framework for proving convergence for tight-frame
algorithms, as developed in {{cite:c3921281419bec53d71201994bd4ffdeef21c52f}}, may be useful here.
These are the directions we will explore in the future.

Allocation Grant 2060408.
