In {{cite:8d786a1f64303e6a4a02c7c4b5885498e5c6759b}}, {{cite:50c99d47155f374dfe5a9e526d256399e9e89bf9}}, {{cite:e9a85289798b4f1d0346cc02061054b72dd26f5c}}, and many others, a tight connection between database schemas and the category-theoretic notion of sketches was presented and investigated. This connection was carried further in {{cite:46bb68c307a45c3dbb22a4518bf779e6dab6e590}} where the existence of three data migration functors was shown to follow as a simple consequences of using categories rather than sketches to model schemas. In this paper we shall show that a modern approach to the study of algebraic topology, the so-called lifting problem approach (see {{cite:61a23fa902c3e8fc240e050318378221fa654fd6}}), provides an excellent model for typical queries and constraints (see {{cite:a6375e3db8266afcdc316f084a6fb8d45dfd7188}}).

A database consists of a schema (a layout of tables in which columns connect one table to another) and an instance (the rows of actual data conforming to the chosen layout). One can picture the analogy between databases and topological spaces as follows. Imagine a database instance {{formula:8b28c2b6-a7a4-44f7-90e5-0947cbe3e352}}  and a database schema {{formula:942b10bb-10e5-4422-a654-bb43099462d7}} , each as an abstract space, and suppose we have a projection from {{formula:e7dcad39-31c8-4883-acbe-6d2e5f011a7e}}  to {{formula:0d01b945-06af-438b-9e3b-2fcaaf88ee63}} . That is, we have some kind of continuous map {{formula:c17312f6-947f-4532-9457-95487a6ae5db}}  from a “data bundle" {{formula:f1acfad4-d5b1-4aa4-9fd3-86075f26b41f}}  to a “base space" {{formula:d1dcaa82-c893-4c9a-8532-1ba876410d6c}} . Points in {{formula:faf2151b-a299-4111-936d-f940d9d126d2}}  represent tables, and paths in {{formula:01c32dd4-e67f-4512-93c1-bc9dff1d1b73}}  represent foreign key columns (or iterates thereof), which point from one table to another. Over every point {{formula:aaefe7ba-3b99-4549-9384-f84ec57af04d}}  in the base space, we can look at the corresponding fiber {{formula:f9d0c512-21b4-4fd8-bb88-a6173db8487b}}  of the data bundle; this will correspond to the set of rows in table {{formula:117c7a38-31fc-4e5f-a0e8-1bb0f610c92e}} .

A query on a database instance {{formula:ab845bf3-d85d-4a90-b9a9-b597577d49bd}}  is like a system of equations: it includes an organized collection of knowns and unknowns. In our model a query takes the form of a functor {{formula:e1adb307-c28e-4612-9dd3-f72fa2528b94}} , such that {{formula:b107f1c9-8a58-4e14-9f3a-e6c64fb231a4}}  (standing for WHERE-clause) corresponds to the set of knowns, each of which maps to a specific value in the instance {{formula:0f60c5a4-1a89-481a-9464-fd7ed9db4ca9}} , and such that the relationship between knowns and unknowns is captured in a schema {{formula:d776a2ee-baad-4b71-9752-e2599f12ad30}} . More precisely, a query on the database instance {{formula:2cedf5fa-1d70-4142-8ba1-e9e961ec9eec}}  is presented as a commutative diagram to the left, which would be roughly translated into the pseudo-SQL to the right,A more general SQL query, with a specific SELECT statement will be discussed in Example REF . in (REF ):
{{formula:a4f8e52b-598a-4c73-b531-5f588879f227}}

A result to the query is any mapping {{formula:d5b3f73d-e118-4664-b60b-cf4c22c4ce76}}  making both triangles commute ({{formula:67c1bb88-9429-41db-a509-db94c81c7931}} ) in the diagram
{{formula:df7047cb-b764-47cf-98ae-28869ebf1769}}

The map {{formula:f13a7cfb-72b8-4851-8ac6-881de58d5076}}  is called a lift, hence the term lifting problem. The idea is that a lift is a way to fill the result schema {{formula:4857bb7a-81e9-47f2-8178-d8ac3e4e9086}}  with conforming data from the instance {{formula:7e25148a-290a-4f0a-aadc-65c8ec90c697}} .

We will now give a simple example from algebraic topology to strengthen the image, and then an example database query to ground it.

Consider an empty sphere, defined by the equation {{formula:9181a5dc-775b-44e8-8211-fc8d717bc565}} ; call it {{formula:1ce56fa7-06ec-4606-b9a2-3ff148e522ae}} . We project it down onto the {{formula:d89cd514-28d0-4187-a701-2560f275c359}} -coordinate plane; call that plane {{formula:b9c9bce7-4805-42ae-8160-41522d2f9455}} . The sphere {{formula:6322fb2b-fe02-4a40-83de-79b380808a31}}  serves as the database instance and the plane {{formula:d997a554-9b12-407f-82ed-46a7fae3c53f}}  serves as the schema. A query consists of some result schema mapping to the plane {{formula:18965cd0-a1fc-4c32-b0cf-8adec05fb981}} , say a solid disk {{formula:ddc25f06-6666-4aea-beee-0376e743fcbc}}  (given by {{formula:c071786f-ec80-4075-9ac4-f09901f0a342}} ), together with some constraints, say on the boundary circle {{formula:61275754-d44b-4254-8066-4edf17ad7a46}}  (given by {{formula:3391c6ba-e845-4218-b31a-bb951acff76b}} ) of the disk. Graphically we have Figure REF  below.
{{figure:d5e3fe64-dfa1-4e25-b926-96a1e1dde9d8}}

The results of the lifting query from Figure REF  are the mappings {{formula:44555248-5c89-49ee-bcfd-a09752328c52}}  making the diagram commute. Under the guidance of (REF ) the query would look something like this:

         S̄ELECT {{formula:ef702aac-1d28-47c3-b5bc-bd69f937aa42}} 
Topologically one checks that there are exactly two lifts—the top hemisphere and the bottom hemisphere—so our pseudo-SQL query above would return exactly two results.

We now provide an example of a situation in which one may wish to query a database, and we show that this query naturally takes the structure of a lifting problem. We break a single example into three parts for clarity.

Example 1.1.1 (Main Example 1: Situation, SPARQL, and schema)

Suppose you have just come home from a party. There, you met and really hit it off with a married couple; the husband's name is Bob and the wife's name is Sue; they live in Cambridge. From your conversation, you know that Bob works at MIT and Sue works in the financial sector. You'd like to see them again, but you somehow forgot to ask for their contact information; in particular you'd like to know their last names.

This is a typical database query problem. It can be phrased as the following SPARQL graph pattern query (which we arrange in two columns for space and readability reasons):

In the following two examples (Examples REF  and REF ) we will show that this query corresponds to a lifting problem for {{formula:818b5738-b5ad-4b35-9fa6-7edbd162f40d}} .

Suppose {{formula:17d0e420-b8be-41af-927b-99fc9f9cde2f}}  is our data bundle, and assume that it contains enough data that the constants in the query have unique referents. There is an obvious functor {{formula:a00cc8c4-8414-420b-b869-8c5ee8483a7c}}  that sends each object in category {{formula:85b6990b-7bcc-4de1-8a59-37a8f2acad30}}  to its referent in {{formula:8be3d1f1-a81d-46f3-badc-d654088bc4d8}} . Thus our query from (REF ) is finally in the form of a lifting problem as in (REF ). We will show in Example REF , after we have built up the requisite theory, that the set of lifts can be collected into a single table, which would look something like this:

This concludes the tour of our main example: we have shown a typical query formulated as a lifting problem. The mathematical basis for the above ideas will be presented in Section .

The purpose of this paper is to:

provide an efficient mathematical formulation of common database queries (modeling both SQL and SPARQL styles),

attach a geometric image to database queries that can be useful in conceptualization, and

explore theory and applications of the derived database {{formula:14529ef6-5fa3-4234-8d7b-ea36c3b8e908}}  of queries on a database {{formula:5370caf1-a248-4703-9f58-67b8b7ffb6f6}} .

We begin in Section  with a review of the categorical approach to databases (see {{cite:46bb68c307a45c3dbb22a4518bf779e6dab6e590}} for more details). Roughly this correspondence goes by the following slogan: “schemas are categories, instances are set-valued functors". In Section REF  we also discuss the Grothendieck construction, which will be crucial for our approach: a database instance can be converted into a so-called relational fibration, which we will later use extensively to make the parallel with algebraic topology and lifting problems in particular.

In Section  we define constraints on a database in terms of lifting conditions and discuss some constraint implications. We give several examples to show how various common existence and uniqueness constraints (such as the constraint that a given foreign key column is surjective) can be framed in the language of lifting conditions. In Section  we discuss queries as lifting problems, and review the paper's main example. In Section , we show that the queries on a given database can be collected into a new, derived database. This derived database of queries and their results can be queried, giving rise to nested queries. We explain how this formulation can be useful for managing the impact of schema evolution. Finally in Section  we briefly discuss some possible directions for future work, including tying in to Homotopy Type Theory (in the sense of {{cite:0dac6ba5791631780ab426c0a70bba405bd70f8b}} and {{cite:847e79ffe6d3ad0200d6ef07f208fa20819e96d4}}) and other projects.

We use the notation {{formula:9ba977e7-6be4-4cdb-b33f-8a484e13716b}}  to denote a set with one element. Given any category {{formula:1bc0ce51-7a52-4133-b917-34da79847a4c}} , we denote the category of all functors {{formula:899f5e7d-582c-439c-9327-c96db539c19e}}  by {{formula:fcf06dff-fc4d-4407-bc9c-ea045cdc9ebc}} . The terminal object in {{formula:6b70d36c-520b-4fb2-aed1-8749456b3bd1}}  sends each object in {{formula:361332ad-c0ab-4c9c-9f41-5ada7e8545cb}}  to {{formula:e5c8848a-3c5f-4ac1-bab7-82edcee2a3eb}} ; we denote it by {{formula:048d2fb2-299c-449c-b7d1-68769648b49e}} . We use {{formula:e85858a6-5256-4860-8794-8d614b134aa2}}  to denote a discrete category with one object. For any category {{formula:cb9d390b-d5d4-4500-9552-3a63d204674f}} , there is a one-to-one correspondence between the objects in {{formula:ec3b0c34-4be3-4c2c-893a-dd46cde31746}}  and the functors {{formula:0da52aea-5388-4429-8b5a-81737ba9dd77}} . Thus we may denote an object {{formula:af1e10a3-4f22-4f8a-af03-f9a3c42912fe}}  by a functor {{formula:a8bd7994-6745-4c3e-9cf9-5aba6da8dfa5}} . In particular, we elide the difference between a set and a functor {{formula:f1852e05-7b55-47f2-a4f1-af3f6fbb2bba}} .

We draw schemas in one of two ways. When trying to save space, we draw our objects as concisely-labeled nodes and our morphisms as concisely-labeled arrows; when trying to be more expressive, we draw our objects as text boxes and put as much text in them (and on each arrow) as is necessary to be clear (see {{cite:786a7e889483b9dc754641133ea5f1fab96d72f5}}). For example, we might draw the indexing category for directed graphs in either of the following two ways:
{{formula:b35830be-5be7-4a34-b7b6-fb8f3e01b3b7}}

When in the typographical context of inline text we are discussing an object that has been elsewhere displayed as a textbox (such as an edge), we may represent it with corner symbols (e.g. as {{formula:b659f44d-acca-40bd-b5e0-dd08f8cad13d}} an edge{{formula:e8e36bed-69d4-4d2b-b168-c84d0a014fdb}} ) to avoid various spacing issues that can arise.

Given two categories, there are generally many functors from one to the other; however, if the objects and arrows are labeled coherently, there are many fewer functors that roughly respect the labelings. We will usually be explicit when defining functors, but we will also take care that our functors respect labeling to the extent possible.

The basic mantra is that a database schema is a small category {{formula:aea49ad8-3f32-4d23-aea5-c97d39830396}}  and an instance is a functor {{formula:9621a244-df3e-4296-a2ac-3d39b442ba7f}} , where {{formula:5ba5f5fc-25bc-4e78-b84c-220c0f07e2ee}}  is the category of sets.If one prefers, {{formula:a32f377f-927c-4fb7-b81b-a05e9650cb54}}  can be replaced by the category of finite sets or by the category Types for some {{formula:f6809178-478e-49bd-b16d-41b43ef01e34}} -calculus. To recall these ideas, we take liberally from {{cite:46bb68c307a45c3dbb22a4518bf779e6dab6e590}}, though more details and clarification are given there. Readers who are familiar with the basic setup and data migration functors can skip to Section REF .

In {{cite:46bb68c307a45c3dbb22a4518bf779e6dab6e590}} a category {{formula:80834321-9c4e-4fe1-8b5b-2b47b936e156}}  of categorical schemas and translations is defined and an equivalence of categories
{{formula:e3125982-5b10-454f-aaef-3db7925fefa8}}

is proved, where {{formula:b8a28364-0416-4ae7-8990-c8ae78d32b0a}}  is the category of small categories. The difference between {{formula:354811df-30b0-44b2-bdf2-da33f5729b15}}  and {{formula:5c4e993e-916e-45c3-b239-f0326e42da35}}  is that an object of the former is a chosen presentation of a category, by generators and relations. Given the equivalence (REF ), we can and do elide the difference between schemas and small categories.

Roughly, a schema {{formula:43a51b45-f7ca-42c5-bfc7-235198c9d33a}}  consists of a graph {{formula:dc9e6ff1-5499-42d9-b46b-9c8d5ecf1aff}}  together with an equivalence relation on the set of paths of {{formula:5726bce8-b8fc-45cb-9484-85d1d6f4b5ef}} . Each object {{formula:01a96570-4b10-4d25-91ad-b9f085d85b33}}  represents a table (or more precisely the ID column of a table), and each arrow {{formula:efc219aa-e787-4203-b1ea-4f58770e2d55}}  emanating from {{formula:c4c4fc62-e5cd-4ff3-9b7e-99612d35bbb8}}  represents a column of table {{formula:02590aa5-80b7-4e0f-b7e5-2999ed5f0ab8}} , taking values in the ID column of table {{formula:ce146be5-84dd-4cee-99f2-a4d3e459fd22}} . An example should clarify the ideas.

the first name of {{formula:5ebb4a8a-003d-4c2a-9add-1547d1056373}} , which is a FirstNameString,

the last name of {{formula:83687a76-6937-4643-bb24-61e4bfd88539}} , which is a LastNameString,

For each department {{formula:9e643424-de82-440c-8c94-b466df0bd644}} , we keep track of

Once we realize that a database schema can be captured simply as a category {{formula:bd063159-5892-476a-93c6-f62b0969a3f5}}  and each instance on {{formula:336e9795-bf19-492a-9131-e2efa55f6cba}}  as a set-valued functor {{formula:7c03a5a9-44b0-417a-9814-f5a25ef640f1}} , classical category theory gives ready-made tools for migrating data between different schemas. The first definition we need is that of schema mapping.

In the Introduction (Section ), we discussed database instances in terms of mappings {{formula:a8dc5064-b824-4c3e-b519-d5dfda9484f8}} , each from a data bundle {{formula:48354dc4-21ca-4ea8-b423-e7ce0744be18}}  to a base space {{formula:ce127059-c038-4763-9b8e-126ccb692496}} . We were referring to exactly the above relational fibration picture.

We have been calling the map {{formula:af562644-4926-41dd-84dc-01f45aabbd26}}  a “relational fibration", but there is a more common category-theoretic term which, to the author, seemed overly technical for the context of this paper. Namely, a functor {{formula:d63955f6-6d71-4591-a46d-ac055cec037d}}  obtained by applying the Grothendieck construction to a set-valued functor {{formula:03a46596-8dde-4c32-a377-eaf189448d89}}  is usually called a discrete opfibration (see {{cite:1c1366f98093cdd3e5d8becac57053db1e2e7481}}). We use the term relational fibration as a more database friendly synonym for the term discrete opfibration.

In Section REF  we will give a definition of relational fibrations in terms of lifting constraints (Definition REF ). First, however, we attempt to understand a relational fibration {{formula:b809346c-0cff-475a-a323-d7fb15b8931d}}  by considering its various fibers and their relationships. More precisely, given an object {{formula:bbbee5c9-5e4d-4037-ac7a-b155c722ac18}} , we consider the fiber {{formula:73667c37-4dac-4455-8682-659b64f113bd}} , and given a morphism {{formula:c2447669-c430-4fd5-af8e-cf97b0ef6390}}  in {{formula:6914bfd8-c424-444d-985c-830bda6945d3}}  we consider how the fibers {{formula:b3257078-b9f7-4f52-ba68-618674f279f1}}  and {{formula:bef34dc8-4404-4864-a11c-7067bd6c5463}}  relate.

If {{formula:399491a6-1898-46aa-a749-09dbfe823ea0}}  were not assumed to be a relational fibration but instead just a general functor, then all we would know about these various fibers would be that they are categories. But the first distinctive feature of a relational fibration (or discrete opfibration) is that the fiber {{formula:e73fdfb8-737c-48e2-86c9-6e315cc3ac1f}}  is a discrete category, i.e. a set, for each object {{formula:75ef137d-2a32-4acc-a4a9-9017af31d13e}} ; that is, there are no morphisms between different objects in a chosen fiber (see Proposition REF ). The pre-image {{formula:7563d26b-8698-45bf-98e6-c6e76f49a9f3}}  of {{formula:76b55c04-33e1-46f7-9633-50283fc2f05f}}  is a set of morphisms from objects in {{formula:409bd60f-8d41-438a-a014-37fa17744e40}}  to objects in {{formula:ad884207-d6fd-4314-b1bb-9f16c5bcb309}} . When {{formula:d2ea209f-ad65-4186-a455-62dfc4d2a1fe}}  is a relational fibration, there exists a unique morphism in {{formula:feadb296-1304-45f5-8b31-d3afb6619a3d}}  emanating from each object in {{formula:a3de2408-7072-4cc4-859f-ba21c5f098a7}} , so the subcategory {{formula:6d6d2cb1-1074-4944-b533-0678f7808c66}}  can be cast as a single function {{formula:b3daf721-2756-44a4-ae32-d498165d90b7}} .

To recap, the relational fibration {{formula:f15554e9-e0ea-4629-b621-10cbcf8426b6}}  of a set-valued functor {{formula:848da656-cc72-42a2-9c37-fc9f43d18d2b}}  contains the same information as {{formula:13e5ef4d-0341-465d-a3f5-01c983956924}}  does, but a different perspective. We have

In algebraic topology (see {{cite:980f7a55dace45667767d3b53ac9a21941cae85a}}), one associates to every topological space {{formula:8ed81788-38cf-4e0c-a6bc-1d784ceac885}}  a fundamental groupoid {{formula:8dcc7535-fc88-44a0-aed3-a76351eacfe6}} . It is a category whose objects are the points of {{formula:45b3e130-8a14-4cc7-83f3-0e7c962db88f}}  and whose set of morphisms between two objects is the set of continuous paths in {{formula:b25b6bf5-33f0-4edf-bed9-5cc64c3958fb}}  from one point to the other. Two paths in {{formula:aaaa3007-dc55-4d83-ab96-b55570cabb10}}  are considered equivalent if one can be deformed to the other (without any part of it leaving {{formula:d31ef23f-d47c-437f-9606-b890931bd91d}} ). Composition of morphisms is given by concatenation of paths.

One can reduce some of the study of a space {{formula:7c674fd4-8eeb-4189-b034-0a282010b3a7}}  to the study of this algebraic object {{formula:77d18c39-0bb4-49f7-bfc2-e4b184961cfd}} , and the latter is well-suited for translation to the language of this paper.

In this section we introduce the lifting problem approach to database constraints. Roughly the same model will apply in the next section to database queries, the idea being that a lifting constraint is a lifting query that is guaranteed to have a result.

Let {{formula:e898b345-8ae1-4a2d-946a-fd4db848d448}}  be a database schema. A (lifting) constraint on {{formula:ea4eaccc-0ab7-4161-8bc1-9d1612d5e1db}} is a pair {{formula:07a1d5bc-572d-48f8-8a89-0a5a7ebd0673}}  of functors

{{formula:ba24fb8b-9eed-4225-bd29-fa88871091de}}

A (lifting) constraint set is a set {{formula:c84cea5d-ed9f-4355-ae4a-1091cbd065fc}} , for some set {{formula:27ce8857-62ba-4d48-b9b7-5919735cd2a2}} . Remark 3.1.2

While not all constraints on databases are lifting constraints (for example, declaring a table to be the union of two others is not expressible by a lifting constraint), lifting constraints are the only type of constraint we will be considering in this paper. For that reason, we often leave off the word “lifting," as suggested by the parentheses in Definition REF .

In this section we will show how to use lifting constraints (see Definition REF ) to declare a number of different properties for tables in a database. Our examples include

declaring a table to be non-empty,

declaring a table to have exactly one row,

declaring a foreign key to be injective,

declaring a foreign key to be surjective,

declaring a binary relation to be reflexive, symmetric, and/or transitive,

declaring a table to be a product or a general limit of other tables, and

declaring that there are no nontrivial cycles in a discrete dynamical system.

We will discuss these in order.

The main example of this was discussed in Example REF . There we were interested in learning more about a married couple, given certain known information about them. After building up the necessary theory in Sections REF  and REF  we will apply it to the case of the married couple in Example REF .

In particular, we provided a SPARQL query to find all instances of married couples with the requisite characteristics (e.g. the husband's and wife's first names being Bob and Sue respectively). In Example REF  our SPARQL query (REF ) only has variables in subject and object positions (the nodes of the schema). It seems that most SPARQL queries used in practice also only have variables in the subject and object positions (see, e.g. {{cite:c4647c91f5ce16538b765822863045867a9e5915}}); still, general SPARQL queries can involve variables in any position including in predicate positions, which correspond to the arrows of the schema. For example, we may use (John ?x Mary) to find all known relationships between John and Mary. To deal with this type of query, one may proceed as follows.

If {{formula:69c9e121-86bc-4143-be23-cb4beb9d69ed}}  is a graph (thought of as a schema with trivial path equivalences, which is in keeping with RDF schemas), then {{formula:2bc45c12-8492-4b9c-80be-69b0af4220f0}}  itself is in fact a database instance on the schema {{formula:c5177c80-471e-49bb-ab6b-99cb62c46e3d}}  from Example REF . A relational fibration {{formula:569dfa93-9289-4497-bbbc-a9359dc971c9}}  can be considered simply as a map of graphs, i.e. a map of instances on {{formula:e3f7e322-169c-41b6-b889-b05faac75aa9}} . Taking its Grothendieck construction yields a map {{formula:79ddc9ac-2194-4745-a0f0-6c6dca66d2fe}} , whereby each arrow from {{formula:c879cd37-1879-45b3-8479-854591295901}}  (representing a foreign key column) and each arrow from {{formula:c2b25ab0-7c2b-440f-8eb9-d394913fd05f}}  (representing a cell in a foreign key column) have become a node. We can perform the original SPARQL query to this derived form of the database because our original predicate can now be accessed as a subject or object. For example our statement (John ?x Mary) would become the pair of statements (?x subject John) (?x object Mary).

In this section we will discuss some formal properties of the machinery developed in earlier sections. For example we will show that the queries on a given database can be arranged into a database of their own and subsequently queried. This process is commonly known as nesting queries. To this end, we define a category of queries and prove that the process of finding solutions is functorial. We do this in Sections REF  and REF . In Section REF  we extend some results from Section REF , giving more detail on the interaction between data migration functors, on the one hand, and query containment and constraint implication on the other.

This section is technical, but it may have fruitful applications. Given any database {{formula:e55eed6f-d696-4230-bcb7-24fd8d9d4789}} , the category {{formula:cef75f85-36d9-4c55-a301-5141430a5744}}  organizes the queries (or views) on {{formula:1b46269a-9e3d-4a6a-9f16-5fa23f5e338e}}  into a schema of their own. There is a canonical instance on {{formula:ad396fb3-f477-4623-b5b0-de7df0a66651}}  populating each table (corresponding to a query) with its set of results. In typical applications, users of a database {{formula:9bc4d2b7-2d3b-468e-b862-d7d098a0d7d3}}  are often better served by interacting with {{formula:b5ba05fe-a160-4664-9beb-2fe10917aa16}}  rather than with {{formula:ae5fa72e-f3b6-4424-b9cb-8eaf14e15d8f}} . It is important to understand how schema evolution affects different parts of {{formula:0729bd3e-873c-4254-b80f-97a6bdb3ec14}} ; this is briefly discussed in Section REF .

This paper has set up an analogy between database queries and constraints on the one hand, and a now classical approach to algebraic topology—the lifting problem—on the other. Data on a schema is analogous to a covering space or fibration: the local quality of this fibration is determined by constraints, and the locating of sections that satisfy a set of properties is the posing of a query.

There are a few interesting directions for future research. The first is to make a connection to the relatively new field of homotopy type theory (HoTT) (see {{cite:0dac6ba5791631780ab426c0a70bba405bd70f8b}},{{cite:847e79ffe6d3ad0200d6ef07f208fa20819e96d4}}). The idea is that instead of two paths through a database schema being equal, one could declare them merely equivalent; if paths are declared equivalent in more than one way, these equivalences may also be declared as equivalent (or not). In this context, two observations on data may not be definitionally equal, but provably equal, and we consider the proofs and the differences between proofs as part of the data. To make this connection, the schema of a database should be a quasi-category ({{cite:b6333a447598473403d06d04c36143b6ff5d7473}},{{cite:c543cc327d7b0b1bd5521dd2f602c0779236f273}}) {{formula:f6b6c90d-67b1-4d8a-a55c-7f59d6ba177b}}  rather than an ordinary category. Each higher simplex encodes a proof that different paths (or paths of paths, etc.) through the schema are equivalent. We might replace the instance data by a functor (map of quasi-categories) {{formula:67ea307a-859a-4ca7-9b98-5fdafc975d13}} , where {{formula:81e78818-3230-47cd-a856-b5c02b61896a}}  is the quasi-category of homotopy types. In this context, classical homotopical questions, e.g. from the theory of model categories ({{cite:1e7f900e82ba0e503bafd7056398bbabab2fea01}}) may be even more applicable.

Another direction for future research is to use topological tools to investigate or “mine" data. For example, given a functor {{formula:813b19dc-fa01-49b8-bc40-00faea37816d}} , we can compose with the functor {{formula:b4ecda00-059d-4109-963f-00754dd5b0b7}}  which sends each set to the corresponding discrete topological space. The homotopy colimit of {{formula:841731a1-1eb7-472e-ac06-e614dbb1c369}}  is a topological space, of possibly any dimension and homotopy type, that encodes the connection pattern of the data. This space is homotopy equivalent to the nerve of the data bundle,
{{formula:f7c223a5-a18b-4023-b9c9-30fd588491ce}}

(see {{cite:61e20f53721ebe845857e406ba7afa9b18f9c5ce}}). Thus we could report homotopy invariants of the data {{formula:b4151dfb-6840-471a-935d-cf859db8f618}} , such as connected components, loops, etc. The question is whether these invariants would be meaningful and useful. For schemas of classical mathematical interest, such as the simplicial indexing category {{formula:728589bb-f811-48eb-bf42-18fc98928b76}} , the homotopy colimit of {{formula:6abf9302-07a5-4bdd-90fa-8744c804595b}}  is exactly what we want; it is the geometric realization of {{formula:2a767d33-e834-48a7-9a60-d9ef80beb1bd}} . It remains to be seen whether such homotopy invariants may be useful in other contexts; e.g. there may be some connection to the analysis given by persistent homology (see {{cite:46a3d501e9ec4fcdeb869413f855c7d16d2d4ddb}},{{cite:e77e8982fce545a025c37d7e19b14a5ba6c269df}}).

A third and fairly straightforward project would be to adapt Garner's small object argument (see {{cite:37da63c2b869e5abfbc1024adb71385a1f02ba27}}) to our notion of constraints. Garner's argument works, and provides nice universal properties, in the case of what we have called “universal constraint sets" (see Section REF ). The question is, if we apply his techniques to local constraints, such as those in Example REF  used to declare that one table is the product of two others, does his procedure still result in a relational fibration with all the nice universal properties enjoyed in the universal case? We conjecture that it will. One should also check whether the results obtained from that procedure agree with those from the so-called universal chase procedure (see {{cite:13ee21f4970c5024af66d3a7235af50d91dacbad}}). Indeed, they should provide equivalent results, since both claim to be universal in the same way.

A third and fairly straightforward project would be to adapt Garner's small object argument (see {{cite:37da63c2b869e5abfbc1024adb71385a1f02ba27}}) to our notion of constraints. Garner's argument works, and provides nice universal properties, in the case of what we have called “universal constraint sets" (see Section REF ). The question is, if we apply his techniques to local constraints, such as those in Example REF  used to declare that one table is the product of two others, does his procedure still result in a relational fibration with all the nice universal properties enjoyed in the universal case? We conjecture that it will. One should also check whether the results obtained from that procedure agree with those from the so-called universal chase procedure (see {{cite:13ee21f4970c5024af66d3a7235af50d91dacbad}}). Indeed, they should provide equivalent results, since both claim to be universal in the same way.
